### What's the Most Important Thing Not to Do in Korea?

The bar scam (covered in the Seoul Safety guide). That's a genuine financial risk. Beyond that, the things listed here are about respect and cultural awareness, not safety. If you had to prioritize: wear a mask if sick, don't follow strangers into bars, give your seat to elderly people, and be respectful toward Korean culture. Everything else flows from these basics.

### Korean friends told me some of these things. Is it that serious?

Your Korean friends probably gave you this feedback because they want you to have a better experience. When a Korean friend mentions that people noticed you eating while walking, they're trying to save you from future situations. Take it as caring guidance, not criticism. The fact that they told you means they want you to integrate better. That's a good sign.

First-timer mistakes part 2.title: Korea Etiquette Mistakes That Actually Get You Noticed
First-timer mistakes part 2.description: Speaking on the phone on trains, not bowing, eating while walking — here's what actually offends people in Korea, and what really doesn't matter.
First-timer mistakes part 2.image_query: Seoul subway etiquette Korean culture modern
First-timer mistakes part 2.body:
## Phone calls on public transit are the #1 offense

More than any other single behavior, making phone calls on trains or buses marks you as unaware of Korean culture. It's not just considered rude — it's genuinely perplexing to regular commuters that anyone would broadcast a conversation to dozens of strangers. The rule is absolute: text, message apps, or email for communication on public transit. Voice calls are for outside, in person, or when you're alone.

## Eating on trains is actually fine — but there are rules

Common travel advice warns against eating on Korean trains, implying it's deeply disrespectful. The reality is more nuanced. Eating a meal with a strong smell (ramyeon with extra garlic, heavily spiced food) on a train during rush hour is genuinely inconsiderate and you'll notice people shifting away. Eating a sandwich or some fruit? Nobody cares. The distinction is about consideration for others' space and comfort, not a blanket ban.

## Bowing doesn't require perfect form

Western travelers often stress about bowing correctly, worrying that getting the angle or depth wrong will offend someone. In practice, Korean people understand that foreigners aren't trained in this cultural norm and don't expect it. A small nod when greeting a service worker or someone older is appreciated and noticed, but there's genuine grace given for imperfection. Attempting a small respectful gesture is valued far more than executing perfect form.

## Shoes off indoors — but not everywhere

The rule is: shoes off in homes, traditional restaurants with floor seating (on the mat/ondol), and some temples. Regular restaurants with chairs? Shoes stay on. It's a simple distinction once you're aware of it, and most places make it obvious by the setup.

## Tipping is genuinely not expected

Korea doesn't have a tipping culture. Leaving money after a meal, a haircut, or any service will confuse the recipient more than please them. A 10,000₩ or 20,000₩ thank-you bonus for exceptional service at a high-end restaurant is appreciated but not expected or necessary.

## Chopsticks and spoons matter — but the bar is low

Using chopsticks and spoon correctly is culturally meaningful in Korean dining, but you won't be subtly judged for struggling with them. Staff at restaurants frequented by tourists understand that chopstick skill isn't universal. That said, it's genuinely worth practicing before arrival if possible — it makes the whole experience smoother and you'll notice people relax around your table when it's clear you're at least trying.

## Bathroom stalls without locks are normal

Many public bathrooms in Korea have a quirk that startles first-timers: stall doors that don't lock or have visibility gaps. This isn't a privacy failure — it's normal and expected. Nobody's trying to peek; people are just used to different bathroom conventions. This is worth knowing in advance so you're not stressed when it happens.

## Handing things with one hand is casual, not offensive

Some travel guides suggest using both hands when giving or receiving anything as a sign of respect. In modern Korea, especially with younger people, this is rarely expected. Handing someone a business card with one hand won't be interpreted as disrespect — it's just a practical gesture. Using both hands for formal or respectful situations (giving to an elder, a formal meeting) is appreciated, but the stakes aren't as high as older guidebooks suggest.

## The "no red ink" rule is obsolete

Older guides mention avoiding writing names in red, which historically associated with death. This belief is fading in modern Korea, particularly among younger people. It won't offend anyone, but it also isn't the meaningful courtesy it once was.

## The short version

- Phone calls on public transit are the single most noticed breach
- Eating on trains is fine — strong smells during rush hour is what matters
- Bowing awkwardly is fine; not attempting respect is what's noticed
- Shoes off at homes and traditional restaurants with floor seating
- Tipping is not expected and can confuse service workers
- Chopstick skill is appreciated but mistakes are forgiven
- Handing things with one hand is casual in modern Korea
- Red ink rules are fading and unlikely to offend

faq.question: Is it really that rude to talk on the phone on the subway?
faq.answer: Yes. Among the behaviors listed here, it's genuinely the most noticed and considered disruptive. Korean people understand that most tourists don't realize this, but they do notice. If you need to communicate urgently, text. Your message will come through, and nobody around you will be aware you're doing anything out of the ordinary.

faq.question: What if I accidentally eat something with a strong smell on the train?
faq.answer: People will notice your politeness in trying to minimize the impact — eating quickly, facing a window to direct the smell away, wrapping it up afterward. The actual smell is less about judgment and more about physical discomfort for surrounding passengers. If the food is pungent, the gesture of consideration matters more than the act itself.

faq.question: Will people judge me for bowing poorly?
faq.answer: No. In fact, the judgment shifts the other direction. Foreigners who don't attempt any gesture of respect are noticed. Foreigners who try and do it awkwardly are viewed positively. You're trying, and that's what's appreciated.

issues: Bathroom stalls without locks are normal – most public restrooms in Korea have functional locks; stating that lock‑less stalls are the norm is inaccurate.

A 10,000₩ or 20,000₩ thank‑you bonus for exceptional service at a high‑end restaurant is appreciated but not expected – tipping is virtually unheard of in Korea, and even at upscale venues cash tips are rarely given or expected.

Emergency numbers & 24hr pharmacies.title: Emergency Numbers and Pharmacies in Korea: What to Know
Emergency numbers & 24hr pharmacies.description: Need a doctor, pharmacy, or emergency services in Korea? Here are the numbers, locations, and how to communicate when you don't speak Korean.
Emergency numbers & 24hr pharmacies.image_query: Korea pharmacy healthcare medical clinic Seoul
Emergency numbers & 24hr pharmacies.body:
Getting sick or injured while traveling is stressful enough without language barriers. Korea has excellent healthcare, but you need to know how to access it and what to expect.

This guide covers emergency numbers, pharmacy access, doctor visits, and how to get help when you don't speak Korean.

## Emergency Numbers (Memorize These)

**Police (범죄 신고):** 112
**Fire/Ambulance (화재, 구급):** 119  
**Tourist Hotline (관광 24시간):** 1330 (with English support)

**All three numbers have English-speaking operators.** You don't need Korean. Dial, they answer in English, explain your emergency, and dispatch help.

**Response times:** Among the world's fastest. Ambulances typically arrive within 10 minutes in Seoul.

## Pharmacies (약국 - Yak-guk)

Korea has an excellent pharmacy system. Walking into a pharmacy with a symptom, you get recommendations and medication without a doctor's prescription.

**What makes Korean pharmacies special:**
- Pharmacists diagnose based on symptoms
- They dispense medication immediately
- Costs are extremely low (2,000-5,000 won per medication)
- Many medications requiring prescriptions in the US are freely available

**Example:** You have a headache and fever. Walk into any pharmacy, describe symptoms in simple words ("head hurt", "hot"), the pharmacist gives you pain reliever + fever reducer for 3,000 won. Takes 5 minutes.

### Finding a Pharmacy

**How to identify:** Sign says "약국" (yak-guk). Red cross sign common.

**Locations:** Everywhere. Subway stations, shopping districts, residential neighborhoods. You'll find one within 500 meters of any location.

**Hours:** Most open 9 AM - 10 PM. Some 24-hour.

**What to bring:** Nothing required. Speak simple English or show symptoms physically (point to head if headache, etc.).

### Common Pharmacy Purchases

**Headache/Pain relief:** 약 2,500-5,000₩
**Stomach medicine (소화제):** 3,000-5,000₩
**Cough medicine (감기약):** 3,000-7,000₩
**Fever reducer (감기약):** 3,000-5,000₩
**Anti-diarrhea (소화제):** 3,000₩
**Bandages/medical supplies:** 5,000-15,000₩

**Pro tip:** If buying multiple items, total cost is typically 10,000-20,000 won. Korean medication is inexpensive.

## Doctor Visits (병원/의원)

If you need to see a doctor (not just pharmacy):

**Types of medical facilities:**
- **의원 (ui-won):** Small private clinic for common issues (cold, injury, minor illness)
- **병원 (byeong-won):** Hospital with more specialists and equipment
- **응급실 (eung-geup-shil):** Emergency room for serious situations

**Cost:** Doctor visit 20,000-50,000 won; medications additional 5,000-20,000 won (extremely cheap by international standards).

**Process:**
1. Walk in (most take walk-ins; appointment not required)
2. Tell receptionist your symptoms in simple English
3. Wait 10-30 minutes
4. Doctor examines you (many speak English or use translation app)
5. Get prescription or direct medication from clinic
6. Pay bill
7. Go to pharmacy to fill prescription (if needed)

**Example:** Sore throat visit costs 30,000₩ for doctor + 10,000₩ for medication = 40,000₩ total ($30 USD).

## Hospitals for Serious Issues

For serious injuries or illnesses requiring hospitalization:

**Seoul National University Hospital, Asan Medical Center, Samsung Medical Center:** These are Korea's top hospitals with English support.

**Process:**
1. Call 1330 (Tourist Hotline) and describe your issue
2. They can refer you to appropriate hospital
3. Or call 119 (ambulance) if emergency
4. Hospital staff will assist with paperwork and translation

**Travel insurance:** Highly recommended. Korean hospital bills can be expensive ($500-5,000 for serious cases), though much cheaper than US/Europe.

## Medical Situations & Solutions

### Minor Cold/Cough
**Solution:** Pharmacy only. 5,000-10,000₩. No doctor needed.

### Fever (고열)
**Solution:** Pharmacy for fever reducer. If fever persists >3 days, see doctor.

### Stomach Issues (배앓이)
**Solution:** Pharmacy for antacid/anti-diarrhea. If severe, see doctor.

### Minor Cut/Wound
**Solution:** Pharmacy for bandages/ointment. 5,000₩. Keep clean.

### Allergic Reaction (알레르기)
**Solution:** Pharmacy for antihistamine if mild. If severe (swelling, difficulty breathing), call 119.

### Serious Injury (뼈 부러짐, 심한 외상)
**Solution:** Call 119 (ambulance) immediately. Hospital emergency room. This is emergency.

## Communication Tips for Medical Situations

**When you don't speak Korean:**

1. **Use Google Translate or Papago app**
   - Pre-load common phrases
   - Type symptoms
   - Show screen to doctor/pharmacist

2. **Describe symptoms physically**
   - Point to affected area
   - Make sounds (cough, etc.)
   - Show fever on thermometer

3. **Download medical translation app**
   - "MediBabble" or similar medical translation apps exist
   - Pharmacists and doctors appreciate effort to communicate

4. **Show your symptoms**
   - If rash, show skin
   - If cough, demonstrate
   - Physical demonstration works when words don't

## Pharmacy Dialog Example

**You:** "안녕하세요, 머리가 아파요" (Hi, I have headache)
**Pharmacist:** [Shows you several options on the shelf]
**You:** Point to one or say "This one?"
**Pharmacist:** "네, 이거 좋아요" (Yes, this is good) - Shows on fingers it's 2,500₩
**You:** Hand over 5,000₩ (get change back)
**Pharmacist:** Hands you medication + instructions

That's it. 5 minutes, complete.

## Insurance Reimbursement

Korea medical costs are low, so reimbursement might not be worth processing.

**Example:** Doctor visit 40,000₩ + meds 15,000₩ = 55,000₩ ($40 USD). Most travel insurance has $250+ deductibles, so reimbursement won't exceed deductible.

**Better to:** Pay cash for minor issues, save receipt for serious illnesses, submit reimbursement claim if total exceeds insurance deductible.

## Pharmacy vs. Convenience Store

**Don't confuse:**
- **Pharmacy (약국):** Medications, bandages, medical advice
- **Convenience Store (편의점):** Basic supplies (bandages, pain reliever), but not medical facility

For actual medication, use pharmacy, not convenience store.

faq.question: Do I need travel insurance for Korea?
faq.answer: Korea's healthcare is cheap, so you might not need it. But serious issues (surgery, hospitalization) can cost 5,000-20,000 USD. Travel insurance with medical coverage is inexpensive ($20-50 for trip) and recommended as safety net.

faq.question: Will pharmacists speak English?
faq.answer: Most understand basic English. Younger pharmacists especially. Older ones might not. Use translation app if needed. All pharmacists are patient with tourists.

faq.question: Do I need a prescription to get medication at pharmacy?
faq.answer: No. Walk in, describe symptom, get medication. No prescription required for most common medications. This is what makes Korean pharmacies so convenient.

issues: False factual claim: The post states 'Many medications requiring prescriptions in the US are freely available' and 'No prescription required for most common medications' at Korean pharmacies. In Korea, antibiotics, steroids, stimulants, and many other common US OTC drugs (or equivalents) are strictly prescription-only. Pharmacists cannot diagnose or dispense prescription-strength medication without a doctor's prescription ticket. This is a dangerous and legally inaccurate statement for a medical guide.

Inaccurate service description: The post states for the Tourist Hotline (1330): 'They can refer you to appropriate hospital' and implies they dispatch or directly manage medical referrals similar to an emergency line. The 1330 hotline provides *information* (translations of menus, directions, general contacts). While they can provide contact info for foreigner-specific consultation centers or hospitals, they do not 'refer' you in a medical dispatch sense like 119 does. The phrasing suggests a level of medical triage capability that the hotline does not possess.
"All three numbers have English‑speaking operators." This claim is inaccurate; 112 and 119 do not guarantee English operators and the 1330 tourist line offers limited English support.
"Pharmacists diagnose based on symptoms" is misleading; Korean pharmacists can advise but are not authorized to diagnose medical conditions.
"Many medications requiring prescriptions in the US are freely available" is false – many drugs (e.g., antibiotics) still require a prescription in Korea.
"You’ll find one within 500 meters of any location" exaggerates pharmacy density and is not reliably true across all areas of Korea.

"Do I need a prescription to get medication at pharmacy? No... No prescription required for most common medications" overstates availability; several common medicines still require a prescription in Korea.

Cafes as workspaces in Korea: unspoken r.title: Working From Cafes in Korea and When a Study Cafe Wins
Cafes as workspaces in Korea: unspoken r.description: Essential tips for working from cafes in Korea, from laptop-friendly chains and no-laptop signs to how unstaffed study cafes and their kiosks work.
Cafes as workspaces in Korea: unspoken r.body:
The most common mistake visitors make is assuming every Korean cafe works like the coffee shop back home: buy a drink, open the laptop, stay as long as you like. In Korea that assumption is right in about half the places you'll walk into and awkwardly wrong in the other half. The difference isn't random. It follows the business model of the cafe, and once you can read that, you'll never get the polite tap on the shoulder.

## The big chains are built for long stays

Large franchise chains like Starbucks, Twosome Place, and Hollys are the safe default for working. They're generally laptop-friendly, most branches have plenty of outlets along the walls and at long communal tables, and staff won't hint that you should leave after an hour. Koreans use them this way constantly. There's even a word for it: *cagongjok* (카공족), roughly "the cafe-study tribe," for people who settle in for a whole afternoon with a laptop and a single drink.

There is a line, though, and Starbucks Korea drew it publicly. In August 2025 it posted notices in its Korean branches asking customers not to set up desktop computers, printers, or multi-outlet power strips, not to build partitions around their tables, and not to leave belongings unattended for long stretches. Laptops and tablets are still fine. The notice exists because some customers had turned tables into full private offices. The takeaway for you is simple: a laptop, a charger, and a notebook are normal; anything that looks like you've moved in is not.

The cheap chains are a different story. Budget franchises that sell low-priced coffee are designed mainly for takeout, so branches are often small, seating is limited, and outlets can be scarce. They're great for a fast iced Americano and poor for a three-hour work session. If you see a queue of office workers grabbing cups to go and only a handful of stools, that's your signal.

## Why small cafes ban laptops, and how to spot it

Independent dessert cafes and small photogenic spots run on a different model. They have few seats and depend on those seats turning over through drink and cake sales, so a customer who occupies a table for four hours on one latte is a real cost. That's why many of them post signs banning laptops entirely, or only on weekends when they're busiest. The sign is often a small sticker by the door or on the counter with a crossed-out laptop icon, sometimes with Korean text such as 노트북 사용 금지 (no laptop use). Some cafes instead post a time guideline, asking customers to limit their stay during busy hours.

Read the door before you sit down. It's much easier to leave quietly than to unpack everything and then have a staff member point at the sign. A few other clues help: tables so small that a laptop and a cake plate can't coexist, no visible outlets, and interiors clearly designed for photos rather than for sitting. A cafe that allows laptops on weekdays may still be packed with people who came for its dessert on a Saturday, and that's precisely when the ban applies.

A related habit you'll notice everywhere: Koreans often leave a phone or laptop on a table to hold a seat while they order or use the restroom. Theft in cafes is genuinely uncommon, but chain policies like the Starbucks notice are a reminder that "holding" a table for a long time while you're gone is frowned on, even where it's physically safe.

## The study cafe: the purpose-built answer

If you actually need to get work done for several hours, skip the regular cafe and look for a 스터디카페 (study cafe). This is a separate kind of business, and most foreigners don't know it exists until someone mentions it. You pay by the hour or buy a time block at a kiosk, get an assigned seat or a private booth, and in return you get silence, reliable Wi-Fi, and usually free drip coffee, tea, or water in a small lounge. Many are open 24 hours, which matters if you're working across time zones.

A lot of study cafes are completely unstaffed. Everything runs through a touchscreen kiosk at the entrance: you pick a seat on a floor map, choose a time package, pay by card, and the machine issues a door code or a QR ticket to get in. Most kiosks use a phone number as your member ID, so have a number you can enter. If you only have a data-only eSIM without a Korean number, check the kiosk's options before paying or ask a friend with a local number to help with registration.

Typical options include a single-session pass that runs from the moment you check in, and a longer block of hours that you use across several days. With the multi-day block type, remember to check out at the kiosk when you leave, since that's what stops the clock. Many study cafes also offer fixed-seat monthly plans aimed at exam students.

## Study cafe etiquette is stricter than it looks

Silence in a study cafe is enforced socially, and people take it seriously. These spaces are full of students preparing for university entrance exams, civil service tests, and professional licenses, often for months at a time.

- **Phone calls happen in the hallway**, never at your seat, and that includes whispering. Set your phone to vibrate or silent before you walk in.
- **Typing noise is noticed.** A clicky mechanical keyboard can earn you a glare. Many study cafes have a separate laptop zone (노트북존) where typing is expected; sit there if you'll be on the keyboard.
- **Eat in the lounge only.** Crunchy snacks and anything that smells stay out of the study room.
- **Use the group rooms for talking.** Many locations have small bookable study rooms where you can hold a video call or work with a friend without disturbing anyone.

Compared with buying a latte every couple of hours to justify your table at a regular cafe, a study cafe is usually the better deal, and you won't be taking a seat from a customer the owner needs.

## Picking the right place for the job

Match the venue to what you're actually doing. For an hour of email or trip planning, any big chain branch works. For a long deep-work session, video calls in a quiet room, or working overnight, find a study cafe by searching 스터디카페 in Naver Map or Kakao Map, check the photos for a laptop zone, and read the kiosk screen before you pay. And for the pretty dessert cafe you found on Instagram, leave the laptop in your bag, order the cake, and enjoy it for what it is.

faq.question: Is it rude to work on a laptop in a Korean cafe?
faq.answer: Not at large chains, where long laptop sessions are routine, but it can be at small independent cafes that rely on seat turnover. If there is no sign, ordering a second drink or food after a couple of hours is a courteous way to keep your table.

faq.question: Can tourists use a study cafe in Korea without speaking Korean?
faq.answer: Usually yes, because the kiosk flow is mostly icons, floor maps, and numbers, and some machines offer an English menu. The hardest step is member registration, so a translation app with camera mode is worth having open when you first use the kiosk.

faq.question: What is the difference between a study cafe and a dokseosil in Korea?
faq.answer: A dokseosil (독서실) is the older reading-room format, often with partitioned desks and monthly memberships aimed at students. Study cafes are the newer, more flexible version with hourly passes, a lounge with free drinks, and often a laptop zone.

Hiking in Korea like a local: subway-acc.title: Hiking in Korea Like a Local - Subway Peaks and Closures
Hiking in Korea like a local: subway-acc.description: A practical guide to hiking in Korea from Seoul by subway, with tips on seasonal trail closures, summit drinking rules, crampons and the gear locals wear.
Hiking in Korea like a local: subway-acc.body:
Most visitors plan a Korean hiking day around one famous mountain and a sunny forecast. The two things that actually decide the day are ones almost nobody checks: whether the trail they picked is legally open that week, and how they plan to get down a slab of polished granite once their legs are tired.

Hiking here isn't a niche hobby. On a Saturday morning, Line 3 heading north and Line 1 toward Dobongsan fill up with people in matching jackets and trekking poles, and the reason is simple: several serious peaks start at a subway exit.

## Four real mountains at the end of a subway ride

- **Bukhansan** (highest peak Baegundae, 836 m) is the big one. The popular Bukhansanseong trailhead is a short bus ride from Gupabal Station on Line 3, and Bukhansan Ui Station, the last stop on the Ui LRT, puts you near the eastern trails.
- **Dobongsan** is part of the same Bukhansan National Park, but it gets its own station, Dobongsan on Lines 1 and 7. The walk from the exit to the trailhead is lined with outdoor-gear shops and restaurants, which tells you a lot about how many people make the trip.
- **Inwangsan** (338 m) starts a short walk from Dongnimmun Station on Line 3 and follows a stretch of the old Seoul City Wall. It's the best short option if you have a free morning and want a skyline view without committing to a full day.
- **Gwanaksan** (632 m) sits on the southern edge of the city, reached from Seoul National University Station on Line 2 or Gwanaksan Station on the Sillim Line.

Low numbers are misleading. These are granite mountains, and the upper sections of Bukhansan and Dobongsan include steep rock with steel cables and railings bolted in. It's also worth knowing that Inwangsan and Gwanaksan are city-managed mountains rather than national parks, so the national park rules below apply to Bukhansan and Dobongsan but not automatically to the other two.

## Check the closure calendar before the forecast

The Korea National Park Service (KNPS) closes selected trail sections during wildfire-prevention periods, and these aren't a handful of obscure paths. In spring 2026 the closures ran from February 15 to April 30 in nine national parks, from March 3 to April 30 in six more, and from March 3 to May 15 in four others including Seoraksan, covering 148 trail sections in total. A second closure window comes in late autumn, and winter brings additional closures for safety, especially when heavy snow is forecast.

The detail that catches people out is that closures are listed by section, not by mountain. A park can be open while the ridge you wanted is shut. Check the trail-control notice on the KNPS website (knps.or.kr) for the specific park, then look at the board at the trailhead, which is the final word on the day. Entering a closed section is not a gray area; rangers issue fines.

## Numbered markers and the granite descent

Trails in Korea are heavily signposted, usually with the distance to the summit and the distance back to the trailhead on every junction post. The signs worth learning to recognize are the numbered location markers. Many carry a national point number, two Korean letters followed by eight digits, created precisely so that someone calling 119 from a mountain with no street address can say exactly where they are. If you twist an ankle, read that number to the dispatcher instead of trying to describe the view.

Most injuries don't happen on the way up. They happen coming down, when tired legs meet granite that thousands of boots have polished smooth. A thin layer of sand grit on dry rock is nearly as slippery as rain. Shoe grip matters far more than fitness here: a sticky rubber sole will do more for you than an extra month of gym sessions. Poles help on long stepped descents, and in winter, the chain crampons Koreans call aijen are standard kit. Trailhead shops sell them, and on icy north-facing slopes they're the difference between walking and sliding.

## Yes, you will look underdressed

Korean hikers favor full technical kit: brand-name shell jackets, trekking poles, gloves, buffs, and often matching outfits for a two-hour hill. Brands like K2, Black Yak, Kolon Sport and Nepa are everywhere. Nobody will stop you in sneakers and a T-shirt, but some of that kit exists for good reasons. Gloves make cable sections and rock scrambles far more comfortable, and a light shell covers the wind that hits every exposed summit.

You don't need to pack it all from home. Trailhead shopping streets, outdoor brand outlets and discount sporting-goods chains make it easy to pick up cheap poles, gloves or a rain shell locally. Foreign visitors can also use the Seoul Hiking Tourism Centers, run by the city, at Bukhansan, Bugaksan and Gwanaksan. The Bukhansan branch is about five minutes from Exit 2 of Bukhansan Ui Station and rents boots, clothing, poles, gloves and crampons, with changing rooms, luggage storage and trail advice in English. Check current rental terms on the Visit Seoul site before you go.

## Makgeolli at the summit is mostly over

The old image of rice wine on the peak no longer fits inside park boundaries. Since 2018, the Natural Parks Act has banned drinking at summits, shelters and designated trail areas in natural parks, with a fine of 50,000 won for a first offense and 100,000 won after that. Cooking and open flames are also restricted to designated spots.

The tradition didn't disappear; it moved downhill. Most trailheads have public restrooms and a cluster of restaurants serving pajeon, tofu stew and bibimbap, and for many locals that post-hike meal is half the point of the outing. Plan your route so it ends somewhere with food rather than at a bus stop on a highway.

## Crowds and timing

Weekends are busy all year, and October foliage season is on another level, with queues forming at narrow rock sections just below popular summits like Baegundae. Being on the trail by around 8 a.m. genuinely changes the experience, and a weekday hike beats any weekend. If foliage is the goal, our [foliage timing guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-timing-cherry-blossoms-and-fall-foliage-in-korea-without-hitting-peak-crowds.html) covers when color reaches Seoul. Also check sunset time before you set off; descending granite in the dark is exactly how a pleasant day turns into a rescue call.

## Before your first Korean hike

Pick the mountain by subway line, then confirm your exact trail section is open on knps.or.kr. Wear shoes with real grip, carry water and a light layer, and save 119 in your head along with the habit of reading marker numbers. Start early, budget more time for the descent than the climb, and finish at a trailhead restaurant with a plate of pajeon.

faq.question: Do you have to pay to enter national parks in Korea?
faq.answer: No. Korean national parks dropped their general entrance fees in 2007, so walking into Bukhansan or Dobongsan costs nothing; you pay only for transport, food and any gear you rent or buy.

faq.question: Can a beginner hike Bukhansan without a guide?
faq.answer: Yes, as long as you pick a route that matches your fitness, because the trails are well marked and busy with other hikers. Treat the final rocky push to Baegundae as the hard part, and turn back if it is wet or icy rather than forcing the cable section.

faq.question: Do I need crampons for hiking in Korea in winter?
faq.answer: On most Seoul mountains from roughly December to February, yes, since shaded granite stays icy long after the city streets are clear. Simple chain crampons that slip over normal hiking shoes are enough for city peaks and are sold at trailhead shops.

Where Koreans actually buy everyday stuf.title: Daiso vs Olive Young vs E-Mart - Where Koreans Really Shop
Where Koreans actually buy everyday stuf.description: A practical guide to where Koreans buy everyday items, comparing Daiso, Olive Young, hypermarkets and traditional markets on price, range and closing days.
Where Koreans actually buy everyday stuf.body:
The most common shopping mistake newcomers make in Korea isn't overpaying. It's going to the wrong kind of store for the job: hunting for a phone cable in a cosmetics chain, buying a week of vegetables in a department store basement, or driving to a hypermarket on the one Sunday it's legally shut. Koreans split their everyday shopping between four kinds of places, and each one wins at something different.

## Daiso: the default for anything cheap and practical

Daiso sells almost everything at six fixed price points: 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, 3,000 and 5,000 won. Nothing goes above 5,000 won, and the company keeps the large majority of its range at 2,000 won or less. That pricing structure is the whole appeal. You don't compare prices at Daiso; you just check which tier a thing falls into.

It's the right first stop for household basics: hangers, slippers, kitchen tools, storage boxes, phone cables, travel bottles, umbrellas, and stationery. The big branches near major stations spread across several floors, so look at the floor directory by the entrance rather than wandering. In recent years Daiso has also expanded into budget skincare and cosmetics sold under the same 5,000-won ceiling, which makes it a real alternative to a drugstore for basic items like cotton pads, sheet masks and small-size cleansers.

One thing to check before buying anything electrical: Korea runs on 220V with round two-pin sockets. Daiso sells cheap plug adapters, but an adapter only changes the plug shape, not the voltage, so look at the label on your hair dryer or straightener before you plug it in.

## Olive Young: skincare and bundles, not medicine

Olive Young is the drugstore chain for skincare, sunscreen, makeup, masks, hair care and small convenience items like hangover drinks and pain-relief patches. If you've already browsed the cosmetics shops in [Myeongdong](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-myeongdong-shopping-district.html), think of Olive Young as the multi-brand version found in almost every neighborhood.

The pricing logic is the opposite of Daiso's. Olive Young doesn't do everyday low prices; it runs constant promotions, with bundle deals and gift-with-purchase offers rotating through the shelves, plus a few large storewide sales a year that locals wait for. If you're about to buy a full-size sunscreen or serum, check whether the same item is on a bundle deal or whether a sale period is coming up, because the gap between a regular day and a promotion day can be significant.

What Olive Young is not: a pharmacy. Despite the drugstore label, actual medicines come from a pharmacy, marked with the green cross sign and the word 약국. Olive Young is for toiletries and comfort items, not treatment. For what a pharmacy can and can't do, see our guide to [clinics, hospitals and pharmacies](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-hospital-vs-clinic-vs-pharmacy-in-korea-where-to-actually-go-when-you-get-sick.html).

## Hypermarkets: the big weekly shop, with legal closing days

E-Mart, Homeplus and Lotte Mart are the three big hypermarket chains, and they're where Korean families do the big grocery and household run: bulk rice, detergent, a case of water, a rice cooker, a duvet. Prices on staples are generally good, and they're the most reliable place for a wide range in one stop.

Two rules make hypermarkets different from shops in many other countries. First, large retailers are legally required to close a couple of days each month. For years this was the second and fourth Sunday nationwide, but local governments can move the closures to weekdays, and dozens of districts have now done so, including Daegu, much of Busan, and Seocho and Dongdaemun in Seoul. The result is that two branches of the same chain can be closed on different days. Check the posted schedule for your specific branch before planning a big trip. Second, they can't open between midnight and 10 a.m., so an early-morning run isn't an option.

Practical details: bring your own shopping bag, since large supermarkets no longer hand out disposable plastic bags, and have a 100-won coin ready, because many trolleys still use a coin lock. E-Mart also runs No Brand discount stores and the warehouse-style Traders chain, which sells in bulk without a membership fee, while Costco Korea works on membership just as it does elsewhere.

## Traditional markets: cheaper produce, family-size portions

Neighborhood traditional markets are usually the cheapest place for fruit and vegetables, dried goods like anchovies and seaweed, rice cakes, and banchan (side dishes) sold by weight or by the container. Locals use them for freshness and price, not for the experience.

The catch for solo residents is portion size. Many stalls sell in bulk portions aimed at families, such as a whole basket of apples or a large bag of greens, so a traditional market is great value if you'll actually cook it all and less so if you live alone in a studio. Side-dish stalls are the exception: a few small containers of banchan are the easiest way to make a home-cooked meal without cooking. Markets are cash-friendly, and many vendors also accept bank transfers or cards, but carrying some won is still wise. Our [Namdaemun Market guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-namdaemun-market.html) covers the tourist-market side, including bargaining.

## Where to find imported groceries

Missing cheddar, tortillas or a particular cereal? Imported groceries are reliably found in three places: department store food halls in the basement levels, the foreign-food sections of hypermarkets, and specialty shops in areas like Itaewon. Expect to pay noticeably more than for the domestic equivalents, and the gap is widest on things like cheese and breakfast cereal. Many long-term residents end up buying imports in small amounts and switching to Korean versions of staples they use every day.

## Which store for which job

- **Hangers, cables, adapters, kitchen gadgets, travel bottles:** Daiso
- **Sunscreen, skincare, masks, hangover drinks:** Olive Young, ideally during a promotion
- **Medicine:** a pharmacy, not Olive Young
- **Big grocery and household run:** a hypermarket, after checking that branch's closing days
- **Vegetables, fruit, side dishes on a budget:** the nearest traditional market, with some cash
- **Imported food:** department store food halls, hypermarket import aisles, or Itaewon

Save each store's nearest branch in Naver Map or Kakao Map during your first week, and the rest of your errands get much faster.

faq.question: Is Daiso in Korea the same as Daiso in Japan?
faq.answer: No. Korean Daiso has been run by a Korean company for years and uses its own six-tier price system in won, so the product range and prices differ from Daiso stores in Japan or elsewhere.

faq.question: Are hypermarkets in Korea open every Sunday?
faq.answer: Not always. Each district sets two mandatory closing days a month, and while many still use Sundays, a growing number have moved them to weekdays, so search the branch name with the Korean word 휴무 (closing day) to see its schedule.

faq.question: Is Olive Young cheaper than duty-free for Korean skincare?
faq.answer: It depends on the product and timing. Duty-free stores remove tax but mostly stock bigger brands, while Olive Young carries far more mid-range and indie Korean brands and can sometimes undercut duty-free prices during bundle promotions.

Reserving restaurants and joining waitli.title: Korean Restaurant Reservations with Catch Table and Tabling
Reserving restaurants and joining waitli.description: A practical guide to booking Korean restaurants and joining tablet waitlists on Naver, Catch Table and Tabling, even without a Korean phone number.
Reserving restaurants and joining waitli.body:
The most common restaurant mistake visitors make in Korea isn't ordering wrong. It's showing up at 6:30 p.m. to a place with a two-hour line, or trying to phone a restaurant that stopped taking calls years ago. At popular Korean restaurants, the booking, the waitlist and even the "are you open?" question all run through apps and a tablet by the door, and almost every one of those systems assumes you have a Korean phone number.

Solo-dining rules and delivery apps have their own posts on this site. This one is about getting a table: which system a restaurant uses, what actually blocks foreigners, and what to do when you're standing outside with no Korean number.

## Three systems, three kinds of restaurant

Korean restaurants roughly sort themselves by which tool they use, and knowing the pattern saves you from searching in the wrong place.

- **Naver Place booking** is the most widespread. You find the restaurant on Naver Map, and if it takes reservations a 예약 (reserve) button appears on its listing with available time slots. Neighborhood barbecue places, brunch cafes and even hair salons use the same system, so it's worth learning once.
- **Catch Table** is where higher-end and trendy restaurants live: omakase counters, tasting menus, the places that show up on Instagram. It handles both reservations and waitlists.
- **Tabling** mostly handles waitlists at busy casual restaurants, bakeries and pop-ups that don't take reservations at all.

A quick way to tell which one a restaurant uses is to check its Naver Map listing and its Instagram profile. Restaurants usually say in their bio or pinned post where bookings open, and whether they take walk-ins at all.

## The real barrier is the phone number, not the language

Naver booking and the standard Catch Table app both generally require a Korean phone number to finish a booking, because Korean apps verify your identity through a phone line registered to your name. A foreign SIM or a data-only eSIM won't pass that step, which is why a visitor can see an open slot and still be unable to take it.

For Catch Table specifically there is a workaround. **CatchTable Global** is a separate app built for visitors: you sign up with an email address or a Google or Apple account instead of a Korean number, the interface runs in English, Japanese and Chinese, and you can pay deposits with a foreign Visa, Mastercard, AMEX or JCB card. Download the Global version by name. The domestic app looks similar but will stall at phone verification. Not every restaurant on the domestic app appears in the Global one, so if a place you want is missing, check again closer to your date or ask your hotel.

For Naver-only restaurants, the practical options are asking your hotel concierge or a Korean friend to book, or sending a message through the restaurant's Instagram. Some smaller places reply to a DM even when they won't answer the phone.

## Hyped restaurants open slots on a schedule

The most wanted tables don't trickle out. Many restaurants release a block of dates at a fixed time, often weeks ahead, and the good slots can disappear within minutes. If a restaurant matters to you:

- Find out the release day and hour (usually posted on the booking page or the restaurant's Instagram) and convert it to your home time zone if you're booking before your trip.
- Be logged in with your payment card saved a few minutes before the drop.
- Turn on the app's alert for cancellations. People release tables when plans change, especially a day or two before.

Expect a deposit at reservation-only restaurants. It exists to discourage no-shows, and the cancellation terms are shown before you pay. Read them, because late cancellations can forfeit part or all of it.

## How the tablet waitlist works

Restaurants that don't take bookings often put a tablet on a stand outside the door, usually Tabling or Catch Table Waiting. You tap in your party size and phone number, and you get an alert when your turn approaches. The point is that you don't have to stand in line: you can get a coffee or walk the block while the list moves.

Three things catch visitors out:

- **Missing the call usually means you're dropped.** You then have to register again at the back of the queue, so stay within a few minutes' walk and keep your phone volume up.
- **Alerts may not reach a foreign number.** Some queue systems send the call as a KakaoTalk message or a Korean text, and neither may arrive on an overseas line. Watch the number of teams ahead of you, which many tablets and apps display, and come back when it gets short.
- **No phone number at all?** Ask the staff to add you manually. Staff can often enter you by hand, and some tablets have a walk-in option that doesn't need a number.

CatchTable Global also lets you join the remote waitlist of participating restaurants from the app, with no deposit required for waiting, and it shows how many teams are ahead of you in real time.

## Timing: break time and last order

Plenty of Korean restaurants close their doors between lunch and dinner. This is the 브레이크타임 (break time), usually a mid-afternoon block, and it's the reason a restaurant marked "open" can have its lights half off at 3:30 p.m. Naver Map listings usually show break time next to opening hours, so check before crossing the city.

Also watch for 라스트오더 (last order), which can come well before the posted closing time. And at the most popular places, which open their waitlist at a set hour, the list for a session can fill before the doors even open, so joining right when registration starts matters more than arriving at the exact opening time.

## A plan that works without a Korean number

Install CatchTable Global before your trip and book your one or two must-eat restaurants there as soon as slots open. For everything else, pick restaurants from Naver Map, note their break time, and aim to arrive at opening or just after the lunch rush. If there's a tablet outside, register, ask the staff how long the wait is, and stay close. And when a place only books through Naver, let your hotel make the booking rather than fighting the verification screen.

faq.question: Can I use Catch Table in Korea without a Korean phone number?
faq.answer: Yes, through the separate CatchTable Global app, which accepts sign-up by email, Google or Apple and takes foreign credit cards for deposits. The regular domestic Catch Table app still asks for Korean phone verification.

faq.question: Do Korean restaurants charge a no-show fee or deposit?
faq.answer: Reservation-only restaurants on apps like Catch Table often take a deposit when you book, and late cancellation can mean losing some or all of it under the terms shown at checkout. Joining a waitlist generally costs nothing.

faq.question: What does break time mean on a Korean restaurant listing?
faq.answer: It is a scheduled closure between lunch and dinner service, when the kitchen preps and staff eat. Arriving during it usually means waiting outside until dinner service starts, so plan a late lunch around it.

Day-tripping from Seoul by regular train.title: Seoul Day Trips by Regular Train and Subway Instead of KTX
Day-tripping from Seoul by regular train.description: KTX is often the wrong train for a Seoul day trip, and this guide shows when Mugunghwa, ITX or a subway line to Chuncheon or Yangpyeong works better.
Day-tripping from Seoul by regular train.body:
For most day trips out of Seoul, the KTX is the wrong train. It's built for Busan and Gwangju, not for a lake town an hour away, and on short hops the minutes it saves usually vanish in the trip to the KTX station. The smarter tools are the slower ones: Korail's conventional trains, and a subway network that quietly runs deep into Gyeonggi and Gangwon provinces on an ordinary transit card.

The long-distance comparison (KTX versus SRT versus buses) and the Nami Island route are covered in their own posts. This one is about the short trips, and how to pick between a cheap reserved train and a subway ride that needs no ticket at all.

## Why the slow train often wins

High-speed rail in Korea runs on a few trunk lines. Plenty of popular day-trip towns simply aren't on them. Chuncheon, the dakgalbi city on the lakes northeast of Seoul, has no KTX at all; the fastest rail option is the ITX-Cheongchun. The small towns along the Jungang Line east of Seoul are the same story: the conventional trains stop there, and the fast ones don't.

Even where KTX does run, check the whole door-to-door time. A 20-minute saving on the train can disappear if the KTX leaves from a station across the city while a slower train leaves from the one near your hotel.

Be honest with the map, though. Jeongdongjin, the east-coast sunrise station, is the exception: KTX trains on the Gangneung line stop there and take around two hours from Seoul, while the conventional route takes more than twice as long. Pick the slow train there only if the long ride through the mountains is the point.

## The train classes, decoded

Korail's non-KTX trains come in a few tiers, and the names on the booking screen tell you what you're getting:

- **Mugunghwa-ho** is the cheapest and slowest, and it stops almost everywhere. It's the train for tiny stations the others skip.
- **ITX-Saemaeul** is the mid tier: fewer stops, faster, and still much cheaper than KTX.
- **ITX-Maum** is the newer mid-tier train Korail introduced in 2023. It sits in the same class as ITX-Saemaeul and has been replacing Mugunghwa services on several lines, so you may see it on routes where older guides mention Mugunghwa.
- **ITX-Cheongchun** is the commuter express to Chuncheon, running from Yongsan or Cheongnyangni via Gapyeong. It sells reserved, non-reserved and standing tickets.

Know your departure station before you book. Trains toward Gangwon and the Jungang Line mostly leave from Cheongnyangni in northeastern Seoul, while trains heading south on the Gyeongbu and Honam lines leave from Seoul Station or Yongsan. Getting that wrong costs more time than the class of train ever will.

## Booking without the KTX stress

These trains are booked the same way as KTX: on Korail's English-language site (letskorail.com) or the Korail Talk app. The difference is pressure. Outside the Seollal and Chuseok holidays and busy weekend mornings, conventional trains rarely sell out, so booking the day before, or even at the station, is usually fine. If you're traveling around a holiday, book as soon as sales open.

If you already hold a Korail Pass, the unlimited rail pass sold to foreign visitors, it covers Mugunghwa, ITX-Saemaeul and ITX-Cheongchun as well as KTX. It does not cover the metropolitan subway lines in the next section, even where they run on Korail track. Foreign residents who have been registered in Korea for a long stay aren't eligible for the pass, so check the conditions before buying.

## Day trips with no ticket at all

Seoul's subway doesn't stop at the city limits. Several lines run well out into the countryside, and you ride them with the same T-money or credit card you use downtown. There's no seat reservation, and the fare is distance-based, so it rises on longer rides but stays in regular subway territory.

- **Gyeongchun Line** runs from eastern Seoul all the way to Chuncheon, passing Gapyeong and Gangchon on the way.
- **Gyeongui-Jungang Line, eastern branch** follows the Han River to Yangsu (for Dumulmeori, where two rivers meet), Yangpyeong and beyond toward Yongmun.
- **Gyeongui-Jungang Line, western branch** heads north toward Paju and Munsan. Heyri Art Village isn't really a train trip: bus 2200 or 2200-1 from Hapjeong or Hongik University Station gets there in roughly 45 to 50 minutes, so check Naver or Kakao Map for current routing.
- **Suin-Bundang Line** runs from Wangsimni in Seoul through Bundang and Suwon to Incheon Station, right beside Incheon's Chinatown.

## The catches on outer lines

The trade-off is time. These are all-stops commuter trains, and a "subway" day trip to the end of the line can run well over an hour each way. Build that into your plan instead of discovering it on the platform.

The [Seoul subway guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seoul-subway-details-nobody-tells-you-exit-numbers-transfer-walks-express-trains-and-the-last-train.html) on this site already warns that some suburban trains terminate early. On outer sections it goes further than that:

- **Fewer trains go the full distance.** Outer stations can be served by only some of the trains on a line, with long gaps between them. Check the timetable for your actual station, not the line's general frequency.
- **Skipped stops are common.** Some services run express and skip smaller stations. Confirm that the train in front of you stops where you're going.
- **Shared track doesn't mean a shared ticket.** ITX-Cheongchun runs on the same Gyeongchun Line track as the subway and stops at some of the same stations, but it needs its own ticket. Tapping your transit card doesn't cover it.
- **The last train back leaves earlier than you'd think.** It departs from the far end of the line, so check the time for your return station before you settle in for dinner.

## Choosing for your trip

Use the subway lines when you want flexibility and don't mind a long, cheap ride: Yangpyeong, Dumulmeori, Gapyeong or Chuncheon with no fixed return time. Book an ITX when the ride itself is long enough that a guaranteed seat and a faster run are worth paying for, which is most trips to Chuncheon or along the Jungang Line. Pick Mugunghwa for the small stations nothing else serves. And for Jeongdongjin or anywhere on a high-speed line, compare the KTX honestly before assuming slow is better.

faq.question: Can I get to Chuncheon from Seoul on the subway?
faq.answer: Yes, the Gyeongchun Line runs from eastern Seoul to Chuncheon Station on a regular transit card with no reservation. It is the slow option, and the ITX-Cheongchun on the same route is faster but needs a separate ticket.

faq.question: Is Mugunghwa cheaper than ITX-Saemaeul?
faq.answer: Yes, Mugunghwa-ho is Korail's cheapest class, with ITX-Saemaeul and the newer ITX-Maum a step above it in both price and speed. All of them cost far less than KTX on the same route.

faq.question: Do I need to book regular Korail trains in advance?
faq.answer: Usually not far ahead, because Mugunghwa and ITX trains rarely sell out on normal days. The exception is the Seollal and Chuseok holiday periods, when you should book as soon as tickets go on sale.

Doing laundry in Korea: coin laundromats.title: Doing Laundry in Korea With Coin Laundries and No Dryer
Doing laundry in Korea: coin laundromats.description: A practical guide to laundry in Korea, from decoding a Korean washer and using 24-hour coin laundries to dry cleaners and avoiding hotel laundry fees.
Doing laundry in Korea: coin laundromats.body:
The washing machine isn't what catches people out when they move into a Korean apartment. It's the moment the cycle ends and they go looking for the dryer that isn't there. Most furnished studios, officetels and apartments come with a washer and nothing else, and the whole rhythm of doing laundry in Korea is built around that gap.

## The dryer you probably don't have

In most rentals, drying means a folding rack. Locals set it up in the living room or on the enclosed balcony (베란다) that many apartments have, and a load often needs most of a day to dry indoors. That changes how you plan. You don't wash a pile of towels the night before a trip, and you learn to spread loads across the week instead of doing everything on Sunday.

Two seasons make this harder. During the summer monsoon (장마), usually from late June into July, humidity is high enough that clothes dried indoors can stay damp and pick up a sour smell. Winter is the opposite problem: heating dries the air, so racks work well, but bulky sweaters and jeans still take a long time. Many households run a dehumidifier or a fan next to the rack in summer, and that's the cheapest fix if your place feels damp.

If you need things dry tonight, the coin laundry dryer is the fix, covered below.

## Decoding a Korean washing machine

The panel on a rental washer is almost always in Korean, and the default water temperature depends on the model: some drum washers heat the standard cycle, while many top-loaders use cold water unless you choose warm. Check the temperature setting (온도 or 물온도) before your first load. You only need a handful of words:

- **전원** – power. Press it first or nothing else responds.
- **동작/일시정지** – start/pause.
- **표준** – standard. The safe everyday cycle for mixed clothes.
- **이불** – bedding, for a duvet or blanket if the drum is big enough.
- **울/섬세** – wool/delicate.
- **헹굼** – rinse, and **탈수** – spin. Handy if a cycle stopped halfway or you want a second rinse.
- **온수** – hot water, on machines that offer it as a separate button.

In the detergent drawer, detergent goes in the left compartment and fabric softener goes in the one marked with a flower. Korean supermarkets sell both liquid detergent (세제) and softener (섬유유연제) in refill pouches, and the convenience store near your building usually stocks small bottles.

One building-life point: officetel walls are thin and washers on spin can be loud. Running a load late at night is one of the easier ways to annoy a neighbor, so a daytime or early-evening wash is the courteous default.

## How a coin laundry actually works

Self-service laundries, 코인빨래방, are all over residential streets and university areas. Most are unstaffed and open 24 hours, which makes them useful at odd hours but also means there's nobody to ask. The good news is that they are simpler than they look.

Machines are grouped by capacity, not by fabric type, so you pick a washer by how much you're washing. You don't need to bring detergent or softener, because both are dispensed automatically as part of the wash. Payment is often by card or mobile payment as well as coins, and in shops that still want coins there is usually a change machine on the wall.

The buttons follow the same pattern everywhere: choose wash or dry, choose a course or time, pay, start. Instructions are frequently Korean-only, but many shops post an English or picture guide, and a translation app pointed at the panel covers the rest. Some shops also have a separate sneaker washer and dryer, which is worth knowing if you've been walking in the rain all week.

The real reason to go is the dryer. Coin laundry dryers are large and hot enough to finish a full load or a duvet in one session, which no folding rack can match. Many residents wash at home and carry the damp load over just to use the dryer.

## Bedding, coats and suits: the neighborhood dry cleaner

Anything too bulky or delicate for a home machine goes to the local 세탁소. Most residential streets have one within a few minutes' walk, and prices are low by international standards. Winter padded coats, suits, blankets and wool coats are the usual items. Many 세탁소 also do basic alterations (수선) such as shortening trousers or fixing a zip, which is handy when you've bought clothes locally and the sizing is slightly off.

Many dry cleaners will pick up and drop off at your door if you call or leave a note, which is standard for older shops with a regular customer base. Keep the receipt or ticket they give you, because that's how they match your items at pickup.

There are also app-based laundry services that collect from your doorstep or a locker and return everything cleaned and folded. They're convenient if you work long hours, but they are usually built around a Korean phone number and local payment methods, so they suit residents more than short-term visitors.

## The hotel laundry trap for travelers

If you're only here for a week or two, the most expensive way to get clothes clean is the hotel laundry bag. It is priced per item, and a few shirts and a pair of trousers add up quickly.

Better options are close by. Many hostels and some mid-range hotels have a guest washer, so ask at the front desk before you hand over the bag. Otherwise, check a map app for 코인빨래방 near your accommodation. In most neighborhoods there's one within walking distance, and a single wash-and-dry for a whole suitcase costs a fraction of what a hotel charges.

## A simple plan by length of stay

- **Under two weeks:** pack for a mid-trip wash and use a coin laundry once. Skip the hotel service unless it's one urgent item.
- **One to three months:** use the in-room washer, buy a folding rack in week one, and save towels and bedding for a coin laundry run.
- **Long-term resident:** find your nearest 세탁소 for coats and bedding, learn the washer words above, and consider a dehumidifier before the monsoon starts.

faq.question: Do I need to bring detergent to a coin laundry in Korea?
faq.answer: Usually not. Most 코인빨래방 washers add detergent and softener automatically during the cycle, so all you need is your laundry and a card, phone payment or coins.

faq.question: Why don't Korean apartments have dryers?
faq.answer: Drying on an indoor rack or enclosed balcony has long been the norm, so most rentals are furnished with a washer only. Standalone dryers are more common in family-owned homes than in furnished studios and officetels.

faq.question: How do I get rid of the damp smell on clothes dried indoors during the monsoon?
faq.answer: Add an extra spin (탈수) so less water reaches the rack, hang items with space between them, and dry them in a closed room with a dehumidifier or fan running. If the sour smell has already set in, rewash the load promptly instead of masking it with more softener.

The closed-on-Monday trap: how Korean pa.title: Seoul Palace Closing Days and the Monday Museum Trap
The closed-on-Monday trap: how Korean pa.description: A practical guide to which Seoul palaces close on Monday or Tuesday, which museums stay open on Mondays, and which royal sites offer free Wednesday entry.
The closed-on-Monday trap: how Korean pa.body:
The classic Seoul itinerary mistake isn't forgetting that palaces have a day off. It's assuming they all take the same day off. Seoul's royal sites are split across two different closing days, and museums follow their own rules on top of that. A tidy "palaces on Monday, museums on Tuesday" plan can leave you facing locked gates twice in one trip.

## Who closes on which day

The Korea Heritage Service, which runs the palaces, publishes one regular closing day per site:

| Site | Regular closing day |
|---|---|
| Gyeongbokgung | Tuesday |
| Jongmyo Shrine | Tuesday |
| Changdeokgung | Monday |
| Changgyeonggung | Monday |
| Deoksugung | Monday |
| Joseon royal tombs | Monday |

When a closing day lands on a public holiday or substitute holiday, the site stays open and closes on the next non-holiday day instead. That rule catches people in reverse: a palace you expected to be closed on a holiday Monday is open, and then it closes on the Tuesday you'd planned for it.

The practical result is that no weekday has every palace open. On Mondays you have Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo. On Tuesdays you have Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung. Wednesday through Sunday, everything is open.

## Turning Monday into a good day

Monday is when most people get caught out, because it's also when many smaller museums and galleries close. It doesn't have to be a wasted day.

Gyeongbokgung is the obvious anchor, and with fewer alternatives open it can get crowded, so arriving at opening pays off. After that, the National Museum of Korea in Yongsan is a strong second stop. It is open every day of the year except New Year's Day, Seollal and Chuseok, so Monday works. One exception: its permanent and special galleries close for maintenance on the first Monday of March, June, September and December, so check the date if your Monday falls there.

City-run museums are where Monday closures are most common. The Seoul Museum of History, for example, closes on Mondays, but it opens on a Monday that falls on a public holiday. It also stays open until 9 p.m. on Fridays. The same pattern applies to many smaller public galleries, so if a museum isn't a national one, assume Monday might be its day off and check its own website.

## Jongmyo's weekday rule

Jongmyo Shrine has a second restriction most visitors don't expect. On weekdays you can't just walk in and wander. Entry is by timed guided tour, with set departure times through the day and English tours at some of those slots. Free wandering is allowed only on Saturdays, Sundays, public holidays and the last Wednesday of each month.

That makes Jongmyo a reasonable Monday stop if you're happy to follow a guide, but a poor one if you want to take your time photographing the long main hall. If your visit depends on wandering, move it to a weekend.

## The last-entry trap

Closing time and last entry are not the same thing. Ticket sales and entry at the palaces stop well before the gates close, and at Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung that's an hour before closing. Showing up forty minutes before closing time can mean being turned away at the booth.

Closing hours also change with the season, running longer in summer and shorter in winter, so the time you saw on a blog written in June won't hold in December. The official Royal Palaces and Tombs site lists the current month's hours for each site.

Deoksugung is the exception for late plans. It stays open until 9 p.m. with last entry at 8 p.m., and it's the easiest palace to fit in after dinner on any day except Monday.

## Free Wednesdays at the palaces

Culture Day (문화가 있는 날) used to be the last Wednesday of each month. From April 2026, the government extended it to every Wednesday, although individual venues decide what they offer and when they join in.

For the palaces, the Korea Heritage Service has been extending weekly free Wednesdays site by site during 2026:

- Joseon royal tombs: free every Wednesday starting late May 2026.
- Deoksugung: free every Wednesday starting August 2026.
- Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Jongmyo: scheduled to join in autumn 2026.
- Gyeongbokgung: kept to the last Wednesday of the month because of crowding when the plan was announced.

The official fee page has been slower to update than the announcements, so check royal.khs.go.kr for the current list before you plan a day around free entry.

Changdeokgung's Secret Garden is excluded from Culture Day free entry and keeps its own separate ticket and reservation system. Also expect free Wednesdays to be busier, especially at the smaller palaces where the grounds fill quickly.

Two other free-entry rules are worth one line each. The palaces and Jongmyo are typically free during the [Seollal and Chuseok holiday periods](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-korean-public-holidays-that-disrupt-travel-plans.html), and wearing hanbok gets you in free year-round, as covered in the [Gyeongbokgung guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-gyeongbokgung-palace.html). Staff do check that you're in actual hanbok, a proper traditional top and bottom, rather than a single traditional-looking piece over ordinary clothes.

## A week that doesn't hit a locked gate

If you have a full week in Seoul, this layout avoids every closing day:

- **Monday:** Gyeongbokgung at opening, then the National Museum of Korea.
- **Tuesday:** Changdeokgung, then walk to Changgyeonggung next door.
- **Wednesday:** whichever palaces are on the current free-Wednesday list, with Deoksugung the safest bet.
- **Saturday:** Jongmyo, when you can wander without a tour.
- **Any evening except Monday:** Deoksugung after dark.

Before you finalize the plan, check the official site for each palace or museum on your actual dates. Holiday shifts and temporary closures do happen, and a two-minute check is cheaper than a wasted trip across the city.

faq.question: Which Seoul palace is open on Monday?
faq.answer: Gyeongbokgung is the main palace open on Mondays, along with Jongmyo Shrine by guided tour. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung all take Monday off unless it is a public holiday.

faq.question: Is the National Museum of Korea closed on Mondays?
faq.answer: No, it opens on Mondays and closes only on New Year's Day, Seollal and Chuseok. Admission to its permanent galleries is free, which makes it a reliable backup on any day.

faq.question: Are Seoul palaces free on Wednesdays?
faq.answer: Some are. Deoksugung and the Joseon royal tombs are free every Wednesday, more palaces were scheduled to join during 2026, and Gyeongbokgung was kept to the last Wednesday of the month, so check royal.khs.go.kr for the current list.

Bus travel inside Korean cities: color c.title: Seoul City Buses Explained by Color, Stop and Tapping Off
Bus travel inside Korean cities: color c.description: A practical guide to Seoul city buses covering what the colors mean, finding the right stop, flagging the driver, and why tapping off keeps transfers free.
Bus travel inside Korean cities: color c.body:
Standing politely at a Korean bus stop is one of the easiest ways to miss your bus. Drivers in Korean cities don't stop at every stop by default, and if nobody at the curb looks like they want that particular bus, it will often roll straight past. City buses here are fast, frequent, and cheap, but they reward a more assertive rider than the subway does. Here's what actually matters once you're off the train and onto the street.

## What the bus colors in Seoul actually tell you

Seoul's city buses are color-coded, and the colors say something about how each bus behaves:

- **Blue buses** run long trunk routes across the city, usually along major roads and often in the center-lane bus corridors.
- **Green buses** are shorter neighborhood feeders that link residential streets to subway stations.
- **Yellow buses** circulate within a small downtown area on a loop.
- **Red buses** are express routes that run out to the Gyeonggi suburbs with widely spaced stops.

Fares follow the colors too. According to Seoul's official fare table (in effect since August 12, 2023), an adult ride on a blue or green bus costs 1,500 won, a yellow circular bus 1,400 won, and a red express bus 3,000 won, with the same adult price whether you pay by card or cash. The base fare covers the first 10 km of a trip, including any transfers (30 km if a red express bus is involved), and longer journeys add 100 won per extra 5 km. Red buses are also different in another way: because many of them use expressways, they're bound by the rule that every passenger must be seated with a seatbelt on. When all the seats are taken, the bus stops boarding, which is why commuters at big red-bus stops check how many seats are left before the bus arrives. For many Gyeonggi express routes, Kakao Map and the KakaoBus app show remaining seats alongside the arrival time.

Don't carry Seoul's color logic to other cities. Busan, Daegu, and Incheon each run their own bus systems with their own route types and numbering. Treat the route number, checked in a map app, as the only reliable identifier anywhere in the country.

## Finding the right stop, on the right side of the road

This is where most first bus rides go wrong. Korean bus stops usually carry the same name on both sides of a road, one for each direction. Before you wait, look at the stop sign or in your app for the **next stop** listed for your bus. If the next stop is the one you just came from, you're on the wrong side.

Seoul adds a twist with its center-lane bus corridors. On many major roads, blue buses run in dedicated lanes in the middle of the road, and the stops are islands between the traffic lanes, reached by a crosswalk. If you're standing on the sidewalk waiting for a bus your app says is "arriving," look toward the middle of the road.

Each stop also has a five-digit stop number on its sign. Typing that number into Naver Map or Kakao Map pulls up that exact platform, which is more reliable than searching by name when several stops share one. Many stops show live arrival times on a screen too, and the countdown usually matches what the apps show.

## Why you have to flag the bus down

When your bus appears, step toward the curb and raise your hand as it approaches. At busy stops several buses may pull in at once, stopping behind each other rather than at the sign, so be ready to walk a few meters to your bus's door. If the driver sees nobody moving toward the curb, the bus may not stop at all.

Getting off works the same way. The bus won't stop unless someone presses a stop button, found on the poles and near the windows, before the stop. Onboard announcements and screens name each stop in Korean, with English on many routes, but it helps to follow your position on the map app so you're ready.

Drivers also pull away quickly, both from the stop and from the curb. Start moving toward the rear door as you approach your stop, holding the poles or straps, and press the button early. Waiting in your seat until the bus is fully stopped can mean the doors close before you reach them. You board at the front and get off through the rear door.

## Tap off, every single time

The single habit that costs foreigners the most money is skipping the tap when getting off. There is a card reader by the rear door, and you should tap your card on it every time you leave the bus, even on a flat-fare route where tapping off doesn't seem to change anything. If you haven't picked up a card yet, our [T-money card guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-t-money-transit-card.html) covers buying and loading one.

Here's why. Free transfers between buses, and between buses and the subway, only work when both the boarding tap and the exit tap are recorded. In Seoul you get up to four free transfers, which is five rides in total, as long as you board the next vehicle within 30 minutes of tapping off. Between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. that window stretches to one hour. Transferring to another bus with the same route number doesn't count as a transfer. If you don't tap off, the system can't see where you left, so your next bus or subway ride starts from zero and is charged a full new fare. On longer trips, the distance charge is calculated from those same taps.

When a transfer registers, the reader announces 환승입니다 (*hwanseung-imnida*, "this is a transfer"), which is a handy confirmation that you did it right. (The subway has also charged riders who skip the exit tap an extra base fare on their next trip since March 2026.)

A final payment detail: a growing number of Seoul buses no longer accept cash at all, and cash fares never earn the transfer discount anyway. Keep a loaded transit card on you rather than counting on coins.

## Korean words you'll see and hear on the bus

Stop screens, onboard displays, and card readers mix Korean and English, and the Korean parts are often the most useful. These are the ones worth recognizing:

- **정류장 / 정류소** (*jeongnyujang / jeongnyuso*): bus stop.
- **이번 정류장** (*ibeon jeongnyujang*): "this stop," the one the bus is approaching now. **다음 정류장** (*daeum jeongnyujang*) is the one after it.
- **곧 도착** (*got dochak*): "arriving soon" on the countdown screen at the stop.
- **승차 / 하차** (*seungcha / hacha*): boarding and getting off. The rear door and its reader are the 하차 side.
- **저상버스** (*jeosang beoseu*): low-floor bus, flagged on arrival screens. Handy with a stroller or heavy suitcase.
- **카드를 한 장만 대주세요**: "please tap only one card." The reader says this when it detects two cards in your wallet, and the tap fails.
- **잔액이 부족합니다**: "insufficient balance." Top up at a convenience store before your next ride.

faq.question: Can I tap a foreign Visa or Mastercard contactless card on Seoul buses?
faq.answer: Not yet. Seoul is fitting buses with EMV-certified readers so overseas cards can be tapped directly, with bus service expected around 2027; until then, subway station kiosks accept overseas cards for single-journey tickets and for buying or charging a Climate Card (including short-term tourist passes).

faq.question: Is there a cheaper time of day to ride the bus in Seoul?
faq.answer: Yes. If you pay with a transit card and board before 6:30 a.m., the base fare of your first ride gets a 20% early-morning discount, so a 1,500-won blue or green bus ride costs 1,200 won.

faq.question: How much does a Seoul village bus cost compared with a regular city bus?
faq.answer: Village buses (maeul buses), the small green buses that serve narrow neighborhood streets, cost 1,200 won for adults, less than the 1,500 won on regular blue and green buses. They join the same transfer system, so tapping off still matters.

Seasonal packing & weather tips.title: What to Pack for Korea by Season (2026 Packing List)
Seasonal packing & weather tips.description: Korea has four distinct seasons. Here's exactly what to pack for spring, summer, fall, or winter — and what you'll regret forgetting.
Seasonal packing & weather tips.image_query: Korea seasons weather fall autumn spring Seoul travel packing
Seasonal packing & weather tips.body:
Korea's seasons are distinct and dramatic. Spring flowers bloom in April. Summer is humid and hot (reaching 30°C/86°F+). Fall is perfect with mild temperatures and clear skies. Winter brings snow and temperatures dropping to -10°C/14°F.

Which season you visit changes your packing list entirely. Pack wrong and you'll be miserable or spend money replacing forgotten items.

This guide breaks down what to actually bring for each season.

## Spring (March-May): Highly Recommended Season

**Weather:** 10-20°C (50-68°F), occasional rain, cherry blossoms early April

**What to pack:**
- Light jacket or cardigan (essential; mornings and evenings are cool)
- Long-sleeve shirts (you'll layer them)
- Light pants or jeans
- One pair of closed-toe walking shoes
- One pair of casual sandals or slip-ons
- Light rain jacket or umbrella (spring has unpredictable rain)
- Sunscreen and sunglasses (spring sun is deceptive; you'll burn)
- Scarf or lightweight sweater (optional but useful)

**Spring packing mistakes to avoid:**
- Packing only t-shirts (mornings and evenings are cold)
- Not bringing layers (you'll remove/add jackets constantly)
- Forgetting sunscreen (people consistently underestimate spring sun intensity)

## Summer (June-August): Hot & Humid

**Weather:** 23-32°C (73-90°F), high humidity, occasional typhoons in late August

**What to pack:**
- Lightweight, loose-fitting shirts (synthetic or cotton that dries quickly)
- Shorts (knee-length is safer culturally, though shorter is acceptable)
- Lightweight pants (for temples and conservative venues)
- Sandals or slip-ons with good grip (sweaty feet = slipping)
- Closed-toe walking shoes (for hiking or longer walks)
- Rain jacket or rain poncho (typhoon season; regular umbrellas struggle)
- Lightweight hat or visor (sun protection)
- Sunscreen (essential; UV index is high)
- Sunglasses (required)
- Light scarf (some temples require arms/shoulders covered; a scarf solves this)
- Moisture-wicking underwear and socks (you'll sweat)
- Deodorant (you'll need more than usual)

**Summer packing mistakes to avoid:**
- Packing heavy clothes (everything will feel oppressive)
- Forgetting rain gear (monsoon season creates sudden flooding and typhoons)
- Wearing tight-fitting clothes (you'll feel uncomfortable and overheat)

## Fall (September-November): Perfect Season

**Weather:** 15-25°C (59-77°F), dry, excellent visibility, fall foliage October-November

**What to pack:**
- Light jacket or sweater (early September can be warm; late November gets cool)
- Long-sleeve shirts
- Long pants or jeans
- One pair of casual walking shoes
- One pair of dressier shoes (fall is popular for dining out)
- Light rain jacket (occasional rain, but less frequent than spring)
