Public bathhouse culture in Korea beyond.title: Mogyoktang Guide to Korea's Neighborhood Bathhouses
Public bathhouse culture in Korea beyond.description: A mogyoktang isn't a mini jjimjilbang. It's an older, plainer bathhouse that's vanishing from Korean neighborhoods. Here's how it differs and how to visit one.
Public bathhouse culture in Korea beyond.image_query: old Korean neighborhood bathhouse mogyoktang exterior
Public bathhouse culture in Korea beyond.body:
Ask most guides about Korean bathing culture and they jump straight to the jjimjilbang, the big spa-sauna complex with themed heated rooms, a snack bar, and a hall where people sleep overnight. The mogyoktang (목욕탕) is the older, plainer institution underneath it. It's a genuinely different place, not a smaller version of the same experience, and knowing the difference saves you from walking in with the wrong expectations. If you haven't been to either yet, our [jjimjilbang etiquette guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-jjimjilbang-etiquette.html) covers the bigger, more tourist-friendly option.

## Mogyoktang vs. Jjimjilbang: What's Actually Different

- **Facilities**: A mogyoktang is just the bathing area: hot and cold tubs, shower stations, and sometimes one small dry sauna. There are no themed spa rooms, no restaurant, and no communal sleeping hall.
- **No overnight stay**: You can't sleep there. A mogyoktang is a place to wash and soak, then leave, while many jjimjilbang run around the clock and let you stay the night.
- **Price**: Closer than most people expect. Official price data from Korea's Consumer 24 (소비자24) service put the average adult bathhouse fee in Seoul at about 11,000 won in July 2026, while a jjimjilbang's daytime entry usually runs around 10,000 to 16,000 won. Prices outside Seoul are often a little lower. You're paying for a simpler place, not getting a bargain.
- **Who goes there**: Mostly residents of the surrounding blocks on a regular routine, many of them older, rather than tourists, families, or weekend groups.
- **Separate and nude**: The bathing floors are split by sex, and everyone bathes fully nude. That's normal and nobody stares.

## Why They're Disappearing

The numbers are dropping fast. Korea had 8,904 public bathhouses in 2000 and 5,656 in 2025, down more than 13 percent from 2020. The reasons cited are rising energy costs for heating all that water and a customer base that is getting older while younger people shower at home or pick a jjimjilbang with more to do. The COVID years hit especially hard, and many of the bathhouses still open are decades old, tucked into older residential streets and run by owners who are aging too. If there's one near where you're staying, it may not be there on your next trip.

## How a Visit Works

The routine is simpler than a jjimjilbang's because there's less to it:

1. **Shoes off at the entrance.** Put them in a small shoe locker and take its key.
2. **Pay at the counter.** Hand over the shoe-locker key with your fee, and you'll get a changing-room locker key, usually on a rubber wristband you wear into the bath.
3. **Undress at your locker.** Go to the bathing area with only your key and a small towel. Many places hand out small towels at the counter, but don't count on a large one.
4. **Wash completely first.** Sit at a shower station and scrub everything before you get into any tub. This rule is the same at every bathhouse in Korea, and skipping it is the one thing regulars will react to.
5. **Soak, rinse, repeat.** Move between the hot and cold tubs at your own pace. Keep your towel out of the water; people fold it on their head or leave it at the edge.
6. **Rinse off, dress, and return the key.** Hand the wristband back at the counter and get your shoe-locker key in return.

Beyond basic bar soap, shampoo, conditioner, and body wash usually aren't provided, so bring your own or buy small packets at the counter if they sell them.

## The Scrub: Seshin

Many mogyoktang have an attendant who does seshin, the famous full-body scrub with a rough mitt called an italy towel (이태리타월). It's a paid extra arranged at the counter or directly with the attendant, and prices are usually posted on the wall. You'll be scrubbed hard enough to see dead skin come off, so soak in a hot tub for a while first; it makes the scrub far easier. If you'd rather do it yourself, the same mitts are sold cheaply at the counter or any convenience store.

## Finding One

Mogyoktang rarely show up in English or on tourist apps, because they aren't built for visitors. Search 목욕탕 directly in Naver Map instead of Google Maps, which lists far fewer of them, and check the hours and recent reviews there before you go, since small, independently run bathhouses keep their own schedules and some close for good with little notice. On the street, look for the Korean word on a sign in older residential neighborhoods rather than in commercial or tourist districts.

## Is It Worth Visiting as a Tourist?

For a first Korean bathhouse, a jjimjilbang is still the easier choice. It's built around newcomers, usually open longer, and more likely to have some English signage in tourist areas. A mogyoktang is worth seeking out if you're staying in one neighborhood long enough to have a routine, or if you want a quiet, no-frills soak closer to how older Koreans actually bathe. Don't expect English: staff rarely speak it, and nobody will walk you through the steps. Knowing the routine above in advance is what makes the visit easy.

## First-Visit Checklist

- Search 목욕탕 on Naver Map and confirm today's hours.
- Bring cash and a card, since some older places prefer cash.
- Pack shampoo, body wash, a comb, and a larger towel if you want one.
- Wash fully at a shower station before touching any tub.
- Keep your towel and hair out of the water.
- Ask at the counter if you want seshin, and soak first.
- Return the wristband key on the way out to get your shoes back.

faq.question: Is a mogyoktang much cheaper than a jjimjilbang?
faq.answer: Not by much anymore. Seoul's average bathhouse fee was about 11,000 won in July 2026, while jjimjilbang daytime entry usually runs about 10,000 to 16,000 won. The real difference is what you get: a mogyoktang is only the bath, with no sleeping hall or extra rooms.

faq.question: Do I have to be naked in a mogyoktang?
faq.answer: Yes. Bathing floors are separated by sex and everyone bathes fully nude. Swimsuits are not worn, and nobody pays attention to other bathers.

faq.question: Can I get a body scrub at a mogyoktang?
faq.answer: Often, yes. Many have an attendant who does seshin, a full-body scrub, for a posted fee. Arrange it at the counter or with the attendant, and soak in a hot tub first so the scrub works better.

Korean winter street food: bungeoppang,.title: Korean Winter Street Food and Where to Find Bungeoppang
Korean winter street food: bungeoppang,.description: Fish-shaped bungeoppang, syrupy hotteok and fish cake broth define a Korean winter, but the stalls are getting harder to find. Here is where they went.
Korean winter street food: bungeoppang,.image_query: bungeoppang fish shaped pastry street stall korea winter
Korean winter street food: bungeoppang,.body:
The first cold week of a Korean winter has a smell: sweet red bean, toasted batter and a little gas from a portable burner. For decades that smell came from a cart on almost every subway exit. Visitors who arrive in December expecting to trip over a bungeoppang stall every few blocks are often surprised, because those carts have been thinning out for years. The snacks haven't gone anywhere. They've moved, and their price has moved too. Here's what to look for and where to find it now.

## The five winter snacks worth knowing

**Bungeoppang (붕어빵)** is the one you'll see in every winter photo: a fish-shaped waffle-like pastry baked in an iron mold, traditionally filled with sweet red bean paste. Custard (called "shu cream") is the common second filling, and newer stalls and cafes add pizza, sweet potato or cheese versions. A close cousin, **ingeoppang** (잉어빵), uses a slightly different, thinner batter and is often what the cart is actually selling, even if everyone calls it bungeoppang.

**Hotteok (호떡)** is a flat, griddle-fried dough pancake with a filling of brown sugar, cinnamon and chopped nuts or seeds that melts into syrup. Eat the first bite carefully. The filling is genuinely hot enough to burn, which is why vendors hand it over folded in a paper cup.

**Gyeranppang (계란빵)** is a small, slightly sweet loaf with a whole egg baked on top. It's a filling snack on a cold morning and easy to eat while walking.

**Eomuk (어묵)**, fish cake threaded on long skewers and kept warm in a pot of broth, is the savory option. At many stands you pay for the skewers and sip the broth from a paper cup with a small ladle. That broth is what people are really there for on a freezing night.

**Gun-goguma (군고구마)**, roasted sweet potatoes, used to come from barrel-shaped street roasters. Today you are more likely to find them in a heated case at a convenience store.

## Why the carts are disappearing, and what that does to the price

Korean media have been covering the shrinking number of street-snack carts for several winters running. The reasons are mostly cost. Red beans, flour, cooking oil and the gas used to fire the molds have all risen sharply. Korean wholesale data reported by several outlets showed domestic red bean prices in late 2025 running 20 to 40 percent above the year before, and more than double what they were three years earlier. Some vendors also pack up their stalls quickly because of street-vending enforcement and neighbor complaints.

The old joke that 1,000 won bought a paper bag full of bungeoppang no longer holds. In December 2025, Financial News reported street prices of around three for 2,000 won, and up to 1,500 won for a single piece in some high-traffic areas such as Gwangjang Market. Koreans now call this "bung-flation." If you see a stall with prices like that, it's normal. You aren't being singled out as a tourist.

## Where to actually find them in 2026

**Convenience stores.** This is the biggest shift. The major chains now bake bungeoppang and roast sweet potatoes in-store during the cold months. GS25 said it began selling winter snacks, including bungeoppang and roasted sweet potatoes, at around 5,000 stores nationwide from October 1, 2026, and CU and other chains have also expanded roasted sweet potatoes and fish cakes for winter. Look for a small heated display near the counter. Our [convenience store guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-convenience-store-hacks.html) covers the rest of what these shops do well.

**Cafes.** Independent cafes have started selling bungeoppang alongside coffee, often with unusual fillings. A YTN report in early 2025 profiled a Seoul cafe owner who said sales rose about 30 percent after adding them.

**Traditional markets and busy stations.** The surviving street carts cluster where foot traffic is heaviest: around large markets and outside major subway exits. Markets such as [Namdaemun](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-namdaemun-market.html) are good bets for hotteok and eomuk.

**Crowd-sourced maps.** Koreans share stall locations on "bungeoppang map" style apps and community maps where users pin a cart when they spot one. Searching 붕어빵 (bungeoppang) in a Korean map app will also surface nearby sellers. It is the same trick locals use, since a cart that was there last winter may not be there now.

## How to pay and order without fuss

Cash is still the safest bet at a street cart. Many carts now display a bank transfer account number, and some accept cards or mobile pay, but a few 1,000-won bills will never fail you. Convenience stores and cafes take cards as usual; our [guide to cards and cash in Korea](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-currency-card-payments.html) explains which foreign cards work where.

Ordering is simple. Point at what you want and hold up fingers for the count, or say the number plus "juseyo" (주세요, "please give me"). Bungeoppang is often sold in sets of two or three, and the price board will show the set price. Hotteok is usually sold one at a time.

## Your winter snack checklist

Before you head out on a cold evening, run through this list:

1. Carry a few 1,000-won bills and coins for carts that don't take cards.
2. Check the nearest convenience store first if you just want bungeoppang or a sweet potato fast.
3. Search 붕어빵 in a Korean map app to find carts near you tonight.
4. Let hotteok cool for a minute before biting into the sugar filling.
5. At an eomuk stand, ask for the broth (국물, gungmul). It usually comes with the skewer.
6. Expect around 2,000 won for a set of bungeoppang, and more in tourist-heavy markets.

Do that and you will eat like a local through the cold months, even if the cart on the corner is gone.

faq.question: How much does bungeoppang cost in Korea now?
faq.answer: Street prices have risen with ingredient costs. Reports from late 2025 put typical carts at about three pieces for 2,000 won, and some busy tourist areas at up to 1,500 won for one piece.

faq.question: When is bungeoppang season in Korea?
faq.answer: Street carts mostly appear when the weather turns cold, roughly from late autumn through winter, and many pack up as spring arrives. Convenience stores and some cafes sell them through the cold months as well.

faq.question: Can I pay for street snacks in Korea by card?
faq.answer: Sometimes, but not always. Some carts accept cards, mobile pay or bank transfer, while others take cash only. Carry a few small bills so you're never stuck.

Skiing near Seoul without a car: Konjiam.title: Skiing Near Seoul Without a Car for First-Time Visitors
Skiing near Seoul without a car: Konjiam.description: You can ski in Korea on a Seoul day trip without renting a car. Here is how the subway, resort shuttles and tour buses work, and what to rent on arrival.
Skiing near Seoul without a car: Konjiam.image_query: ski resort slopes korea winter gyeonggi gangwon
Skiing near Seoul without a car: Konjiam.body:
Plenty of visitors land in Seoul in December or January and only then realize Korea has real ski resorts, some under an hour from the city. The question that stops most of them is getting there. Car rental sounds like the obvious answer, but icy mountain roads, Korean-language navigation and resort parking on a weekend make it the hardest option for a first trip. You don't need a car. Here's how first-timers actually get to the slopes and what to expect once they arrive.

## When the season runs

Korean ski resorts make most of their snow, so opening dates depend on how cold it gets. For the 2026/27 season, published resort notices checked in mid-November gave these planned dates: Phoenix Snow Park in Pyeongchang moved its opening to November 26, Oak Valley in Wonju listed December 11 with a planned closing of February 20, 2027, and Konjiam said only "in December," with a close in early March. Resorts often change these dates with the weather, so treat them as plans, not promises, and check the resort's own notice before you book anything you can't cancel.

In practice, the most reliable window for a short trip is late December through mid-February. Weekends and the Korean school winter break are the busiest times, so a weekday trip means shorter lift lines and an easier time at the rental counter.

## Three ways to get there without a car

**Option 1: Subway plus the resort shuttle (cheapest, a little effort).** Two resorts close to Seoul are reachable by rail. Konjiam Resort in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, is the closest large resort to the capital, roughly 40 to 50 minutes by road from Gangnam. Take the Gyeonggang Line to Gonjiam Station and catch the resort's shuttle from outside the station. Elysian Gangchon in Chuncheon sits near Baegyang-ri Station on the Gyeongchun Line, which you can reach by changing at Mangu Station on the Gyeongui-Jungang Line. Shuttle times change each season, so check the resort's website for the current timetable. If rail and transfers are new to you, our [guide to day trips by regular train](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-day-tripping-from-seoul-by-regular-train-mugunghwa-itx-saemaeul-and-the-gyeongui-jungang-line.html) explains how these lines work.

**Option 2: The resort's own shuttle bus from Seoul.** Most major resorts run seasonal shuttle buses from pick-up points in Seoul, such as large subway stations. Seats usually need booking ahead on the resort website, which can be Korean-only, so this works best if you have a Korean speaker to help or a booking platform that resells the seats.

**Option 3: A packaged day tour (easiest, most expensive).** Travel platforms sell ski day trips that bundle a round-trip bus from central Seoul (pick-up points such as Hongdae or Myeongdong vary by operator), clothing rental, equipment rental and optional lift tickets. These bundles cost noticeably more than doing it yourself, and adding a lift pass raises the price further, so compare current listings, since prices change each season. You pay for convenience, but someone else handles the Korean-language rental desk, which matters a lot on your first day.

## What to rent, and what to bring from home

Korean resorts are set up for people who arrive with nothing. Skis or a snowboard, boots, poles and helmets can all be rented on site, usually priced by session length such as four or six hours. Ski clothing, both jacket and pants, is a separate rental at most resorts and many day tours include it. You'll often also need to buy or bring gloves and goggles, and these are worth packing from home because resort shop prices are high.

Dress in layers under the rental suit. Korean mountain resorts are much colder than Seoul, especially for night skiing, which many resorts offer and which is a good way to dodge daytime crowds. Our [seasonal packing guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seasonal-packing-weather-tips.html) has more on dressing for Korean winters.

## Lift tickets and lessons

Lift passes are sold by time block (for example half-day, four hours or a full day) instead of per run. Prices change each season and resorts often run online discounts, so compare the resort's own site with ticket platforms before you pay at the window.

If you've never skied, book a lesson. Larger resorts have English-speaking instructors, but they're limited, so request one when you book, not on arrival. Beginner slopes in Korea can get crowded and you'll be sharing them with plenty of fast snowboarders, so a lesson is the safest way to start.

## Your first-trip checklist

1. Check the resort's official opening notice the week of your trip, since dates move with the weather.
2. Pick your transport: subway plus shuttle for Konjiam or Elysian Gangchon, a resort bus, or a bundled day tour.
3. Go on a weekday if you can, and avoid Korean school winter break weekends.
4. Pack gloves, goggles, a warm hat and thermal layers. Rent the rest.
5. Book an English-speaking lesson in advance if you're a beginner.
6. Have your passport handy, since rental desks may ask for ID or a deposit.

Get those six things right and a ski day from Seoul is no harder than any other day trip.

faq.question: What is the closest ski resort to Seoul?
faq.answer: Konjiam Resort in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, is the closest large ski resort to Seoul, about 40 to 50 minutes by road from Gangnam. It is also reachable by the Gyeonggang Line to Gonjiam Station plus a resort shuttle.

faq.question: When does ski season start in Korea?
faq.answer: Usually between late November and mid-December, depending on temperatures. For 2026/27, Phoenix Snow Park planned to open November 26, Oak Valley December 11, and Konjiam sometime in December. Always check the resort's official notice before going.

faq.question: Can I rent ski clothes in Korea?
faq.answer: Yes. Most resorts rent ski jackets and pants separately from skis or snowboards, and many Seoul day tours include clothing rental. Gloves and goggles are often not included, so bring your own.

New Year's Eve in Korea: the Bosingak be.title: New Year's Eve in Seoul at Bosingak and the First Sunrise
New Year's Eve in Korea: the Bosingak be.description: Koreans ring in the year with 33 strikes of the Bosingak bell, then many chase the first sunrise. Here is how to do both and get home that night.
New Year's Eve in Korea: the Bosingak be.image_query: bosingak bell pavilion jongno seoul night
New Year's Eve in Korea: the Bosingak be.body:
If you're in Korea on December 31, you'll notice that New Year's here has two parts. The first is midnight, when a huge crowd in central Seoul counts down as the Bosingak bell is struck. The second comes about seven and a half hours later, when people climb hills and drive to the east coast to watch the first sunrise of the year, called haedoji (해돋이). Most visitors know about one of these at most. Here's how to do either or both without getting stuck in the crowd or stranded at 1 a.m.

## Midnight at Bosingak: the bell ringing

The Jeya-ui Jong (제야의 종) bell-ringing ceremony at Bosingak pavilion in Jongno has been held since 1953 and is Seoul's signature New Year's event. At midnight the bell is struck 33 times. The ringers are the Seoul mayor and other officials along with citizen representatives chosen through a public nomination, and for the 2026 ceremony nominations ran from November 6 to 30.

Last year's program gives a good idea of the shape of the night. The event ran from 10:50 p.m. on December 31 to 12:20 a.m., with pre-show performances, introductions, the countdown, the 33 strikes and a short after-show. Expect something similar this year. Crowds are very large. When the ceremony returned after a three-year pause, around 100,000 people were expected.

Recent years have also had countdown events at Gwanghwamun Square, Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP) and Lotte World Tower, so Bosingak isn't the only place to be at midnight. Gwanghwamun has run large media countdown shows on the screens around the square.

## Getting there and getting home

This is the part that catches visitors out.

**Roads close early.** For the last ceremony, the roads around Bosingak were closed to traffic from 6 p.m. on December 31 until 7 a.m. on January 1, including stretches of Jongno, Cheonggyebuk-ro and Ujeongguk-ro. Don't plan on a taxi drop-off at the pavilion.

**The nearest station may skip stops.** In recent years, Jonggak Station on Line 1 has run trains straight through without stopping for part of the night to prevent crush risk. One year this was set from 11 p.m. to 1 a.m. Plan to walk in from Jongno 3-ga, City Hall or Gwanghwamun instead.

**Last trains run later that night.** Seoul usually extends subway and bus service after midnight on New Year's Eve. The exact extension and route list are announced in late December, so check the Seoul city notice or the TOPIS transport site that week. Our [Seoul subway guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seoul-subway-details-nobody-tells-you-exit-numbers-transfer-walks-express-trains-and-the-last-train.html) explains how to check last-train times for your line.

**Shared bikes and scooters are switched off.** Seoul's Ttareungyi bike stations near Jonggak and private e-scooters around Bosingak have been shut down for the night. Don't count on them as a backup.

## The first sunrise: where and when

On January 1 a lot of Koreans get up in the dark to see the sun rise. Sunrise times calculated by the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute for January 1, 2027 include 7:40 a.m. at Gangneung (for Jeongdongjin), 7:33 a.m. at Pohang (for Homigot) and 7:32 a.m. in Busan and Ulsan. In Seoul it is later, about 7:47 a.m., which was the time for January 1, 2026. Higher ground sees the sun a minute or two earlier.

**In Seoul.** You don't need to leave the city. Seoul lists hills such as Inwangsan, Eungbongsan and Ansan as good city sunrise spots. Several are short climbs, but they're icy and dark at 7 a.m., so take a headlamp and shoes with grip. Our [hiking guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-hiking-in-korea-like-a-local-subway-accessible-peaks-seasonal-trail-closures-and-the-gear-culture.html) covers which peaks are easy to reach by subway.

**On the east coast.** Jeongdongjin in Gangneung is the classic choice, along with Ganjeolgot in Ulsan, which has held sunrise festivals with drone and fireworks shows starting around 5 a.m. Pohang's Homigot and the beaches of Busan, such as Haeundae and Gwangalli, are popular too. Trains, buses and lodging on these routes book out early for December 31, so reserve as soon as you decide.

## Practical tips for the night

Midnight in Seoul in late December is usually well below freezing, and you'll be standing still for an hour or more. Wear thermal layers, gloves and a hat, and bring hand warmers from a convenience store. Keep your phone charged, because crowded areas can have weak signal and you'll need maps to find an open station. January 1 is a public holiday, so some shops and restaurants close, and our [holiday guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-korean-public-holidays-that-disrupt-travel-plans.html) explains what to expect.

## Your New Year's checklist

1. Decide on midnight, sunrise or both. Doing both is possible in Seoul, but very tiring if you also travel to the coast.
2. For Bosingak, arrive on foot by about 10:30 p.m. from a station other than Jonggak.
3. Check Seoul's late-December notice for extended subway and bus times.
4. For a coastal sunrise, book train or bus seats and a room the moment you decide.
5. Note your sunrise time: about 7:47 a.m. in Seoul and about 7:32 to 7:40 a.m. on the east and south coasts.
6. Dress for hours in sub-zero cold and carry hand warmers.

Done that way, you see the year arrive twice and still make it back to bed.

faq.question: How many times is the Bosingak bell rung on New Year's Eve?
faq.answer: The bell is struck 33 times at midnight. The ringers include the Seoul mayor and citizen representatives selected through a public nomination process.

faq.question: Does the Seoul subway run late on New Year's Eve?
faq.answer: Usually yes. Seoul has extended subway and bus service past the normal last train on December 31 in recent years. The exact times are announced in late December, so check the city's notice that week.

faq.question: What time is sunrise on January 1 in Korea?
faq.answer: For January 1, 2027, published times are about 7:32 a.m. in Busan and Ulsan, 7:33 a.m. in Pohang and 7:40 a.m. at Gangneung for Jeongdongjin. Seoul is later, around 7:47 a.m.

Shipping souvenirs home from a Korean po.title: How to Ship Souvenirs Home From a Korean Post Office
Shipping souvenirs home from a Korean po.description: Bought too much in Korea? A post office box and an EMS form often cost less than an extra bag fee. Here is how the counter works and which service to choose.
Shipping souvenirs home from a Korean po.image_query: korea post office counter parcel boxes woocheguk
Shipping souvenirs home from a Korean po.body:
It usually happens on the second-to-last day of a trip. The skincare, the snacks, the extra jacket from the market, and suddenly your suitcase won't close. Airline excess baggage fees are expensive, and many travelers don't realize Korean post offices are set up to solve exactly this problem. You can walk in with a pile of shopping, buy a box at the counter, pack it there and send it home the same afternoon. Here's how the process works and how to pick the right service for what you're sending.

## Find a post office and go early

Korea Post (우체국, ucheguk) has branches all over the country, and the easiest way to find one is to search 우체국 in a Korean map app. Most branches are open weekdays, roughly 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., and closed on weekends and public holidays. Parcel counters can stop accepting international mail earlier than closing time at some branches, so arriving by mid-afternoon is a safe habit. Larger central branches tend to be busier but are more used to foreign customers.

Don't worry about the language barrier. Staff deal with international parcels every day, and Korea Post publishes a Postal Service Guide for Foreigners on its EMS website.

## Buy a box and pack at the counter

Post offices sell official cardboard boxes in several sizes, plus tape, and most have a packing table where you can assemble and fill the box right there. Pack tightly. Wrap anything breakable in clothing and fill gaps, because international parcels get handled many times on the way.

Size matters as much as weight. Since December 2020, Korea Post has charged air parcels, EMS and small packets by actual weight or volumetric weight, whichever is higher. Volumetric weight is length times width times height in centimeters, divided by 6,000. A big, light box of puffy jackets can cost more than you'd expect, so choose the smallest box your items fit in.

## Pick a service: EMS, small packet or sea mail

**EMS (국제특급, international express).** This is the fast, tracked option and the one most travelers use. EMS can carry up to 30 kg to most countries, although some destinations, such as Spain, Argentina and Bangladesh, cap it at 20 kg. You get a 13-character tracking number you can follow online in English.

**Small packet (소형포장물).** For light items up to 2 kg, the small packet service is cheaper than EMS. It suits a few cosmetics, books or small gifts.

**Sea mail (선편소포).** Surface mail parcels are the cheapest way to send heavy, non-urgent items such as clothes, books and kitchenware, but delivery takes weeks or even months. Only use it for things you won't miss for a while.

Prices depend on the destination zone and the weight. Korea Post's site has a rate calculator for EMS and parcels, so you can check before you go.

## Fill in the customs form properly

Every international parcel needs a customs declaration. You'll list each type of item in English, how many there are and their value. Be specific: write "cosmetics (cream, 3 pcs)" instead of just "gifts." Vague descriptions are a common cause of customs delays at the other end. Have your destination address and the recipient's phone number ready, and your own Korean contact details such as your hotel address.

You can also fill in the form online before you go using Korea Post's international mail smart acceptance service, on the website or in the app. Non-contract customers who register an EMS shipment this way get a 5 percent discount, and it saves time at the counter.

## Check your country first

International mail rules have changed a lot since 2025, so check Korea Post's notices for your destination before you pack. Korea Post stopped accepting EMS and parcels for the United States in August 2025 after US duty-free rules for low-value packages ended, then resumed in September 2025 with new steps, including customs declarations and the sender prepaying duties. In 2026, new EU customs rules led Korea Post to restrict EMS and K-Packet to several EU countries, in some cases only for low-value shipments. Shipping companies reported limits for Denmark and Romania from June and for Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands from July, and from October 23, 2026, EMS for shipments declared at 150 euros or less was suspended to a longer list of EU countries. EMS Premium, a partner express service you can book at the same post office counter, has stayed available in many of these cases. Ask at the counter which option works for your country.

## What you can't send, and two traps to avoid

Every destination has its own list of banned or restricted items. Typical problem items include loose lithium batteries and power banks, aerosols and flammables, and some foods, especially meat, fresh produce and anything with seeds. Perfume is often restricted because of its alcohol content. Ask at the counter if you're unsure, since a rejected item means repacking on the spot.

Two other things catch travelers out. First, if you're planning to claim a VAT refund on goods, check the rules before shipping them, because refunds for higher-value purchases can require showing the items at departure. Our [tax refund guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-tax-refund-tax-free-shopping.html) explains when that applies. Second, your home country may charge import duty or tax on the parcel when it arrives. That's set by your destination, not by Korea Post.

If you'd rather not deal with a post office at all, luggage forwarding companies can send bags to the airport or your next hotel instead. Our [luggage storage and forwarding guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-luggage-storage-forwarding-services.html) compares those options.

## Your shipping checklist

1. Check Korea Post's notice for your destination country, especially for the US or EU.
2. Find the nearest 우체국 in a Korean map app and go on a weekday, ideally before mid-afternoon.
3. Bring your passport, the full destination address and the recipient's phone number.
4. Buy a box at the counter and pick the smallest size that fits.
5. Choose EMS for speed, a small packet for items under 2 kg, or sea mail for heavy things you can wait for.
6. List every item clearly in English on the customs form, or register online first for a 5 percent EMS discount.
7. Keep your receipt and tracking number until the box arrives.

A half-hour stop at the post office can save you an expensive extra bag and a stressful airport check-in.

faq.question: Can a tourist send a parcel from a Korean post office?
faq.answer: Yes. You don't need residency or a Korean bank account. Bring your passport, the destination address and the recipient's phone number. You can buy a box at the counter, pack it there and pay by card or cash.

faq.question: What is the maximum weight for EMS from Korea?
faq.answer: EMS from Korea can carry up to 30 kg to most countries, but some destinations limit it to 20 kg. Charges use either the actual weight or the volumetric weight (L x W x H in cm / 6,000), whichever is higher.

faq.question: What is the cheapest way to ship things home from Korea?
faq.answer: Sea mail parcels are the cheapest for heavy items, but delivery takes weeks or months. For light items up to 2 kg, the small packet service is cheaper than EMS. EMS is the fastest and fully tracked.

Gwangjang Market: what to eat, when stal.title: Gwangjang Market Food Guide and How to Avoid Overpaying
Gwangjang Market: what to eat, when stal.description: Gwangjang Market is Seoul's most famous food market, and its price complaints are famous too. Here is what to eat, when to go and how to pay a fair price.
Gwangjang Market: what to eat, when stal.image_query: gwangjang market food stalls bindaetteok seoul
Gwangjang Market: what to eat, when stal.body:
Gwangjang Market shows up in almost every Seoul food video. There are rows of stalls under one long roof, mung bean pancakes frying in oil, and stacks of tiny gimbap rolls. It also shows up in Korean news for a different reason: repeated complaints that some vendors overcharge or under-serve customers, especially foreign tourists. Both things are true. The food is worth the trip, and a little preparation keeps you from paying more than you should. Here's how to approach it.

## What Gwangjang Market is

Gwangjang Market in Jongno is Seoul's largest traditional market and is often described as Korea's first permanent market, with more than a century of history. Most of the building is wholesale and retail shops selling fabric, bedding, hanbok and used clothing. The famous part is the food alley at its center, a crossroads of open stalls where you sit on a bench and eat at the counter. It was featured in the Seoul episode of Netflix's Street Food series, which brought it a big wave of international visitors.

The closest stations are Jongno 5-ga on Line 1 (exit 8, about a 3-minute walk) and Euljiro 4-ga on Lines 2 and 5 (exit 4, about 5 minutes).

## When to go

The food alley runs every day, typically from morning until late evening, around 9 a.m. to 11 p.m. Many individual stalls don't open until 10 or 11 a.m., and some take Sundays or Mondays off. The non-food shops in the rest of the market keep shorter hours, and most close on Sundays.

The quietest time is a weekday late morning or mid-afternoon. Evenings and weekends are crowded, with queues at the best-known stalls, and that's when the market feels most like a tourist attraction.

## What to eat

**Bindaetteok (빈대떡).** The market's signature dish is a thick, crispy pancake made from freshly ground mung beans, fried in plenty of oil. You'll see vendors grinding the beans on site. It goes well with makgeolli, a milky rice wine.

**Mayak gimbap (마약김밥).** These are small, finger-length seaweed rice rolls with simple fillings such as carrot, pickled radish and spinach, served with a mustard and soy dipping sauce. The name means "narcotic gimbap," a joke about how addictive they are, not anything sinister.

**Yukhoe (육회).** Korean-style raw beef tartare, usually seasoned with sesame oil and pear, has its own cluster of specialist restaurants on the market's edge. Several have long lines.

**Kalguksu (칼국수).** Hand-cut noodle soup is a cheap, filling choice on a cold day, served at counter stalls inside the market.

**Mandu, sundae and tteokbokki** round out the menu, so you can graze across several stalls.

## The overcharging problem, and what changed

In November 2023 a Korean YouTuber showing Vietnamese friends around the market posted a video of a 15,000-won mixed jeon (pancake) platter with only about ten pieces. It caused a public backlash. Seoul City and the market's merchant groups announced measures including weight labels next to menu prices, sample models of signature dishes, and mystery shoppers to check stalls. Merchants opposed the weight labels and that plan stalled. A multilingual QR menu showing portion photos was added in 2024 instead. Complaints surfaced again in November 2025, and the response that time included more mystery-shopper checks and a requirement that street stalls display the operator's name.

None of that means you'll be cheated. Most stalls serve honest portions, but it's worth protecting yourself.

## How to make sure you pay a fair price

- **Read the posted price before you sit down.** Stalls are supposed to display prices. If you can't see one, ask "eolmayeyo?" (얼마예요, "how much is it?") and point at the dish before ordering.
- **Order one dish at a time.** It's easier to keep track of what you've had, and you can move on to another stall.
- **Be careful with "set" or mixed platters.** These are where most of the complaints came from. Ask what's included and how many pieces you'll get.
- **Check your bill against what you ordered.** If something looks wrong, point to the price board. Many vendors now accept cards, but carry some cash too, since not every stall accepts foreign cards. Our [guide to paying in Korea](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-currency-card-payments.html) covers what works where.
- **Go with a friend if you can.** Most dishes are sized for sharing. If you're alone, our [guide to eating solo](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-eating-alone-in-korea-which-restaurants-refuse-solo-diners-and-where-honbap-works.html) applies here too, since counter stalls are among the easiest places to eat by yourself.

If you want a market with a different feel, [Namdaemun Market](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-namdaemun-market.html) is better for shopping and its own food alleys.

## Your Gwangjang Market checklist

1. Go on a weekday between late morning and mid-afternoon to avoid the worst crowds.
2. Arrive via Jongno 5-ga exit 8 or Euljiro 4-ga exit 4.
3. Start with bindaetteok and mayak gimbap, then graze through other stalls.
4. Confirm the price and portion before you order, especially for mixed platters.
5. Carry a card and some cash.
6. Avoid Sundays if you also want to shop, since most non-food stores close.

Follow those steps and the market becomes what it should be: a cheap, loud, delicious lunch.

faq.question: Is Gwangjang Market open on Sundays?
faq.answer: The food alley is generally open every day, although some individual stalls close on Sundays or Mondays. Most of the market's non-food shops, such as fabric and clothing stores, are closed on Sundays.

faq.question: What is Gwangjang Market famous for?
faq.answer: It is best known for bindaetteok, a crispy mung bean pancake, and mayak gimbap, small seaweed rice rolls with a mustard dipping sauce. Yukhoe (raw beef) and kalguksu noodle soup are also popular.

faq.question: Do Gwangjang Market stalls overcharge tourists?
faq.answer: There have been several well-publicized complaints, starting with a viral 2023 video of a small 15,000-won jeon platter. Most stalls are fair, but check the posted price and portion before ordering, especially for mixed platters.

Changdeokgung Secret Garden: how the tim.title: Changdeokgung Secret Garden Tickets and How to Get a Spot
Changdeokgung Secret Garden: how the tim.description: You can't just walk into Changdeokgung's Secret Garden. Entry is by timed, capped sessions that sell out. Here is how booking works and when to go.
Changdeokgung Secret Garden: how the tim.image_query: changdeokgung secret garden huwon pavilion pond
Changdeokgung Secret Garden: how the tim.body:
Most first-time visitors to Seoul head to Gyeongbokgung, the biggest of the city's palaces. Many people who have seen both prefer Changdeokgung, and the reason is behind it: Huwon (후원), the royal rear garden usually called the Secret Garden in English. It's a wooded valley of pavilions, ponds and old trees that Joseon kings used for rest and study. The catch is that you can't wander in. The garden only opens in timed sessions with a capped number of people, and the popular ones sell out. Here's how the system works so you get in on the day you want.

## Two tickets, not one

Changdeokgung has two separate areas, each with its own ticket. The palace buildings, with the throne hall, offices and royal quarters, are the general admission area. Adult admission is 3,000 won. The Secret Garden is a separate, additional ticket: 5,000 won for adults and 2,500 won for ages 7 to 18. You need the palace ticket as well, because you walk through the palace grounds to reach the garden gate.

Visitors wearing hanbok get free entry to the palace grounds, a long-standing rule at the Seoul palaces that has been under review, so check the current policy before you go. It doesn't make the Secret Garden session free.

## How Secret Garden booking works

Each Secret Garden session admits a maximum of 100 people. Half the places are sold online in advance and half are released for on-site sale on the day.

**Online booking** opens at 10 a.m. six days before your visit date, through the official royal palaces reservation site, which has an English interface. Seats go first come, first served and can sell out fast in spring and autumn, so be online right at 10 a.m. Korea time if you're aiming for a peak-season weekend.

**On-site tickets** go on sale at the palace ticket office from the morning of the visit. In peak season people queue before the office opens. In winter it's much quieter, and Seoul's official media outlet has noted that same-day booking is usually easy in the colder months.

A tip that saves a lot of stress: take a screenshot of your confirmation. Allow about 10 minutes to walk from the palace entrance to the garden gate, and be there at least 10 minutes before your session.

## Guided sessions and language

Visits to the Secret Garden are guided. You walk the route with a palace guide and the group, and you can't wander off on your own. The walk lasts roughly an hour to an hour and a half and covers hilly paths, so wear comfortable shoes. English sessions are offered at set times that change by season, with fewer slots in winter, so check the current timetable on the reservation site. Korean-language sessions run more often. If you don't mind not understanding the commentary, a Korean session can be easier to book.

## When to go

Changdeokgung is closed on Mondays, like most of Seoul's palaces. If a Monday is a public holiday, the palace usually opens and closes on the next weekday instead, a pattern covered in our [guide to palace and museum closing days](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-the-closed-on-monday-trap-how-korean-palaces-and-museums-schedule-their-days-off.html). From November to January the palace is open from 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., with last entry at 4:30 p.m. Hours are longer from February to October.

Each season changes the garden. Spring blossoms and autumn foliage are the most famous and the hardest to book. Winter is the easiest time to get a session, and a light snow on the pavilions is beautiful. Summer is green but hot on the hill paths.

There's also the separate Moonlight Tour, a ticketed evening program in the garden held for limited periods in spring and autumn. It sells out very quickly and is booked through a different channel, so don't expect to add it at the last minute.

## Getting there and pairing it with other sights

The closest station is Anguk on Line 3. Exit 3 is about a five-minute walk. Jongno 3-ga Station (Lines 1, 3 and 5) is about a 10-minute walk. There's no dedicated parking, so use public transport. Donhwamun, the main gate, is under repair until mid-2027, so expect to enter through another gate and have your ticket ready.

Changdeokgung sits right next to [Bukchon Hanok Village](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-bukchon-hanok-village.html), so a morning garden session followed by a walk through the hanok lanes makes an easy half day. If you're also planning to see [Gyeongbokgung](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-gyeongbokgung-palace.html), do it on a different day. Two palaces back to back is a lot of walking.

## Your Secret Garden checklist

1. Pick a day that isn't a Monday, and avoid peak spring and autumn weekends if you can.
2. Six days ahead, be online at 10 a.m. Korea time to book a session in your language.
3. If you miss out, go early on the day to try for one of the on-site tickets.
4. Budget for both tickets: the palace and the garden.
5. Wear walking shoes and arrive at the garden gate early with your confirmation.
6. Pair it with Bukchon on the same morning.

Book it that way and you give yourself the best odds of seeing the most beautiful spot in Seoul's palaces, instead of gambling at the ticket window.

faq.question: How much does the Changdeokgung Secret Garden cost?
faq.answer: The Secret Garden ticket is 5,000 won for adults and 2,500 won for ages 7 to 18. You also need a palace admission ticket, which is 3,000 won for adults, because the garden is reached through the palace grounds.

faq.question: How far in advance can I book the Secret Garden?
faq.answer: Online booking opens at 10 a.m. Korea time, six days before your visit date. Half of each session's 100 places are sold online and half on site on the day.

faq.question: Can I visit the Secret Garden without a guide?
faq.answer: No. Visits are guided group sessions at set times, and you follow the route with the guide. English sessions are available at fixed times that change by season.

Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival: ice fi.title: Hwacheon Ice Festival 2027 Trout Fishing Guide From Seoul
Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival: ice fi.description: Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival 2027 guide: dates, ice fishing fees and vouchers, grilling your trout, and how to get there from Seoul by bus or tour.
Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival: ice fi.image_query: hwacheon sancheoneo ice festival ice fishing korea
Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival: ice fi.body:
Every January, a frozen stretch of Hwacheoncheon Stream in Gangwon Province fills with thousands of people crouched over small holes in the ice, jigging short rods and waiting for a sancheoneo (산천어), a trout raised in cold, clean mountain water. This is the Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival, which CNN listed among its "Seven Wonders of Winter" in 2011 and which drew more than 1.86 million visitors in 2025, about 122,000 of them from abroad. It is a fun day out, but it rewards planning. Below are the six things that decide how your day goes: the dates, the ticket, the fishing itself, eating your catch, getting there from Seoul, and staying warm and safe on the ice.

## 1. The 2027 dates, and why they can move

The 2027 festival is listed by the Korea Tourism Organization's festival database for **January 9 to January 31, 2027**, but that listing says its details are still based on the 2026 edition and will be updated. Treat the dates as planned rather than guaranteed. For comparison, the 2026 festival ran 23 days, from January 10 to February 1.

The dates can move because everything depends on the ice. In 2020, unseasonably warm weather delayed the opening twice: it was scheduled for January 4 and only opened on January 27, once the ice reached the roughly 20 centimeters organizers needed. Hwacheon County says it controls water flow from an upstream spillway, checks ice thickness continuously, runs daily underwater inspections and CCTV, and maintains the ice every night. If the ice is not safe, the fishing grounds stay closed. Check the official site, narafestival.com, or the festival line at 1688-3005 the day before you travel, especially during a mild spell.

## 2. How the ticket and voucher system works

The fee is for the ice fishing program, not for entering the town. Here is how it worked in **2026**, the most recent edition:

- **15,000 won** for general visitors from middle school age up.
- **10,000 won** for foreign tourists holding a foreign passport, the same reduced rate given to elementary students, people aged 65 and over, and a few other groups. Bring your passport as proof.
- **Free** for children younger than elementary school age, when accompanied by a guardian.
- Paying adults received a **5,000-won voucher** for local farm products, usable at the festival grounds. In effect, part of your fee comes back as Hwacheon produce or snacks.

Tickets came two ways. Online reservations were capped at 4,000 people a day: you paid in advance and swapped your booking for a wristband on site. On-site registration took up to 8,000 people a day, first come, first served, and could sell out early on weekends. Registration opened at 8:30 a.m. on weekdays and 7 a.m. on weekends.

The 2027 prices are **not final**. In October 2026 the county said it was reviewing a rise in the adult fee to about 25,000 won, with the returned value growing to about 15,000 won in farm-product vouchers and Hwacheon Sarang gift certificates, so the real out-of-pocket cost would stay roughly the same. Confirm the final numbers on narafestival.com before you book.

## 3. The fishing, and what else there is to do

**Ice fishing** is the main event. Daytime fishing in 2026 ran from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays and from 8:30 a.m. on weekends. Night fishing ran from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m., with registration from 6:30 p.m. Some areas were reservation-only and others were for on-site ticket holders. In 2026 the festival also set aside **fishing spots and rest areas reserved for foreign visitors**, which take some of the pressure off on crowded weekends.

**Bare-hand catching** is the event you see on the news: participants in festival T-shirts and shorts wade into a cold pool and grab trout by hand. It is a separate program from ice fishing, with its own sign-up, so check its fee and session times on the official site.

Beyond fishing, the 2026 program included sledding on a 40-meter snow slope and a 60-meter ice track, traditional Korean ice sleds, an ice bobsleigh, ice soccer, curling, a zipline, an indoor ice-sculpture plaza made with Harbin ice lantern makers, and the lantern-lit Seondeung Street night festival on weekends. Some of these have extra fees.

## 4. Eating the trout you catch

You can take your trout to the festival's cooking areas, where it is grilled or served as raw slices. Grilled sancheoneo is the classic way to end the day, and one fish makes a good snack. Expect a cooking charge and a queue at lunchtime. Many vendors deal in cash, so bring some won. Note one rule: tents, stoves and gas equipment are not allowed on the ice, so you cannot cook your catch yourself on the river.

## 5. Getting there from Seoul

Hwacheon is about 90 km northeast of Seoul and about 25 km south of the inter-Korean border. The festival grounds are at 137 Sancheoneo-gil, Hwacheon-eup, close to the town center.

**Intercity bus.** Intercity buses from Dong Seoul Bus Terminal (Gangbyeon Station, Line 2) take roughly 2.5 to 3.5 hours to Hwacheon, depending on the route and traffic, so check the timetable before you go. Buy a return seat early for weekend afternoons, because the trip back to Seoul fills up. You can top up your [T-money card](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-t-money-transit-card.html) for the subway leg, though intercity tickets are bought separately.

**Day tours and shuttles.** Several operators run day trips that bundle round-trip transport, the fishing ticket and rod rental. One 2027 tour listed for January 9 to 31 picks up at Hongik University Station Exit 4 (6:30 a.m.), near Myeongdong (6:50 a.m.) and Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station Exit 10 (7 a.m.), leaves Hwacheon around 4 p.m. and is back in Seoul around 6:30 to 7:10 p.m. Read the refund terms. Some tours promise a full refund if warm weather cancels or postpones the festival, while others become non-refundable a day before departure.

If you also want to ski that week, our guide to [skiing near Seoul without a car](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-skiing-near-seoul-without-a-car-konjiam-elysian-gangchon-and-shuttle-buses.html) covers the shuttle buses to Gangwon resorts.

## 6. What to wear and how to stay safe

You will sit or stand still on ice for hours, which feels much colder than walking around Seoul. Wear thermal base layers, waterproof boots with warm socks, gloves you can fish in, and a hat. Pack disposable hand warmers. Our [seasonal packing and weather guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seasonal-packing-weather-tips.html) covers what a Korean January actually feels like.

On the ice, stay inside the marked fishing zones. Do not walk onto unmarked parts of the stream, and leave if staff close an area. Weekdays are calmer than weekends, so a Tuesday or Wednesday visit means shorter queues for tickets and grilling.

## Your Hwacheon checklist

1. Check narafestival.com for confirmed 2027 dates and the final fee, and call 1688-3005 if the weather has been mild.
2. Decide on a tour or the bus. For a tour, read the warm-weather refund rule. For the bus, book a return seat from Dong Seoul.
3. Book online if you can. Otherwise arrive before registration opens: 7 a.m. on weekends, 8:30 a.m. on weekdays in 2026.
4. Pack your passport for the foreign-visitor rate, and cash for grilling and food stalls.
5. Dress in thermal layers, waterproof boots and gloves, and carry hand warmers.
6. Spend your farm-product voucher before you leave the grounds.
7. Pick a weekday if you can, and stay inside the marked zones on the ice.

faq.question: When is the Hwacheon Sancheoneo Ice Festival in 2027?
faq.answer: It is listed for January 9 to January 31, 2027, but the listing is still based on 2026 details. The festival depends on the ice reaching about 20 cm, and warm weather has delayed it before. In 2020 the opening moved from January 4 to January 27. Check narafestival.com before you go.

faq.question: How much does ice fishing cost for foreigners?
faq.answer: In 2026 the ice fishing ticket was 15,000 won for general visitors and 10,000 won for foreign tourists with a foreign passport. Paying adults got back a 5,000-won farm-product voucher. For 2027 the county is reviewing an adult fee of about 25,000 won with about 15,000 won returned in vouchers, so confirm the final price on the official site.

faq.question: How do I get to Hwacheon from Seoul?
faq.answer: Intercity buses from Dong Seoul Bus Terminal take roughly 2.5 to 3.5 hours to Hwacheon, and the festival grounds are close to the town center. Day tours also run from Hongik University, Myeongdong and Dongdaemun with transport, the fishing ticket and rod rental included. They leave Hwacheon around 4 p.m. and reach Seoul around 6:30 to 7:10 p.m.

Christmas in Korea: a couples' holiday,.title: Christmas in Korea for Couples, Lights and What Opens Dec 25
Christmas in Korea: a couples' holiday,.description: Christmas in Korea is a public holiday built for dates, not family dinners. Where the 2026 lights are, why to pre-order cake, and what opens on Dec 25.
Christmas in Korea: a couples' holiday,.image_query: shinsegae department store myeongdong christmas media facade seoul
Christmas in Korea: a couples' holiday,.body:
If you're in Korea over Christmas, the day will feel familiar and strange at once. December 25 is a national public holiday, the streets are full of lights and carols, and every bakery window is stacked with cakes. But the people filling Myeongdong on Christmas Eve are mostly couples on a date, not families heading home for dinner. This guide covers why Christmas works that way here, which light displays to plan around, the two bookings you should make weeks ahead, and exactly what is open on Friday, December 25, 2026.

## Why Christmas in Korea is a date night

Christmas has been a legal holiday in South Korea since the US military government period of 1945 to 1948, and Korea is often described as the only East Asian country to make it one. Most Koreans aren't Christian, though. As of January 2024, about 63% of Koreans said they had no religion, with Protestants at about 17% and Catholics at about 8%. So for most people the day is secular.

History pushed it toward romance. Under the nationwide night curfew that ran from 1945 to 1982, Christmas Eve was one of the few nights people could stay out freely, and it became the night couples went out. Today Korean and foreign media compare it to Valentine's Day with Santa added. The big family holidays are Seollal and Chuseok, each three days long. Christmas is a single day, and for many people it's about a partner or friends rather than relatives.

What that means for you: Christmas Eve, which falls on a Thursday in 2026, is the crunch night. Romantic restaurants, hotel rooms and photo spots are busiest on the 24th and the evening of the 25th, not over a long family lunch.

## Book these two things early: dinner and cake

**Restaurant tables.** In 2024, fine-dining places such as Gortz showed as fully booked for December 24 and 25 on the Catch Table app by mid-December, and restaurants at N Seoul Tower reported full houses on Christmas Eve. Hotels with rooms left were reported to at least double their Christmas Eve rates. If you want a specific restaurant on the 24th, book as soon as its December slots open. Our guide to [reserving restaurants with Catch Table, Naver and Tabling](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-reserving-restaurants-and-joining-waitlists-in-korea-catch-table-naver-booking-and-the-tabling-tablet.html) explains how the apps work for foreign visitors. Casual places, chicken shops and Korean barbecue are much easier, so you can always fall back on those.

**Christmas cake.** Buying a whole decorated cake is the one Christmas ritual almost everyone shares, and it runs on pre-orders. Paris Baguette, Korea's largest bakery chain, opened 2026 pre-orders on November 11. They run until December 19, with pickup at your chosen store from December 21 to 25. Discounts reach up to 30% through its own Paba app and up to 20% through Kakao gift and reservation channels. Hotel and cafe cakes are the status version. In 2024, the Starbucks Korea and Josun Hotels tree cake cost 89,000 won and sold out 13 minutes after pre-orders opened. At the other end, convenience stores sell mini cakes, with GS25's at 7,500 won that year. If you walk into a bakery on the afternoon of the 24th without a reservation, expect the popular designs to be gone.

## The light displays and what's confirmed for 2026

**Shinsegae Department Store main building, Myeongdong.** The giant LED wall on the main store, called Shinsegae Square, is Seoul's most photographed Christmas screen. In 2025 it covered about 1,354 square meters. The 2026 Christmas film went live on November 6, 2026 and runs daily from 5 p.m. to midnight until January 31, 2027. The 3-minute-40-second story follows a bear delivering Christmas wish letters, scored with Beethoven's Ninth played by a 60-piece orchestra. The best view is from across the road in front of Seoul Central Post Office. On Christmas Day 2025, crowds there spilled onto nearby roads around the 5 p.m. show, so arrive a little early or come on a weeknight before the 24th.

**Lotte Department Store main store, Sogong-dong.** Lotte's 2026 theme, Lotte Town Dream Light Garden, switched on October 30, 2026. It has about 20,000 bulbs on the building's exterior, a light street of roughly 100 meters leading from Euljiro 1-ga Station, and a 15-meter "Heart Light Tree" hung with heart-shaped lights. Lotte has also announced a new 1,614-square-meter media facade called Lotte Town Light on the Young Plaza building, to start during the December 2026 Christmas season. No exact switch-on date was published at the time of writing, so check before you go. Both department stores are a short walk from the shops covered in our [Myeongdong shopping guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-myeongdong-shopping-district.html).

**Lotte World Park, Jamsil.** The 2026 Lotte Town Christmas Market runs on the outdoor lawn from November 19, 2026 to January 3, 2027. General entry is free, and a light and video show plays on the hour from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.

**The Hyundai Seoul, Yeouido.** Hyundai's 2026 theme is Christmas in New York City. A village of 13 brick buildings up to 10 meters tall opened on the 5th floor on November 10. Entry is by advance reservation, through the Hyundai app or Klook for overseas visitors, or by joining a same-day on-site waitlist via QR codes in the store. It runs until December 31, and waits can be long near Christmas.

**Seoul Winter Festa: Gwanghwamun and Cheonggyecheon.** For 2026, the Seoul Lantern Festival runs along Cheonggyecheon (Cheonggye Plaza to Samil Bridge) from December 11, 2026 to January 31, 2027, 6 p.m. to 11 p.m., free, and the Gwanghwamun Market is announced for December 11, 2026 to January 10, 2027. Check the city's festival site for program details before you go. For a sense of the crowds, here's last year: in 2025 the Winter Festa ran from December 12 to January 4. Gwanghwamun Square became a Santa-village market with a 15-meter tree and a carousel. The Seoul Lantern Festival lit Cheonggyecheon stream from Cheonggye Plaza to Samil Bridge from 6 p.m., with closing time pushed from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m. mid-run. It drew a record 2.77 million visitors in its first 20 days. On Christmas night 2025, the wait to enter the Gwanghwamun market topped an hour, with the line reaching Exit 9 of Gwanghwamun Station and a wind chill of minus 8°C.

**Myeongdong Cathedral.** The cathedral puts up a large outdoor tree and becomes a gathering point at Christmas. In 2025 the Seoul archdiocese held a Christmas Day Mass at noon, and afterward about 20 holiday booths opened in front of the Catholic Center selling rosaries, candles, stained glass and roasted chestnuts. Mass schedules change yearly, so check the cathedral's notice if you plan to attend.

## What's open on Friday, December 25, 2026

**Palaces: all open.** Palaces close on a fixed weekly day, not on holidays. Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo close on Tuesdays. Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung close on Mondays. Christmas 2026 is a Friday, so every palace keeps normal hours. Christmas isn't a free-entry day, though. The holiday free entry applies at Seollal and Chuseok. Winter closing times are earlier, and ticket sales at Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung stop an hour before closing.

**Department stores and the big displays: open.** The Myeongdong department stores trade on Christmas Day, and the facade shows run every evening. On Christmas afternoon 2025, Myeongdong was busy enough that police and staff with whistles were directing pedestrian flow.

**Closed: banks, government offices and post offices.** They follow the public-holiday calendar, and so does any errand that needs one. Do your currency exchange at a private money changer or use an ATM instead.

**Transit: running, on the holiday timetable.** The subway and buses run on December 25 but follow the weekend and holiday timetable, with longer gaps between trains. Because the 25th is a Friday, it also creates a three-day weekend for Koreans, so trains out of Seoul on Friday morning and back on Sunday evening are busier than a normal weekend.

For New Year's Eve plans, the Bosingak bell and first-sunrise trips have their own [New Year's Eve guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-new-year-s-eve-in-korea-the-bosingak-bell-late-subways-and-first-sunrise-spots.html).

## Your Christmas-in-Korea action list

1. **Now:** pre-order a Christmas cake if you want one. Paris Baguette takes orders until December 19, with pickup December 21 to 25.
2. **As soon as December slots open:** book Christmas Eve dinner on Catch Table or Naver. Have a casual backup in mind.
3. **Any weeknight before December 24:** see the Shinsegae screen (5 p.m. to midnight) and Lotte's light street together. They're a short walk apart.
4. **From December 11:** plan a Gwanghwamun or Cheonggyecheon night between then and the holiday, and expect hour-long queues on the 24th and 25th.
5. **If you want The Hyundai Seoul's Christmas village:** reserve a slot ahead if you can, because reservation rounds sell out fast and the on-site waitlist can be long near Christmas.
6. **For December 25:** plan a palace morning (all are open), then department stores and lights after dark. Change money before the holiday, and dress for temperatures below zero.

faq.question: Is Christmas a public holiday in South Korea?
faq.answer: Yes. December 25 has been a legal holiday since the US military government period of 1945 to 1948, so banks, government offices and post offices close. In 2026 it falls on a Friday.

faq.question: Are Seoul palaces open on Christmas Day 2026?
faq.answer: Yes. Palaces close on a fixed weekly day: Tuesday for Gyeongbokgung and Jongmyo, and Monday for Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung. December 25, 2026 is a Friday, so all of them open at normal hours. It is not a free-entry day.

faq.question: When does the Shinsegae Christmas media facade in Myeongdong run?
faq.answer: The 2026 Christmas film plays daily from 5 p.m. to midnight on the Shinsegae Department Store main building, from November 6, 2026 to January 31, 2027. The best view is from in front of Seoul Central Post Office across the road.

Gyeongju from Seoul: the KTX, the bus to.title: Gyeongju from Seoul by KTX - Buses to Bulguksa and Tombs
Gyeongju from Seoul: the KTX, the bus to.description: Take the KTX to Gyeongju Station (once Singyeongju), ride buses 10, 11 and 12 to Bulguksa and Seokguram, then see the tomb park and Wolji Pond at night.
Gyeongju from Seoul: the KTX, the bus to.body:
Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for close to a thousand years, and it still looks the part: grassy royal burial mounds sit right in the middle of town, a 7th-century stone observatory stands in a field, and two of Korea's best-known Buddhist sites sit on a mountainside to the southeast. From Seoul it is a little over two hours by KTX, which makes it doable as a long day trip. The catch is that the high-speed station is nowhere near the sights, the buses to the temples are a separate puzzle, and the tombs are spread across several sites with different rules. This guide covers all three: the train, the buses to Bulguksa and Seokguram, and the order to see the tombs in.

## Step one: the KTX, and the station name that changed

KTX trains leave Seoul Station for Gyeongju in about 2 hours 10 minutes, with a standard adult fare of roughly 45,000 to 49,300 won depending on the train and day (check Korail for the exact price). If you are staying in southern Seoul, the SRT from Suseo Station also stops there and takes a similar time. Our [KTX vs SRT comparison](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-ktx-vs-srt-vs-intercity-bus-for-long-distance-travel.html) explains which one is easier to book from where you're staying.

The name is where most people get confused. The high-speed station opened in 2010 as **Singyeongju Station** ("new Gyeongju"). The old downtown Gyeongju Station closed in December 2021 when the Donghae line was rerouted, and on December 28, 2023 Singyeongju was officially renamed **Gyeongju Station**. Older blogs, maps and guidebooks still say Singyeongju. It is the same place. When you book on Korail, search for "Gyeongju" (경주).

What matters more is location. The station is in Geoncheon-eup, west of the city, not in the historic center, so you need a bus or taxi either way.

## Getting from Gyeongju Station into town

City buses leave from the stop outside the station. Board at the front and tap a T-money or other Korean transit card on the reader. The routes you need:

- **Buses 60 and 61:** to the downtown historic area around Cheonmachong, Hwangnidan-gil and Cheomseongdae. It takes about 20 to 30 minutes depending on the stop.
- **Buses 50, 51, 70 and 710:** to the Gyeongju Express and Intercity Bus Terminal, about 18 minutes. The terminal is roughly 700 to 800 meters from Daereungwon, and it is where the main tourist bus loop begins.
- **Bus 711:** a direct but infrequent route from the station through the terminal, past Hwangnidan-gil and the Cheonmachong rear gate, and on to Bulguksa, about 47 minutes to the temple.
- **Bus 700:** another infrequent direct route to Bulguksa that also passes the bus terminal and Donggung Palace, then continues through the Bomun Lake resort area, about 55 minutes.

Buses 700 and 711 run only a handful of times a day. Check the next departure in Naver Map or KakaoMap before you rely on them. For how tagging on and off and transfers work, see our guide to [city buses in Korea](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-bus-travel-inside-korean-cities-color-codes-tag-off-transfers-and-why-you-must-flag-the-bus.html).

## Bulguksa and Seokguram: buses 10, 11 and 12

Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto were inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995. They are about 15 kilometers from downtown, so you'll need a bus.

- **Buses 10 and 11** run the same loop in opposite directions. Both connect the bus terminal and downtown with Gyeongju National Museum, Bomun Lake and Bulguksa. From the downtown side, plan on about half an hour to the temple.
- **Bus 12** goes uphill from Bulguksa to the Seokguram parking lot in about 15 to 20 minutes. It runs infrequently, so look up the return time as soon as you arrive. From the parking lot it is a short walk to the grotto.

Both temples became free to enter in May 2023, when the government started covering the cultural-heritage admission fees that Buddhist temples used to charge. Bulguksa and Seokguram both open around 9 a.m., with last entry about an hour before closing. Hours shift with the season, so check before you go. Inside Seokguram the Buddha statue is behind glass and photography is not allowed.

Go to the temples first, in the morning. They close earliest of anything on this list, and the downtown sites stay open late into the evening.

## Which tombs to see first

Gyeongju has more than one tomb park, and they have different rules. Here is the order that works on foot.

**1. Daereungwon and Cheonmachong.** Daereungwon is the walled park of 23 large Silla mounds in the middle of town. Entry to the park itself has been free since 2023. The one paid part is **Cheonmachong**, the only tomb you can walk inside. Tickets are 3,000 won for adults, 2,000 won for teens and 1,000 won for children. Excavated in 1973, it is where the famous painted "heavenly horse" saddle flap and a gold crown were found, and inside you can see a cross-section of how the tomb was built. The main gate is open 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. (last entry 9:30 p.m.), and Cheonmachong and the rear gate close at 9:30 p.m. If you only go inside one tomb, make it this one.

**2. Hwangnidan-gil.** About 150 meters from the Cheonmachong rear gate, this street of hanok cafés, bakeries and small shops is where most people stop for lunch or coffee.

**3. Cheomseongdae.** About 670 meters on foot from the center of Daereungwon, this stone tower is often called the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia. Entry is free, and it's open 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. in summer and until 9 p.m. in winter. The open fields around it, dotted with more mounds, are the easiest place to walk among the tombs without a fence.

**4. Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond.** About 890 meters past Cheomseongdae, this restored Silla detached palace is best after dark, when the pavilions are lit and reflected in the water. Admission is 3,000 won for adults, 2,000 won for teens and 1,000 won for children. It's open until 10 p.m. with last entry at 9:30 p.m. Arrive around sunset, and expect crowds on weekend evenings.

This walk, from Daereungwon to Donggung, is about two kilometers in total.

## Bikes, taxis and the timing question

The downtown sites are flat and close together, so many visitors rent a bicycle. Rental shops cluster near Daereungwon and the bus terminal and charge by the hour, and prices vary by shop. A bike works well for the tomb-and-pond circuit. Riding to Bulguksa is a different matter: it's around 15 kilometers each way with traffic, and the bus is easier.

**Day trip or overnight?** A day trip from Seoul is realistic if you take an early KTX. Spend the morning at Bulguksa and Seokguram, do the tombs in the afternoon, and finish at Wolji Pond at dusk before a late train back. If you're traveling by regular train elsewhere on your trip, our guide to [day trips from Seoul by regular train](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-day-tripping-from-seoul-by-regular-train-mugunghwa-itx-saemaeul-and-the-gyeongui-jungang-line.html) covers the slower lines. But Wolji Pond at night and the last KTX back don't leave much margin. Staying one night, near Hwangnidan-gil or at Bomun Lake, lets you see the pond lit up without watching the clock and catch Bulguksa the next morning before the tour buses.

## Your Gyeongju plan, step by step

1. Book a morning KTX from Seoul Station (or an SRT from Suseo) to **Gyeongju Station**, the former Singyeongju.
2. Check the next bus 711 or 700 departure. If one is soon, ride straight to Bulguksa. If not, take bus 50, 51, 70 or 710 to the bus terminal and switch to bus 10 or 11.
3. Visit Bulguksa, then take bus 12 up to Seokguram. Note the return bus time when you arrive. Both temples are free.
4. Ride bus 10 or 11 back downtown.
5. Walk Daereungwon (free) and pay 3,000 won to go inside Cheonmachong.
6. Eat on Hwangnidan-gil, about 150 meters from the rear gate.
7. Walk or bike to Cheomseongdae (free), then on to Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond (3,000 won) for sunset and the lights.
8. Take bus 60 or 61, or a taxi, back to Gyeongju Station for your train, or stay the night and keep the next morning free.

faq.question: Is Singyeongju Station the same as Gyeongju Station?
faq.answer: Yes. The KTX station opened as Singyeongju in 2010 and was renamed Gyeongju Station on December 28, 2023, two years after the old downtown Gyeongju Station closed. It's west of the city center, so you need a bus or taxi to reach the sights.

faq.question: Which bus goes from Gyeongju to Bulguksa and Seokguram?
faq.answer: Buses 10 and 11 run between the bus terminal, downtown and Bulguksa in opposite directions. Buses 711 and 700 run directly from Gyeongju Station but only a few times a day. Bus 12 goes from Bulguksa up to the Seokguram parking lot in about 15 to 20 minutes.

faq.question: Do you have to pay to see the tombs in Gyeongju?
faq.answer: Entry to Daereungwon is free, and so is the area around Cheomseongdae. The one paid tomb is Cheonmachong, which you can walk inside, at 3,000 won for adults. Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond also cost 3,000 won, while Bulguksa and Seokguram have been free since May 2023.
