Ttareungyi, Seoul's public bike: buying.title: Ttareungyi Seoul Bike Pass for Visitors and Han River Rides
Ttareungyi, Seoul's public bike: buying.description: How foreign visitors buy a Ttareungyi day pass with an overseas card, unlock and return Seoul Bike, avoid overtime fees and ride the Han River paths.
Ttareungyi, Seoul's public bike: buying.body:
Along the Han River in Seoul you'll see rows of green-and-white bikes parked at small docking stations. That's Ttareungyi (따릉이), the city's public bike, officially called Seoul Bike. A day pass costs about the same as a convenience-store coffee, and the riverside paths are among the best ways to see the city at ground level. The catch for visitors is the buying step: the pass system for foreigners is different from the one locals use, and a few details trip people up. This guide covers how to buy the pass, unlock and return a bike, what overtime costs, and which Han River stretches are worth riding, including what changes in late autumn and winter.

## What Ttareungyi is

Ttareungyi is an unmanned public bike-sharing service run for the Seoul Metropolitan Government by the Seoul Facilities Corporation. It launched in October 2015 and is open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, to anyone aged 13 or older. You rent a bike at one station and return it at any station in the city, not necessarily the one you started from. Stations sit near subway exits, bus stops and inside the Han River parks.

There are two bike sizes. The standard bike has dark green wheels and a larger frame. The smaller, lighter "Saesak" (새싹) Ttareungyi has light green wheels and suits teenagers and shorter riders. Both have three gears: first for hills, second for flat ground, third for faster flat riding. The front basket fits a day bag.

## Buying a pass as a foreign visitor

Short-term visitors don't sign up the way residents do. According to the Seoul Facilities Corporation's own FAQ, you buy a dedicated foreigner pass in one of two ways:

- **On the Ttareungyi website (bikeseoul.com):** choose English, Chinese or Japanese as the language, then buy the foreigner pass.
- **In the Ttareungyi app:** on the first screen, choose the foreigner option, then buy the pass.

Two payment rules matter. First, the foreigner pass must be paid with a **credit card issued overseas**. Second, each card can buy only **one** pass, so a couple sharing one card will need a second card for the second bike. Foreign residents with a Korean phone number can instead join as regular members, the same way Korean nationals do.

The day pass comes in 1-hour (**1,000 won**), 2-hour (**2,000 won**) and, since November 2025, 3-hour (**3,000 won**) versions. Check in the app whether the 3-hour option is offered on the foreigner pass. The hour count is the length of a single ride, not of your whole day: return the bike to a station before the time runs out, then rent again. If you've already bought a Discover Seoul Pass, it can also be used for Ttareungyi; follow the pass's own instructions for linking it in the Ttareungyi app.

You'll need mobile data for the app, because renting uses your phone's camera, Bluetooth and GPS. If you haven't sorted that yet, see our [eSIM and mobile data guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-esim-mobile-data.html).

## Overtime charges

Overtime is where small mistakes turn into charges. If you keep the bike past your base time (1, 2 or 3 hours), you pay **200 won for every 5 minutes** over, charged automatically to the card you used for the pass. Twenty minutes over on a 1-hour pass adds 800 won. That's small, but it adds up on a long, slow river ride. You can't rent again until any unpaid extra fee is settled.

The way to avoid it is simple. On a long ride, pull into a station before your time is up, return the bike, wait for the return notification, then rent again. You can check your rental and return history in the app.

## Unlocking a bike

Most bikes now use a QR terminal on the rear wheel. The official steps are:

1. Open the Ttareungyi app and tap the rental button.
2. Scan the QR code on the bike's terminal. If it won't scan, enter the 5-digit bike number printed beside the right pedal.
3. The lock opens automatically, and the rental is complete.

If it doesn't work, the corporation's FAQ suggests turning on Bluetooth and GPS, disconnecting earbuds or a smartwatch (other paired devices can block the rental) and checking that the app has camera permission. Before riding off, squeeze both brakes and set the saddle height. On newer bikes you lift the black lever, adjust, and press it down. On older bikes you pull the silver lever outward.

## Returning a bike properly

A bike isn't returned just because you park it near a station. To return it:

1. Ride to any Ttareungyi station.
2. Park the bike at the rack and pull the rear-wheel lock until it's fully closed.
3. Wait for the return confirmation by app notification, KakaoTalk message or text. Don't walk away before it arrives: until the return is registered, the rental and its overtime clock keep running.

If every rack is full, stand the bike as close to the racks as you can and lock it. Keep it off the yellow tactile paving and out of the way of pedestrians. If no confirmation arrives, the lock may not have closed fully or the network may have failed. Call the Ttareungyi call center on 1599-0120. Locking the bike somewhere other than a station only pauses it and doesn't end the rental. Your clock keeps running, and the app's temporary-unlock function lets you continue the ride.

## Helmets and insurance

Korea's Road Traffic Act has required cyclists to wear a helmet since September 28, 2018. When the rule took effect, it came with no penalty for adult riders, and that's why most people riding Ttareungyi along the river go without one. If you want a helmet, bring your own. Don't count on finding one at a station.

Ttareungyi users are covered by a policy the city arranges with DB Insurance. It applies from the moment your rental completes until the return process begins. It covers medical expenses up to 3 million won (you pay the first 100,000 won, and only treatment within a year of the accident counts), liability for injuring someone or damaging their property up to 2 million won (also with a 100,000 won deductible), and accidental death or permanent disability up to 20 million won. Terms are renewed each year, so confirm the current limits with the call center or on bikeseoul.com. Death cover doesn't apply to riders under 15. Accidents during normal use are claimed directly with DB Insurance on 02-1899-7751 (check its opening hours before calling). Claims about a defective bike go through the Seoul Facilities Corporation on 1599-0120. The policy names Ttareungyi users as the insured but doesn't specifically mention nationality, so check with the call center if you're relying on it.

## Han River stretches worth riding

The Han River parks have continuous bike paths on both banks, and Seoul asks riders to keep to **20 km/h** on them. AI cameras and speed displays at busy points such as Ttukseom and Jamsil show green at or below that speed and red above it. Pedestrians cross the paths often at Yeouido, Ttukseom, Banpo and Nanji, which have raised crosswalks.

- **Yeouido Hangang Park:** the most popular start. It's flat and wide, with views of the National Assembly and the 63 Building and plenty of stations. It's also busy on weekend afternoons.
- **Banpo Hangang Park:** home to the Banpo Bridge Moonlight Rainbow Fountain and Sebitseom, the floating islands. The fountain runs seasonally, so in winter don't plan your ride around it.
- **Ttukseom Hangang Park:** on the north-east side, popular with cyclists and easy to pair with Seoul Forest nearby.
- **Mangwon to Nanji:** quieter, with Mangwon's riverside park and the Nanji Ecological Wetland further west.

For a full day, Seoul's official media outlet suggests the loop from Jamsugyo Bridge to Haengjudaegyo Bridge, crossing both banks, at about 50 km. At 20 km/h that's around 150 minutes of riding, more than a 2-hour pass allows, so either dock and re-rent along the way or, if the app offers it to you, choose the 3-hour pass. To find stations and the parks' subway exits, the map apps in our [best travel apps guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-useful-travel-apps.html) work better than Google Maps here.

## Riding in late November and winter

Ttareungyi doesn't close for winter, but the conditions change. It gets dark before about 5:30 p.m. in late November and December, and the wind off the river is noticeably colder than in the streets. Phone batteries drain faster in the cold, and your phone is your key for both renting and confirming the return, so start with a full charge. Gloves make a real difference on metal handlebars. After rain or snow, shaded underpass sections can stay icy, so slow down there. For what to wear, see our [seasonal packing guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seasonal-packing-weather-tips.html).

## Your Ttareungyi checklist

1. Install the Ttareungyi app and make sure you have mobile data before you go to the river.
2. Have an overseas-issued credit card ready, one card per pass, or use a Discover Seoul Pass.
3. Choose the foreigner option and buy a 1-hour (1,000 won) or 2-hour (2,000 won) pass, or a 3-hour (3,000 won) pass if the app offers it.
4. Turn on Bluetooth, GPS and camera permission, and disconnect your earbuds if the rental fails.
5. Scan the rear-wheel QR code, or type the 5-digit number by the right pedal.
6. Check the brakes and saddle, then keep to 20 km/h on the river paths.
7. Dock and re-rent before your time runs out to avoid the 200-won-per-5-minutes charge.
8. Pull the rear lock fully closed and wait for the return message before you leave.
9. Save 1599-0120 for problems, and in winter finish before dark with your phone charged.

faq.question: Can a foreign tourist pay for Ttareungyi with a foreign credit card?
faq.answer: Yes. According to the Seoul Facilities Corporation, the foreigner pass is bought on bikeseoul.com (in English, Chinese or Japanese) or in the app after choosing the foreigner option. It must be paid with an overseas-issued credit card, and each card can buy only one pass. A Discover Seoul Pass can be used instead.

faq.question: How much does a Seoul Bike day pass cost and what if I ride too long?
faq.answer: The day pass costs 1,000 won for 1 hour and 2,000 won for 2 hours, and a 3-hour version (3,000 won) has been sold since November 2025, though you should check in the app whether it is offered on the foreigner pass. The time is per ride. Going past it costs 200 won for every 5 minutes, charged to your card, so on a long ride, return the bike at a station and rent again before your time runs out.

faq.question: How do I know my Ttareungyi bike has been returned?
faq.answer: Park it at any station rack, pull the rear-wheel lock until it is fully closed, and wait for the return confirmation by app notification, KakaoTalk or text. If no message arrives, the lock may not be fully closed. Call 1599-0120, because the rental and its overtime clock keep running until the return is registered.

Seoul Winter Festival 2026: Cheonggyeche.title: Seoul Winter Festival 2026 Guide to Lanterns, Market, Rink
Seoul Winter Festival 2026: Cheonggyeche.description: Seoul Winter Festival 2026 runs Dec 11 to Jan 31. Dates, hours and prices for the free Cheonggyecheon lanterns, Gwanghwamun market and Seoul Plaza ice rink.
Seoul Winter Festival 2026: Cheonggyeche.body:
Walk out of Exit 5 of Gwanghwamun Station on a December evening and you'll see a strip of light running east along Cheonggyecheon stream, a lit-up market on Gwanghwamun Square and, a few minutes south, skaters circling the ice in front of Seoul City Hall. All of it belongs to one city-run event. For 2026 it has a new name, the Seoul Winter Festival (서울윈터페스티벌), with the theme "Fantasia Seoul". Until last year it was called Seoul Winter Festa. The city announced the 2026 program on November 25. It runs for 52 days, from December 11, 2026 to January 31, 2027, and for the first time it reaches the Han River.

The program is big, and each part has its own dates. This guide covers each part of the festival, when it runs, what's free, and how to see several in one evening without spending half of it in a queue.

## The festival at a glance

The venues are Gwanghwamun Square, Cheonggyecheon, Seoul Plaza, Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP), Bosingak and, new this year, Ttukseom Hangang Park. The main light events start on Friday, December 11. The opening ceremony follows on Saturday, December 12, at 6 p.m. on Gwanghwamun Square. It has a K-performance contest, a musical gala, a citizen choir and a light parade the audience can join, and it ends with the lighting ceremony for Gwanghwamun and Cheonggyecheon.

| Event | Dates | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Seoul Lantern Festival | Dec 11 – Jan 31 | Cheonggyecheon |
| Seoul Light Gwanghwamun | Dec 11 – Jan 10 | Gwanghwamun Square |
| Gwanghwamun Market | Dec 11 – Jan 10 | Gwanghwamun Square, Sejongno Park |
| Seoul Plaza Ice Rink | Dec 18 – Feb 9 | Seoul Plaza |
| Seoul Light DDP | Dec 11 – Jan 31 | DDP |

There's also a stamp tour. If you visit at least three of the five main events, you get a voucher for local shops. Check the festival's official site for how to collect stamps.

## 1. Seoul Lantern Festival on Cheonggyecheon

This is the free centerpiece of the festival, lit every night for the full 52 days. The Seoul Lantern Festival (서울빛초롱축제) fills about 1.2 km of the stream, from the fountain at Cheonggye Plaza down to Samil Bridge. It's open every evening from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m., from December 11 to January 31. The 2026 theme is "Seoul's Romance: Symphony of Light". The route is split into four zones, each designed differently, and traditional hanji paper lanterns are mixed with media art and character displays.

You walk along the lower path beside the water, so the route goes in one direction and narrows at bridges. Start at Cheonggye Plaza, near Gwanghwamun Station and City Hall Station, and walk east. You can climb up to street level at almost any bridge if you don't want to go the whole way.

Cheonggye Plaza has its own program until December 31. It includes a media wall of messages from the public, artworks by artists with developmental disabilities, and the returning Dream Light Train. A new Dream Light Castle is added this year.

## 2. Seoul Light Gwanghwamun and Gwanghwamun Market

**Seoul Light Gwanghwamun** is a media facade show projected on Gwanghwamun, the main gate of Gyeongbokgung, with light sculptures and wish-making activities on the north side of the square. The theme is "Glimmer, Surface of Time". Seoul's festival listing gives it as December 11 to January 10, from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m. The show cycle isn't out yet, so check the timetable on the day.

**Gwanghwamun Market** runs on the same dates, December 11 to January 10. This year's theme is "Santa Village Where Time Stopped", and the market grows beyond the square to Gamsa Garden and Sejongno Park. It has booths from other countries, stalls run by Namdaemun Market merchants and a Seorojangteo local market. Daily hours for 2026 aren't out yet. Last season the market opened from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m. Our [Christmas guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-christmas-in-korea-a-couples-holiday-light-displays-and-what-stays-open-on-december-25.html) covers how crowded it got on Christmas night and the department-store light displays nearby. In short, avoid December 24 and 25 if you dislike queues.

From January 2 to 3, Gwanghwamun Square hosts a New Year weekend with traditional games and a hanbok runway event.

## 3. Seoul Plaza Ice Rink

The outdoor rink in front of City Hall opens a week after the lights, running from December 18, 2026 to February 9, 2027. At last season's price, it's one of the cheapest ways to skate in Seoul. Last season, a one-hour session cost 1,000 won, and that included skate and helmet rental. Half of the tickets were sold online through the rink's booking site and half on the spot. The 2026 price isn't out yet, so check the booking site before you go.

What's confirmed for 2026 is longer night hours. The rink has transparent outer walls and new lighting. On Fridays and Saturdays it stays open until 12:30 a.m., and on December 24 and December 31 it stays open until 1 a.m. the next morning. Last season's regular hours were 10 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. from Sunday to Friday and 10 a.m. to 11 p.m. on Saturdays and public holidays.

The nearest station is City Hall, on Lines 1 and 2. On a busy weekend, book your session online first. Then walk the lantern route while you wait, because Cheonggye Plaza is only a few minutes away.

## 4. Seoul Light DDP and the year-end events

At DDP in Dongdaemun, **Seoul Light DDP** plays media art across the building from December 11 to January 31. The nearest station is Dongdaemun History & Culture Park, on Lines 2, 4 and 5. DDP also hosts the Winter Hibernation Contest on December 20, with room for 300 participants this year, and SEOULCon, a global influencer expo, from December 29 to January 1.

On December 31, Bosingak, Gwanghwamun Square and DDP share a countdown video with Seoul's mascot Haechi. Bosingak gets a media facade for 2027, the Year of the Red Sheep, and the bell is struck 33 times at midnight. Late trains, road closures and sunrise spots are covered in our [New Year's Eve guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-new-year-s-eve-in-korea-the-bosingak-bell-late-subways-and-first-sunrise-spots.html).

## 5. The new Han River part at Ttukseom

This is the first year the festival reaches the river. From December 24 to 31, Ttukseom Hangang Park hosts the **Han River Night Sauna**, a Finnish-style outdoor sauna looking out over the winter river. There's also a Han River Christmas market with food and activity booths and busking. Sauna prices and booking aren't out yet; check the official site.

## Money-saving extras

- **Night cashback:** Pay with Seoul Love gift cards (서울사랑상품권) in Jongno-gu or Jung-gu between 5 p.m. and midnight and you get 5% back.
- **Show discounts:** A receipt from a local shop in Jongno-gu or Jung-gu gets you 10% off tickets for Sejong Center season performances, Seoul Philharmonic Orchestra concerts and Daehakro Theater Quad.

## A one-evening plan and checklist

1. **Pick your date.** The lantern festival and DDP run until January 31, but the Gwanghwamun light show and market close on January 10, and the rink opens only on December 18. Go between December 18 and January 10 to see all of them.
2. **Avoid the peak nights** of December 24, 25 and 31 unless the crowds are part of the fun.
3. **Book a rink session** online if you're going on a Friday or Saturday.
4. **Start at Gwanghwamun around 5:30 p.m.** for the facade show and the market.
5. **Walk south to Cheonggye Plaza** and follow the lanterns east. They're lit from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m.
6. **Finish at Seoul Plaza** with a late skate. It's open until 12:30 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.
7. **Collect stamps** at three of the five main events for the local shopping voucher.
8. **Dress for standing in the cold.** Wear layers, gloves and a hat, and bring a hot snack from the [winter street food stalls](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-korean-winter-street-food-bungeoppang-hotteok-and-where-the-stalls-went.html).

faq.question: When is the 2026 Seoul Winter Festival?
faq.answer: It runs from December 11, 2026 to January 31, 2027, a total of 52 days. The opening ceremony is on December 12 at 6 p.m. on Gwanghwamun Square. Individual events have their own dates. Gwanghwamun's light show and market run until January 10, and the Seoul Plaza rink runs from December 18 to February 9.

faq.question: Is the Seoul Lantern Festival on Cheonggyecheon free?
faq.answer: Yes. The Seoul Lantern Festival is free and open every evening from 6 p.m. to 11 p.m., from December 11 to January 31. It covers about 1.2 km of Cheonggyecheon, from Cheonggye Plaza to Samil Bridge.

faq.question: How much does the Seoul Plaza ice rink cost?
faq.answer: Last season a one-hour session cost 1,000 won, including skate and helmet rental, with half the tickets sold online and half on site. The 2026 price hadn't been published at the time of writing. This season the rink opens December 18 and stays open until 12:30 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.

Jeonju Hanok Village from Seoul: KTX vs.title: Jeonju Hanok Village from Seoul by KTX or Bus - What to See
Jeonju Hanok Village from Seoul: KTX vs.description: Take the KTX from Yongsan or a bus from Central City, then a city bus from Jeonju Station to Gyeonggijeon, Omokdae, the bibimbap street and hanok stays.
Jeonju Hanok Village from Seoul: KTX vs.body:
When you get off a KTX at Jeonju Station, there are no hanok rooftops anywhere in sight. The station has a hanok-style building, but Jeonju Hanok Village is across town, about 25 minutes away by city bus. Most first-time visitors from Seoul don't realize this until they're on the platform. This guide covers the whole trip in order: train or bus from Seoul, the station-to-village step, the four sights worth your time (Gyeonggijeon Shrine, Jeondong Cathedral, Omokdae and Pungnammun Gate), what to eat on the main street, and whether to do it as a day trip or stay a night in a hanok.

## KTX from Yongsan or express bus from Central City

**By KTX.** Trains to Jeonju run on the Jeolla line, and most leave from **Yongsan Station**, not Seoul Station. The fastest KTX takes about 1 hour 32 minutes, and most take about 1 hour 40 minutes. KTX fares on the Honam and Jeolla lines came down by an average of about 10% on September 1, 2026, when KTX and SRT started operating as one service. A standard adult seat from Yongsan to Jeonju is now about 31,600 won. The slower Mugunghwa costs 17,600 won but takes around 3 hours or more. There are roughly 26 to 31 trains a day from Jeonju back to Yongsan, and the last one leaves Jeonju around 11:10 p.m. Check the Korail app for the exact times on your date. If you're staying in Gangnam, SRT trains from Suseo also run on the Jeolla line. Our [KTX vs SRT vs intercity bus comparison](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-ktx-vs-srt-vs-intercity-bus-for-long-distance-travel.html) covers how to book each one as a visitor.

**By express bus.** Buses to Jeonju leave from the Honam-line side of **Seoul Express Bus Terminal (Central City)** in Gangnam, which is Express Bus Terminal subway station. According to the Jeonju Hanok Village official site, the ride takes about 2 hours 40 minutes. Buses leave very often, roughly every 10 to 20 minutes for most of the day, from about 5:30 a.m. to midnight. Seoul Nambu Terminal also has intercity buses to Jeonju. Buses cost less than the KTX, but they get stuck in highway traffic on Friday evenings, weekends and holidays. A bus does have one real advantage: Jeonju Express Bus Terminal is much closer to the village than the train station.

## The step everyone forgets: getting to the village

Neither the train station nor the bus terminal is in the hanok district. The Jeonju Hanok Village official site lists these connections:

- **From Jeonju Station:** board a city bus at the station stop and get off at **Jeondong Catholic Church (Hanok Village)**. Routes include 79, 101, 112, 119, 508, 536, 542, 545, 546 and 999. The ride takes about 25 minutes. A taxi costs roughly 6,000 to 7,000 won.
- **From Jeonju Express Bus Terminal:** take bus 79, 999 or 1994 from the stop on the terminal side (signed for the Buddhist hall) to the same Jeondong Catholic Church stop. It takes about 15 minutes. A taxi costs roughly 5,000 to 6,000 won.

Tap a transit card when you board and again when you get off, as you would in Seoul. On a weekend morning, a taxi for two or three people often costs about the same as the bus and saves time.

## What to see: four sights in walking order

The village covers about 298,000 square meters. According to the city's figures, it has more than 700 hanok and is the largest hanok district in Korea that sits inside a city center. Unlike [Bukchon in Seoul](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-bukchon-hanok-village.html), where people still live in quiet residential lanes, much of Jeonju's village is shops, cafés, guesthouses and cultural sites. The whole district is non-smoking. The four sights below are all within a short walk of each other.

**1. Jeondong Cathedral.** The bus stop is named after it, so it's usually the first thing you see. This red-brick Romanesque church was built between 1908 and 1914 on the site where Korean Catholics were executed during the Joseon dynasty. Some of its bricks came from Jeonju's demolished city wall. Entry is free, and the official site lists visiting hours as 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., except during Mass. On Sundays there are several morning Masses, so a weekday visit is easier if you want to see the inside. Dress modestly and keep your voice down.

**2. Gyeonggijeon Shrine.** Across the street from the cathedral, this walled shrine was built in 1410 to hold the royal portrait of King Taejo (Yi Seong-gye), who founded the Joseon dynasty. Jeonju was his family's ancestral home. Admission is 3,000 won for adults, 2,000 won for ages 13 to 24 and 1,000 won for ages 7 to 12. The ticket also covers the Royal Portrait Museum inside the grounds. Entry is free on Culture Day, the last Wednesday of each month. From November to February it's open 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with last entry an hour before closing, and it stays open later the rest of the year. One thing to check before you go: the main hall (jeongjeon) has been closed for repainting work that was scheduled to run until mid-December 2026. The rest of the grounds and the museum stayed open during the work.

**3. Omokdae.** Walk east to the end of the main street and up a short slope to this hilltop pavilion. General Yi Seong-gye stopped here to celebrate a victory over Japanese raiders in 1380, a few years before he founded Joseon. It's free, and it has the best view of the village: rows of tiled roofs with the city behind them. Go in the late afternoon, when the light is low.

**4. Pungnammun Gate.** At the western edge of the village, toward Nambu Market, stands the south gate of the old Jeonju walled town. It was rebuilt in 1768 and is designated Treasure No. 308. The town once had four gates, and this is the only one that survived early-20th-century redevelopment. Viewing it from outside is free. Once you've seen the gate, keep walking to Nambu Market.

## Bibimbap and the main-street snack crawl

Jeonju was named a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2012, and Jeonju bibimbap is the dish it's best known for. Specialist restaurants in and around the village serve it in a brass bowl or a hot stone bowl with a spread of side dishes. Jeonju's kongnamul gukbap (bean sprout soup with rice) is the local breakfast and costs much less.

The main street running from the cathedral toward Omokdae is lined with snack stalls. On weekends the queues get long, and the area gets crowded with people walking and eating. On **Friday and Saturday nights from 6:30 to 11 p.m.**, the **Nambu Night Market** sets up just past Pungnammun. According to the official site, stalls sell grilled skewers, samgyeopsal gimbap, meat pancakes, beef sushi and tanghulu. If you're on a day trip, the night market only works if your return train leaves late enough.

## Day trip or a night in a hanok stay?

**Day trip.** With a morning KTX from Yongsan, a day trip works well. Arrive mid-morning, see the cathedral and Gyeonggijeon, eat bibimbap for lunch, walk to Omokdae and Pungnammun in the afternoon, and catch an early-evening train back. The village is compact, so 5 to 6 hours is enough for the main sights. If you're also planning slower rail trips closer to Seoul, see our guide to [day-tripping by regular train](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-day-tripping-from-seoul-by-regular-train-mugunghwa-itx-saemaeul-and-the-gyeongui-jungang-line.html).

**Overnight.** The city counts about 200 places to stay inside the village, and many are hanok guesthouses. Rooms usually have a sleeping mat (yo) on a heated ondol floor rather than a bed. Bathrooms may be shared, and walls are thin, so read the listing details before you book. Staying the night lets you see the lanes after the day-trippers leave, visit the Friday or Saturday night market without watching the clock, and get to Gyeonggijeon at 9 a.m. before the crowds. If you want to rent a hanbok, an overnight stay also gives you a full morning in it. Hanbok rental shops line the main street. Gyeonggijeon gives a 50% discount to visitors wearing hanbok on the fourth Saturday of each month.

## Your Jeonju checklist

1. Book a KTX from **Yongsan** (not Seoul Station) to **Jeonju**, about 1 hour 40 minutes and about 31,600 won. Or take an express bus from Central City, about 2 hours 40 minutes.
2. Note your return time. The last KTX leaves Jeonju around 11:10 p.m.
3. At Jeonju Station, take bus 79, 119, 999 or another listed route to **Jeondong Catholic Church** (about 25 minutes), or a taxi for about 6,000 to 7,000 won.
4. Visit Jeondong Cathedral (free, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., outside Mass times).
5. Visit Gyeonggijeon (3,000 won, museum included). Check whether the main hall has reopened after its repainting.
6. Eat Jeonju bibimbap for lunch, or kongnamul gukbap if you're starting early.
7. Walk up to Omokdae for the rooftop view, then west to Pungnammun.
8. On a Friday or Saturday, stay for the Nambu Night Market (6:30 to 11 p.m.) or book a hanok room so you don't have to rush for the train.

faq.question: Is Jeonju Station within walking distance of the Hanok Village?
faq.answer: No. Jeonju Station is across town. City buses such as 79, 119 and 999 run to the Jeondong Catholic Church (Hanok Village) stop in about 25 minutes, or a taxi costs roughly 6,000 to 7,000 won. Jeonju Express Bus Terminal is closer, about 15 minutes by bus.

faq.question: How long does it take to get from Seoul to Jeonju?
faq.answer: Most KTX trains from Yongsan Station take about 1 hour 40 minutes, the fastest about 1 hour 32 minutes, and a standard adult seat costs about 31,600 won. Express buses from Seoul Express Bus Terminal (Central City) take about 2 hours 40 minutes, longer in weekend traffic.

faq.question: How much is admission to Gyeonggijeon Shrine?
faq.answer: Adults pay 3,000 won, ages 13 to 24 pay 2,000 won and ages 7 to 12 pay 1,000 won, and the ticket includes the Royal Portrait Museum. Entry is free on the last Wednesday of each month, and the main hall was closed for repainting scheduled until mid-December 2026.

Templestay in Korea: booking on templest.title: Templestay in Korea for Foreigners, from Booking to 108 Bows
Templestay in Korea: booking on templest.description: How to book a Korean templestay on templestay.com, day vs overnight programs, the 4 a.m. wake-up, 108 bows, monastic meals and refund rules at Seoul temples.
Templestay in Korea: booking on templest.body:
At 4:00 a.m. at Bongeunsa, across the road from COEX in Gangnam, the overnight templestay schedule says "Waking up." Twenty minutes later you're in the main hall for the dawn ceremony, and by 5:00 you're on your knees for 108 bows. That's the real shape of an overnight templestay, and it surprises people who booked expecting a quiet spa night in a temple. This guide covers how booking works on the official site, the difference between day and overnight programs, what happens at yebul, the 108 bows and the monastic meal, what to wear and bring, and which Seoul temples run programs in English, with their listed prices and cancellation rules.

## Booking on templestay.com

Templestay programs are listed on templestay.com, run by the Cultural Corps of Korean Buddhism (the Jogye Order's culture arm). The English site lets you search by region, temple, program type and number of people, then book a specific date from each program's calendar. Each program page has its own price list, schedule, "What to bring" list, refund policy and regulations, and those differ from temple to temple. Read the page for the exact program you pick rather than assuming one rule fits all.

A few booking rules from the official pages are worth knowing before you click:

- **Payment confirms the booking.** Jogyesa's page states that a reservation isn't confirmed until payment is complete, and unpaid reservations are cancelled automatically after a set time.
- **Payment method varies.** Jogyesa asks you to pay in advance, by card online (recommended) or bank transfer, and doesn't take cards on the spot. Geumsunsa's rest program says you can pay by card or cash on arrival.
- **Booking windows vary.** Bongeunsa opens reservations one month before the date. Jogyesa's day program closes bookings three days before; Bongeunsa's overnight program, one day before.
- **No printout needed.** The official FAQ says every temple keeps its own reservation list, so you don't have to bring a confirmation letter. Some temples don't send one at all; you can email the temple or support@templestay.com with your booking name, date and temple to check.
- **Changes and cancellations** go to the temple directly or to support@templestay.com. Check the calendar for open dates before asking to move.

## Day programs vs overnight stays

The official site groups programs into three types:

- **One-day:** usually two or three hours, built around a temple tour, meditation and a tea ceremony. The site pitches it at foreign tourists who don't have a whole day.
- **Experience-oriented:** typically one night, often on weekends, with the morning chanting, 108 prostrations, the formal monastic meal and meditation, plus a craft such as lotus lanterns or prayer beads.
- **Rest-oriented:** a looser stay where you rest, join the ceremonies if you like and keep the rest of the time free.

The FAQ adds that you can skip a session if you're unwell or tired. Tell the staff. Some temples allow stays of up to about ten days by combining programs, and the maximum depends on the temple.

## Seoul temples with English programs

The official FAQ names seven temples inside Seoul that are easy to reach by bus or subway: Bongeunsa, Geumsunsa, Hwagyesa, Jinkwansa, Jogyesa, Myogaksa and the International Seon Center. Three of them have current English listings worth comparing (prices as shown on templestay.com in November 2026; they can change):

- **Jogyesa (Jongno, central Seoul).** The "Jogyesa Always Templestay" is described as a program prepared for foreigners. You meet at 10:00 at the information center to the left of the main entrance, take a 40-minute temple tour, then make a lotus lantern until about 11:20. It's listed at **10,000 won** per person. Jogyesa also lists an overnight program; its page asks you to email jogyesa01@templestay.com in advance about single rooms. Jogyesa is a short walk from Insadong, covered in our [Insadong guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-insadong-traditional-culture-street.html).
- **Bongeunsa (Gangnam).** The overnight program is listed at **120,000 won**. It starts at 13:50 with room assignment and uniforms, then temple etiquette, a temple tour, a monastic meal at 17:00 and evening yebul. Day 2 runs from the 4:00 wake-up to tea with a monk at 9:00 and closing at 11:00. The nearest subway is Bongeunsa Station (Line 9), Exit 1, about 100 m away; Samseong Station (Line 2) Exit 6 is about 600 m. Bongeunsa also runs BONG-PASS, a drop-in temple experience every Tuesday from 10:00 to 16:00, payable by card or cash at the temple. The temple's templestay office lists Monday as its regular closing day.
- **Geumsunsa (Bukhansan, Jongno).** A rest-oriented stay at a temple inside Bukhansan National Park in Gugi-dong, listed at **80,000 won** per adult per night. Check in by 2:30 p.m. Dinner is at 17:30 and evening chanting at 18:10. Next morning the monks' wake-up chant is at 4:40, dawn chanting at 5:00, then free time until a 10:30 check-out. Payment is by card or cash on arrival, and the program is for individual bookings only.

For meditation-focused stays, the FAQ points to the International Seon Center and the Lotus Lantern International Meditation Center. The latter runs an intensive course once a month lasting three nights and four days.

## The 4 a.m. morning: yebul and 108 bows

**Yebul** is the ceremony that opens the temple day, paying respect to the Buddha, the bodhisattvas and his disciples. Participants sit in assigned places and follow the moktak (wooden percussion instrument) signals, as Bongeunsa's guidelines put it. Most overnight programs also include the evening yebul, often after watching the monks play the dharma instruments such as the drum and bell.

Most experience programs include the **108 prostrations**, and the timing varies. At Bongeunsa they follow the dawn ceremony, from 5:00 to 5:50. At Jogyesa's overnight stay they're an optional evening session at 18:25. Each prostration takes you from standing down to the floor and back up again. Fifty minutes of that is a real workout for knees and thighs, so pace yourself. Bongeunsa's schedule includes a temple etiquette session on the first afternoon, before any of the ceremonies.

## Barugongyang, the monastic meal

The formal monastic meal (written *balwoogongyang* on templestay.com) uses a set of four nesting bowls: from largest to smallest, rice, soup, side dishes and water. The official site describes three principles behind it: equality (everyone shares the same food), cleanliness and thrift (nothing is wasted). In practice that means:

- Eat in silence and don't comment on the food.
- Take only what you can finish. Nothing should be left in the bowls.
- At the end, the bowls are rinsed in turn with tea or water and a piece of pickle saved for the purpose, then you drink the rinse and eat the pickle.
- The clean water is collected and checked. In the traditional practice described in The Korea Times, if food bits remain, the diner drinks it.

Not every program serves the full ritual meal; some list a simpler monastic meal. Check the program schedule.

## What to wear and pack

Temples provide a uniform of a vest and pants. Most provide only soap and toothpaste, according to the official site, and some add towels or a hair dryer. Bongeunsa lists soap, a hair dryer and tissue; Jogyesa's overnight program lists one towel and soap per person. Bring:

- Your own toiletries and a towel unless the page says one is provided
- A T-shirt to wear under the uniform, plus socks (Bongeunsa says bare feet aren't acceptable in the halls)
- Sneakers, a tumbler or water bottle, and any medication
- Warm layers in winter. The official site warns that mountain temples can be much colder than you expect, and see our [seasonal packing guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seasonal-packing-weather-tips.html)

Sleeveless shirts and flip-flops aren't allowed or recommended at Geumsunsa and Jogyesa.

## Etiquette that matters

- **Hapjang and a half-bow:** greet people with palms together and a slight bow, and bow toward the Buddha when entering or passing the main hall.
- **Chasu while walking:** hands folded in front, right over left.
- **Quiet:** keep conversation low across the grounds, especially near halls.
- **No alcohol or smoking**, and avoid heavy makeup or strong scents.
- **Separate rooms:** the FAQ says men and women can't share a room. Rooms are often shared, but some temples offer private rooms for two to four people for an extra fee.
- **Return the uniform** and tidy your room before check-out.

## Cancellation rules, temple by temple

Refund rules are set per program, so compare before you pay:

- **Jogyesa:** 100% refund up to 7 days before; no refund 1 to 6 days before. If the minimum number of participants isn't met, the program is cancelled with a full refund.
- **Bongeunsa:** 100% refund 14 days before, 70% at 7 days, none from 6 days. No-shows can lead to being restricted from future Bongeunsa programs.
- **Geumsunsa:** 100% refund up to 4 days before; no refund from 3 days to 1 day.

## Your templestay checklist

1. Pick one-day, experience or rest on templestay.com, then read that program's own page.
2. Note the booking window: Bongeunsa opens a month ahead, and Jogyesa's day program closes 3 days before.
3. Pay how the page says: in advance at Jogyesa (online card recommended, or bank transfer), card or cash on arrival at Geumsunsa.
4. Screenshot the refund rule: 7 days at Jogyesa, 14 days for a full refund at Bongeunsa, 4 days at Geumsunsa.
5. Pack toiletries, a towel, socks, a T-shirt, a tumbler and warm layers. No sleeveless tops or flip-flops.
6. Arrive on time: 10:00 at Jogyesa, 13:50 at Bongeunsa, by 2:30 p.m. at Geumsunsa.
7. Expect lights-out around 9 p.m. and a 4 a.m. wake-up on overnight stays.
8. Practice hapjang and chasu, eat in silence and leave nothing in your bowls.
9. Email the temple or support@templestay.com if you need to change plans. Never just no-show.

faq.question: Can foreigners book a templestay in Seoul without speaking Korean?
faq.answer: Yes. The English templestay.com site lists programs by temple and date. Jogyesa runs the Jogyesa Always Templestay, described as a program prepared for foreigners, and Bongeunsa and Geumsunsa have English program pages with schedules, prices and refund rules.

faq.question: How much does a templestay in Seoul cost?
faq.answer: Prices listed on templestay.com in November 2026: Jogyesa's day program is 10,000 won per person, Geumsunsa's rest-oriented stay is 80,000 won per adult per night, and Bongeunsa's overnight program is 120,000 won. Prices can change, so confirm on the program page.

faq.question: What time do you wake up at a templestay?
faq.answer: Early. Bongeunsa's overnight schedule has the wake-up at 4:00 a.m., yebul at 4:20 and 108 bows from 5:00 to 5:50. At Geumsunsa, the monks' wake-up chant is at 4:40 and dawn chanting starts at 5:00. You can skip a session if you're unwell; just tell the staff.

Seoul City Wall (Hanyangdoseong): the si.title: Seoul City Wall Trail Guide, Which Section to Walk First
Seoul City Wall (Hanyangdoseong): the si.description: Walk Seoul's 18.6 km city wall the smart way: the six sections compared, Naksan at night, current Baegak hours and rules, the free museum and wall badges.
Seoul City Wall (Hanyangdoseong): the si.body:
Step out of Exit 2 at Hyehwa Station after dark, walk uphill for about fifteen minutes, and you reach Naksan Park, where a lit stone wall runs along the ridge with central Seoul glowing below. That wall is Hanyangdoseong, the Seoul City Wall, and it is not a single attraction but a loop of roughly 18.6 km that ties together four mountains and the city's old gates. Most visitors see one gate from a taxi window and never realise they can walk the wall itself. This guide breaks the loop into its six official sections, says which one suits a first walk, explains how the Baegak section works now that it is fully open, and covers the free museum and the two badge programmes.

## What the wall is and how the loop is divided

King Taejo, founder of the Joseon dynasty, ordered the wall in 1395, and most of the wall was built in 1396, with Sungnyemun, the main south gate, completed in 1398. It traced the ridgelines of four mountains around the capital: Baegak (also called Bugaksan) to the north, Naksan to the east, Namsan (Mongmyeoksan) to the south and Inwangsan to the west. There were four main gates, Heunginjimun (Dongdaemun), Sungnyemun (Namdaemun), Donuimun (Seodaemun, now only a site) and Sukjeongmun, plus four smaller ones, including Hyehwamun, Changuimun and Gwanghuimun. The wall is designated Historic Site No. 10.

The official Seoul City Wall website (seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr) splits the loop into six courses. These are the figures it currently lists:

| Section | Route | Length | Time | Official difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baegak | Changuimun to Hyehwamun | 4.7 km | about 3 hr | 5 stars |
| Naksan | Hyehwamun to Heunginjimun | 3.2 km | about 1 hr | 2 stars |
| Heunginjimun | Heunginjimun to Jangchung Gymnasium | 1.8 km | about 1 hr | 1 star |
| Namsan | Jangchung Gymnasium to Baekbeom Square | 6.7 km | about 3 hr | 3 stars |
| Sungnyemun | Baekbeom Square to Donuimun site | 1.8 km | about 1 hr | 1 star |
| Inwangsan | Donuimun site to Changuimun | 4.0 km | about 2 hr 30 min | 5 stars |

Two things the table hides. First, the flat sections (Heunginjimun and Sungnyemun) are where the wall has largely disappeared under roads and buildings; around Jangchung-dong it is no longer visible, and the official site recommends researching the Sungnyemun route beforehand because the original line is hard to follow. Second, the two five-star sections are steep and rocky. The Inwangsan page specifically warns about the rock sections, especially in winter.

## The best first section is Naksan, ideally at night

If you only walk one stretch, make it Naksan. It is the gentlest mountain section, the official site describes it as relatively easy because of its gentle slope, and it is open 24 hours with lights along the trail, so an evening walk is normal rather than risky.

A simple plan that ends near food and transport:

1. Take Line 4 to **Hyehwa Station** and leave by **Exit 2**. Naksan Park's upper area is about a 15-minute walk; Ihwa Village is about 20 minutes.
2. Walk around the top of **Naksan Park** for the night view over the city. Ihwa Village, on the slope, has had murals and installations on its buildings since 2006.
3. Follow the wall downhill toward **Heunginjimun**. On the way, look for stones with carved inscriptions near Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park and at the end of the trail. They recorded who built each stretch.
4. Finish at **Dongdaemun Station**. Exit 10 is about two minutes from Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park, and Heunginjimun is about a minute from Exits 6 and 7.

To start from the other end, ride Jongno Town Bus 03 from Dongdaemun Station Exit 5 to Naksan Junction and walk downhill instead. Parts of the route pass through Bukjeong and Ihwa neighbourhoods where people live, and the official site asks walkers to keep their voices down. At night that matters more.

## Baegak section, hours and rules in late 2026

Baegak, the mountain behind Cheong Wa Dae (the Blue House), is the section that changed most. Public access was cut after the January 1968 infiltration by North Korean commandos, known as the 1·21 incident, and the trails reopened in stages. The final piece, a 1.32 km trail on the southwestern slope starting from the Dolphin Rest Area above Changuimun, opened at 9 a.m. on 17 October 2026, which means every Baegak trail is now open.

**Hours:** The official course page for Baegak lists it as open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and in March 2026 the Presidential Security Service said the trail would stay fully open around the clock. You will still find seasonal hours (such as 9:00 to 17:00 in winter) in older guidebooks and some recent articles. The six information booths (Changuimun, Cheongundae, Gokjang, Sukjeongmun, Malbawi and Samcheong) reopened on 9 March 2026 and are staffed daily from 9:00 to 18:00. Walking in daylight, inside booth hours, is the sensible choice on a five-star rocky section anyway.

**ID:** Older guides describe a passport check and a visitor badge you wore and returned on the way down. Current official pages do not mention an ID requirement. Carrying your passport costs nothing, but you should not expect to show it.

**Rules on the trail:**

- Stay on the marked trail.
- Filming is restricted around military facilities and restricted zones, so follow the posted notices.
- Spotted deer live on the mountain. Signs ask you not to feed or approach them.

**Getting there:** From Gyeongbokgung Station Exit 3, take green bus 7212, 1020 or 7022 to Jahamungogae and walk two minutes to Changuimun. The other end is Hyehwamun, five minutes from Hansung University Station Exit 5. That makes Baegak and Naksan a natural pair: Baegak in the morning, Naksan after dark from almost the same point.

## Inwangsan and Namsan, briefly

**Inwangsan** (4.0 km, about 2 hr 30 min) runs from the Donuimun site, two minutes from Seodaemun Station Exit 4, over rocky ground with formations such as Seonbawi and Chimabawi, to Changuimun by way of Yun Dong-ju Hill. For the hiking side of Inwangsan and gear rental, see our guide to [hiking in Korea like a local](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-hiking-in-korea-like-a-local-subway-accessible-peaks-seasonal-trail-closures-and-the-gear-culture.html). The Yun Dong-ju Literary Museum at the end closes on Mondays.

**Namsan** (6.7 km, about 3 hr) is the longest section and passes the restored Mongmyeoksan beacon mound, first built in 1423. The Namsan area is open 24 hours, and the second floor of the N Seoul Tower observatory has displays about the wall. For the tower itself, see our [N Seoul Tower guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-n-seoul-tower-namsan.html).

## Seoul City Wall Museum at Dongdaemun

The Seoul City Wall Museum opened on 31 July 2014 inside Heunginjimun Park (Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park), on floors 1 to 3 of the Seoul Design Support Center, a short walk north of Dongdaemun Station. **Admission is free.** It is open 9:00 to 18:00, Tuesday to Sunday, and closed every Monday and on 1 January (it does open on other public holidays). Exhibits cover the wall from the Joseon period through damage under Japanese rule and modernisation to its restoration, with a model of the whole loop and a digital tour of its 18.627 km. Visiting before a Naksan walk gives you the context for the inscribed stones. If you are planning a Monday, our post on [how Korean museums schedule their days off](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-the-closed-on-monday-trap-how-korean-palaces-and-museums-schedule-their-days-off.html) covers the pattern.

## Badges and the completion certificate

There are two separate programmes, and finishing one does not count for the other.

- **Four-gate stamp tour:** Collect stamps at Heunginjimun, Sungnyemun, the Donuimun site and Sukjeongmun, either on the paper map or, since October 2022, in the official Seoul Hanyangdoseong app (open it near a gate and choose the stamp tour). Once your stamps are confirmed you receive a white commemorative badge.
- **Mayor-issued completion certificate:** Take a photo of yourself, face clearly visible, at each of four summit markers: the Inwangsan summit sign, the Baegak Cheongundae (or Baegak Maru) marker stone, the Naksan summit sign and the Namsan beacon mound. Apply through the completion certificate menu on seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr with your name, date of birth, phone number and the photos, then collect the printed certificate at the Hanyangdoseong On-site Museum on Namsan or the Hyehwa-dong Exhibition and Visitor Center, where staff confirm your identity. You also get a badge whose colour changes by season. You can do it once per quarter, and completing all four seasons earns a special metal badge.

## Your Seoul City Wall checklist

- Pick one section. For a first walk, choose Naksan from Hyehwa Station Exit 2 down to Dongdaemun, about 1 hour.
- Go to Naksan after dark for the lit wall and city view, and keep quiet through residential lanes.
- Visit the free Seoul City Wall Museum first, any day except Monday, 9:00 to 18:00.
- For Baegak, start at Changuimun (bus 7212, 1020 or 7022 from Gyeongbokgung Exit 3), walk in daylight, stay on the trail, follow filming notices and leave the deer alone.
- Leave Inwangsan and Baegak for dry days, because both are rated five stars and have rocky sections.
- Install the Seoul Hanyangdoseong app if you want the four-gate stamp badge.
- For the certificate, photograph yourself at all four summit markers and apply on the official site.
- Check seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr the day before for any notices on hours or closures.

faq.question: Which section of the Seoul City Wall is best for a first visit?
faq.answer: Naksan, from Hyehwamun to Heunginjimun. It is about 3.2 km and takes around an hour, the official site rates it as relatively easy, and it is open 24 hours with lights along the trail. Start from Hyehwa Station Exit 2 and finish at Dongdaemun Station.

faq.question: Do I need my passport to walk the Baegak (Bugaksan) section?
faq.answer: Older guides describe an ID check and visitor badge, but current official pages do not mention an ID requirement. The official course page lists Baegak as open 24 hours, and information booths are staffed daily from 9:00 to 18:00. Stay on the trail and follow filming notices near military facilities.

faq.question: Is the Seoul City Wall Museum free, and when is it closed?
faq.answer: Yes, admission is free. The museum in Heunginjimun Park near Dongdaemun Station is open 9:00 to 18:00, Tuesday to Sunday, and closed every Monday and on 1 January.

Korean drinking etiquette: soju pouring.title: Korean Drinking Etiquette, Soju Rules and Pojangmacha Nights
Korean drinking etiquette: soju pouring.description: Pour for others, never yourself. Soju rules, how to use a Seoul pojangmacha, December hoesik rounds, the 19 age rule and Korea's 0.03% driving limit.
Korean drinking etiquette: soju pouring.body:
Under an orange tarp on a side street in Jongno, a plastic table holds a plate of tteokbokki, a few skewers of eomuk and one green bottle of soju. The foreigner at the table cracks the cap, fills his own shot glass, and drinks it facing his Korean friend's father. Nobody says anything. But in two small moves he has broken two of the most basic rules of drinking in Korea: you do not pour for yourself, and you do not knock back a drink face-on in front of an elder.

None of this is hard once you know it. This guide covers the pouring rules, what a pojangmacha actually is and how to use one, how December year-end company dinners work, and the legal lines that apply to visitors as much as to locals.

## The soju pouring rules, in the order you will need them

**Never fill your own glass.** Hite Jinro, the company behind Chamisul and Jinro soju, calls this one of the most fundamental rules: people at the table look after each other and refill other glasses before their own, and someone else will fill yours. If your glass is empty and you want more, the polite move is to fill someone else's first. That usually prompts them to return the favour.

**Use two hands with anyone older or more senior.** When an older person or a boss pours for you, hold your glass with both hands. When you pour for them, hold the bottle with both hands, or hold it in your right hand and support your wrist or forearm with your left. The Wikipedia entry on soju sums up the traditional rule simply: the youngest person in the group pours for their elders, and both hands are used to pour and to receive.

**Turn your head away when you drink in front of elders.** With a senior at the table, angle your head and glass slightly to the side as you sip. Hite Jinro explains it as a traditional value: drinking face-to-face with a senior is considered impolite. Among friends of the same age, nobody expects it.

**Wait for the toast before the first sip.** Even when every glass is full, people wait until the group is ready and someone calls "geonbae" (cheers). Drinking before that moment reads as impatient.

**You can say no.** If you do not drink, say it once, clearly: "jeoneun sureul mot haeyo" (I can't drink alcohol). Guides to Korean workplace dinners note that most hosts will find you a soft drink and stop there. You can still take part in the toasts with a glass of water or cider.

## What is actually in that green bottle

Soju is the default drink at almost every Korean table, and it is stronger than many visitors assume because it comes in tiny glasses. Diluted soju sold today usually sits below 20% alcohol, and versions under 17% are widely available, according to Wikipedia's summary of the market. The familiar green bottle holds about 360 ml. In 1994 one maker introduced green 360 ml bottles and other brands copied them, and in 2009 seven soju companies agreed to use the same bottle so it could be returned and reused.

Because the people around you keep refilling your glass, it is easy to lose count. Pace yourself by sipping rather than finishing every shot in one go, and eat while you drink. Korean drinking food has its own name, anju, and ordering it is part of the etiquette, not an extra.

## How to use a pojangmacha

A pojangmacha, often shortened to pocha, literally means "covered wagon". It is a street stall in a small tent, selling foods like tteokbokki, sundae, eomuk (fish cake), mandu and anju to go with drinks. Many pochas serve soju, makgeolli and beer in the evening, and some set out cheap plastic chairs or benches for late-night drinkers. Wikipedia notes there were about 3,100 pochas in Seoul as of 2012, and names Jongno as the best-known area, with more at Gwangjang Market. Stalls in Jongno and elsewhere sometimes offer set plates that combine gimbap, tteokbokki and sundae.

A few practical points for a first visit:

- **Order food, not just drinks.** Pochas exist to feed people as they drink. Pick at least one anju dish for the table. Common choices include dakbal (spicy chicken feet), twigim (fried snacks), gyeranmari (rolled omelette) and eomuk.
- **Bring some cash as a backup.** Some small street stalls work more smoothly with cash, so it is worth carrying a little in case the card terminal is busy or missing.
- **Indoor pochas count too.** Bars that copy the tent look are called "indoor pojangmacha" (silnae pojangmacha). The same pouring rules apply inside as under the tarp.

## Year-end hoesik nights: what December looks like

Hoesik is the Korean company dinner. Its biggest season is December, when teams hold a songnyeonhoe, a year-end party to say goodbye to the year. You may also hear the older word mangnyeonhoe ("forget the year"). It comes from the Japanese bonenkai, and the National Institute of Korean Language recommends songnyeonhoe instead.

A traditional hoesik runs in rounds:

1. **1-cha (first round): dinner.** This is the main meal, and even people who do not drink usually attend.
2. **2-cha (second round): drinks.** The group moves on to a bar, a hof (Korean-style pub) or a pojangmacha.
3. **3-cha (third round): noraebang.** A karaoke room. Fewer people make it here, and going home after the second round is normal. If you do go, read our [noraebang etiquette guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-noraebang-etiquette-how-korean-karaoke-actually-works-for-first-timers.html) first.

The format is changing fast. Lunch parties, one-round dinners and nights with no drinking at all are now normal at many firms. In one survey cited by Homes in Korea, only 47.5% of people in their 20s said a year-end party was necessary, compared with 68.9% of people aged 50 and over. A separate, small 2024 survey of 124 workers found 9 pm was the most popular finishing time.

If a Korean company invites you as a colleague or partner, attending the first round signals respect, and leaving after it is not read as rude. Restaurants and party rooms fill up in December, especially the Saturdays before Christmas, so groups book early.

## The legal lines: age, driving and getting home

**Drinking age is based on birth year, not birthday.** Under Korea's Youth Protection Act, people can buy alcohol from January 1 of the year in which they turn 19 under the international age system. KBS reported in 2023 that this rule stayed in place even after Korea adopted international age for most legal purposes. Your exact birthday does not matter. Convenience stores and bars may ask for ID, so carry your passport.

**The drink-driving limit is 0.03% BAC.** Driving with a blood alcohol content of 0.03% or higher counts as drunk driving in Korea. Penalties rise in bands (0.03% to 0.08%, 0.08% to 0.2%, and above 0.2%) and range from fines and licence suspension to prison. Refusing a breath test is also penalised. If you have rented a car, leave it parked and take a taxi or the subway.

**Plan the trip home before the second round.** Hoesik and pocha nights often run late, and the subway does not run all night. Check the last-train time for your station before you settle in. Our [Seoul subway guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seoul-subway-details-nobody-tells-you-exit-numbers-transfer-walks-express-trains-and-the-last-train.html) explains how last trains work and why the final departure from your station may be earlier than you expect.

**The morning after: haejang-guk.** Korea has a whole category of "soup to chase a hangover", called haejang-guk (also sulguk). It usually combines dried napa cabbage, vegetables and meat in a hearty beef broth. Seonjiguk adds congealed ox blood, and sundaeguk is made with blood sausage. Look for restaurants with 해장국 on the sign the morning after a long night out.

## Your Korean drinking etiquette checklist

Save this before your first night out. For wider manners beyond the table, see our [first-timer etiquette guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-first-timer-etiquette-common-mistakes.html).

- Do not pour your own glass. Fill someone else's first, and let them return it.
- Pour and receive with two hands when the other person is older or more senior.
- Turn your head slightly away when you drink in front of an elder.
- Wait for "geonbae" before the first sip.
- If you don't drink, say "jeoneun sureul mot haeyo" once and take a soft drink.
- Order at least one anju dish at a pojangmacha. Never drink on an empty stomach.
- Carry a little cash for small street stalls, and your passport for ID checks.
- Bottled soju is usually just under 20% alcohol or lower, and your glass keeps getting refilled. Sip, don't race.
- At a December hoesik, stay for the first round. Leaving after it is fine.
- Never drive after drinking. The limit is 0.03% BAC.
- Check your last train before the second round starts.
- Next morning, find a bowl of haejang-guk.

faq.question: Is it rude to pour my own soju in Korea?
faq.answer: Traditionally, yes. At a Korean table people refill each other's glasses rather than their own. If your glass is empty, fill someone else's first and they will usually return the favour. Among close friends of the same age the rule is looser, but it is still the safe default.

faq.question: What is the legal drinking age in Korea for visitors?
faq.answer: Under the Youth Protection Act you can buy alcohol from January 1 of the year in which you turn 19, regardless of your actual birthday. The same rule applies to tourists, and bars or convenience stores may ask for ID, so carry your passport.

faq.question: Do I have to stay for every round of a Korean hoesik?
faq.answer: No. A traditional hoesik runs as dinner, then drinks, then noraebang. Attending the first round shows respect, and leaving after it is normal. Many companies now hold one-round dinners, lunch parties or events with no drinking at all.

National Museum of Korea: free entry, th.title: National Museum of Korea Free Entry Guide and Top Galleries
National Museum of Korea: free entry, th.description: National Museum of Korea guide with current hours, closed days, free vs paid exhibits, Ichon Exit 2, the floor order and the Room of Quiet Contemplation.
National Museum of Korea: free entry, th.body:
Step out of Exit 2 at Ichon Station in Yongsan and the first thing many visitors do is look for a ticket counter. At the National Museum of Korea there usually isn't one to queue at. The permanent galleries are free, and the mistake people make is the opposite one: they assume something this big and free can be "done" in an hour, wander the first floor in the order the doors suggest, and run out of energy before they reach the two rooms most people came for: the Room of Quiet Contemplation on the 2nd floor and the Celadon Gallery on the 3rd. This guide covers what is actually free, what charges, how to get there, and the order that gets you to the best galleries while you still have fresh legs.

## What is free and what you pay for

Admission to the permanent exhibition halls is free. So is the Children's Museum, and so are special exhibitions the museum runs as free shows. The only thing that charges is a ticketed special exhibition, which is held in the separate Special Exhibition Galleries and sold on its own. If a poster at the entrance shows a ticket price, that price is for that one show, not for the building.

The outdoor exhibition area and the Pagoda Garden are free as well, with no ticket at all, and they keep longer hours than the galleries.

## Opening hours and the closed days that changed

Older blogs list 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Those hours are out of date. According to the museum's official viewing-hours page, the current schedule is:

- **Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday:** 9:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., last admission 5:00 p.m.
- **Wednesday and Saturday:** 9:30 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., last admission 8:30 p.m.

Admission closes 30 minutes before closing time, and staff start guiding visitors to the exit 10 minutes before closing. The outdoor exhibition area is open from 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.

The museum closes only on January 1, Lunar New Year's Day and Chuseok day itself. Separately, the permanent and special galleries close on the first Monday of March, June, September and December for maintenance. The museum noted there would be no such closure in March 2026, and the Pagoda Garden stays open on those days. Monday is otherwise a normal open day here, which is why it pairs well with a palace day; our guide to the [closed-on-Monday trap](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-the-closed-on-monday-trap-how-korean-palaces-and-museums-schedule-their-days-off.html) covers which palaces close when.

The two late nights matter more than most people realize. On a Wednesday or Saturday you can stay from 9:30 a.m. until 9:00 p.m., which means no rushing through the upper floors before closing.

## Getting there from Ichon Station

Take Line 4 or the Gyeongui-Jungang Line to Ichon Station. The museum's own directions say to leave by **Exit 2** and walk about 150 meters toward Yongsan Family Park. For how exit numbers and longer transfer walks work in general, see our guide to [Seoul subway details nobody tells you](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-seoul-subway-details-nobody-tells-you-exit-numbers-transfer-walks-express-trains-and-the-last-train.html).

## The galleries to see first

The main building has three floors of permanent galleries:

- **1st floor:** Prehistory and Ancient History, and Medieval and Early Modern History.
- **2nd floor:** Calligraphy and Painting, the Donated Collection, and the Room of Quiet Contemplation.
- **3rd floor:** Sculpture and Crafts, and World Art.

A full visit takes at least half a day. If you have two or three hours, do it in reverse. Take the elevator or stairs straight up to the 3rd floor and work downward. The 3rd floor holds the Celadon Gallery (Room 303) and the Buncheong Ware and White Porcelain Gallery (Room 304), which reward slow looking. Check the closure notice first: the Buddhist Sculpture (301) and Metal Crafts (302) galleries on the 3rd floor, Buddhist Painting (203) and Wood and Lacquer Crafts (204) on the 2nd floor, and Calligraphy and Painting Rooms 202-3 and 202-4 are closed for renovation until January 28, 2027, and reopen on January 29, 2027. Then drop to the 2nd floor for the Room of Quiet Contemplation, and save the history halls on the 1st floor for whatever time and energy you have left. Most first-time visitors start on the 1st floor, spend an hour in the prehistoric galleries, and arrive upstairs tired.

On the way in, don't walk past the Ten-story Stone Pagoda of Gyeongcheonsa Temple. It stands 13.5 meters tall inside the building on the first floor, and it's a designated National Treasure. An inscription dates it to 1348, during the Goryeo period, and it is carved from marble rather than the granite used for most Korean pagodas. It was smuggled to Japan in 1907, returned in 1918, reassembled at Gyeongbokgung in 1960, and moved indoors here in 2005 because acid weather was damaging the stone. If you are also visiting Gyeongbokgung, where the pagoda stood from 1960 to 2005, see our [Gyeongbokgung guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-gyeongbokgung-palace.html).

## The Room of Quiet Contemplation

This 2nd-floor gallery was created for just two objects: a pair of gilt-bronze Pensive Bodhisattva statues, each a designated National Treasure, made in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. You reach them through a dark, quiet corridor, and they sit side by side in a dim room. Each figure has its right leg crossed over the left and the fingers of the right hand lightly touching the cheek.

The museum asks everyone, including guided groups, to keep silent inside so people can look in peace. It's one of the busiest rooms in the building, so if you want it quieter, try arriving close to opening or using a Wednesday or Saturday evening. Flash, tripods, selfie sticks and gimbals are prohibited throughout the museum, so plan on handheld photos without flash.

## Tours, the app, lockers and the shop

**Free guided tours in English** run at 10:30 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. on weekdays and weekends. They gather in front of the Korean Empire section of the 1st-floor permanent exhibition hall.

**The museum's exhibition guide app** is free on Google Play, the App Store and One Store. It uses Bluetooth beacons to give location-based commentary in Korean, English, Chinese, Japanese and Vietnamese, plus gallery maps and recommended routes. The museum recommends downloading content over Wi-Fi before you go, and you'll need location and Bluetooth turned on.

**Bags and coats:** free coat storage is on the west side of the main gate, and there are lockers in front of the museum shop and the Children's Museum. Wheelchairs and strollers are free to borrow in the Great Hall. Food, drinks and pets aren't allowed in the galleries.

**The museum shop** is a sight of its own. The museum's goods, branded MU:DS (museum plus goods), are produced by the National Museum Foundation. The craze is usually traced to a miniature Pensive Bodhisattva figure released in 2020, and some later items have sold out on the day they went on sale. There are three museum shops in the building plus an online store, so if a bestseller is gone on-site, check online.

**The Children's Museum** is free but runs in five timed sessions a day, from 9:30 a.m. to 5:20 p.m., with 320 online reservations per session. Visitors with a reservation enter by showing their confirmation. From December 15, 2026, reservations are canceled automatically if you don't enter within 20 minutes of your slot, instead of the previous 30.

## Your National Museum of Korea checklist

1. Pick a Wednesday or Saturday if you can, and arrive by 9:30 a.m. or plan an evening visit before the 8:30 p.m. last entry.
2. Avoid January 1, Lunar New Year's Day, Chuseok and the first Monday of March, June, September and December.
3. Take Line 4 or the Gyeongui-Jungang Line to Ichon Station and use Exit 2.
4. Download the free exhibition guide app over Wi-Fi and switch on Bluetooth and location.
5. Leave big bags in the lockers or the free coat storage.
6. Stop at the Gyeongcheonsa pagoda, then go straight up to the Celadon Gallery on the 3rd floor and work down to the Room of Quiet Contemplation on the 2nd. Until January 28, 2027, Rooms 301, 302, 203, 204, 202-3 and 202-4 are closed for renovation.
7. Stay silent inside the Room of Quiet Contemplation, and leave the flash off everywhere.
8. Join a free English tour at 10:30 a.m. or 1:00 p.m. if you want context.
9. Only buy a ticket if you want a specific paid special exhibition.
10. Book Children's Museum sessions online in advance and arrive within 20 minutes of your slot.

faq.question: Is the National Museum of Korea free?
faq.answer: Yes. The permanent exhibition halls, the Children's Museum and free special exhibitions cost nothing. Only ticketed special exhibitions in the Special Exhibition Galleries charge, and that price covers that one show.

faq.question: What are the National Museum of Korea's opening hours?
faq.answer: It opens 9:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday, and until 9:00 p.m. on Wednesday and Saturday. Last admission is 30 minutes before closing. It closes on January 1, Lunar New Year's Day and Chuseok, and the galleries also close on the first Monday of March, June, September and December.

faq.question: Where is the Room of Quiet Contemplation?
faq.answer: It's on the 2nd floor of the main building. It displays two gilt-bronze Pensive Bodhisattva statues from the late 6th and early 7th centuries, both National Treasures, and visitors are asked to keep silent inside.
