Andong Hahoe Village from Seoul: the KTX.title: Andong Hahoe Village from Seoul by KTX-Eum and Bus 210
Andong Hahoe Village from Seoul: the KTX.description: How to reach Andong Hahoe Village from Seoul: the KTX-Eum, city bus 210 to the village, the 5,000-won ticket and shuttle, and the 2 p.m. mask dance.
Andong Hahoe Village from Seoul: the KTX.body:
At the bus stop outside Andong Station, a lot of first-time visitors stand waiting for bus 246 because a guidebook or blog told them to. That number is out of date. According to the Hahoe Village management office's own timetable, the city bus to Hahoe has run as **bus 210** since March 2022, and even some 2026 articles still print the old number. Get the bus right, time your arrival around the 2 p.m. mask dance, and Hahoe works well as a long day trip from Seoul. Get it wrong and you can spend an hour of a short winter afternoon at a bus stop.

This guide covers the KTX-Eum from Seoul, the bus out to the village, the ticket and shuttle, the mask dance schedule, and what to eat and where to sleep if you stay the night.

## Getting from Seoul to Andong by KTX-Eum or express bus

The fast option is the **KTX-Eum on the Jungang Line**, which leaves from **Cheongnyangni Station** in northeast Seoul. When KORAIL put KTX trains on this line in January 2021, Korea Tourism Organization reported that the trip to Andong dropped from 3 hours 54 minutes to about **2 hours** (an average of 2 hours 3 minutes). On the way the train stops at Yangpyeong, Seowonju, Wonju, Jecheon, Danyang, Punggi and Yeongju.

There are not many departures. At launch it was about seven or eight trains each way per day, and timetables and fares have changed since, so check the KORAIL website or the Korail Talk app before you plan the day around one train. Weekend trains sell out, so book your return when you book the outbound trip.

If you would rather take the bus, **express and intercity buses** run to Andong from Seoul terminals including Dong Seoul and the Seoul Express Bus Terminal. They are usually cheaper but slower than the KTX-Eum, and traffic decides how long the trip takes. Check current times on the Kobus or Bustago apps. For a full comparison of rail and road for trips like this, see our guide to [KTX vs. SRT vs. intercity bus](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-ktx-vs-srt-vs-intercity-bus-for-long-distance-travel.html).

Train or bus, the transfer at the other end is easy. In December 2020 Andong Station moved from the old downtown site to a new building on the edge of town, **right next to Andong Bus Terminal**. Train and bus arrivals end up in the same place. If an older guide sends you to an Andong Station "downtown by the river", it means the closed station.

## Bus 210 from Andong to Hahoe Village

Hahoe is about 50 minutes from downtown Andong by **city bus 210**. The adult cash fare on the village office's table is 1,500 won, and a transport card works too. If you have never used a Korean city bus outside Seoul, read our explainer on [bus travel inside Korean cities](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-bus-travel-inside-korean-cities-color-codes-tag-off-transfers-and-why-you-must-flag-the-bus.html). The main point is that you flag the bus down and tag your card when you board.

The bus runs roughly once an hour, with gaps. The official table lists departures from the downtown start of the route at 06:30, 07:30, 08:20, 09:20, 10:20, 11:00, 12:30, 13:10, 14:05, 15:10, 16:00, 17:20 and 18:20. Buses leave Hahoe for Andong at 07:35, 08:50, 09:45, 10:30, 11:30, 12:40, 13:40, 14:20, 15:45, 16:30, 17:00, 18:20 and 19:10. Three runs a day also loop past **Byeongsan Seowon**, the riverside Confucian academy. Times are given for the downtown start, so add a little if you board near the station, and check the times on the day with Kakao Map or Naver Map. A missed bus can leave you waiting more than an hour.

The bus drops you at the **ticket office and car park**, not in the village. Cars are not allowed into the village itself. You buy your ticket at the office and ride the **free shuttle** to the village entrance.

## Tickets, opening hours, the shuttle and Buyongdae

Prices on the official Hahoe Village site:

- Adults (19–64): **5,000 won**
- Youth (13–18): 2,500 won
- Children (7–12): 1,500 won
- The shuttle, parking and the **Hahoe World Mask Museum** next to the ticket office are free.

Last entry is **17:30 from April to September** and **16:30 from October to March**, and the village opens at 09:00. In winter, plan around that earlier 16:30 cutoff. Entry is free on January 1 and on the main day of Seollal and of Chuseok.

Why is the whole village protected? In 2010 UNESCO listed Hahoe together with Yangdong Village near Gyeongju as the "Historic Villages of Korea". Hahoe is a clan village of the Pungsan Ryu family, set in an S-shaped bend of the Nakdonggang River. Tiled yangban houses and thatched commoners' houses still stand side by side, and people still live in many of them. Keep your voice down and don't walk through gates marked private.

For the postcard view of the river bend, go to **Buyongdae Cliff** on the opposite bank. The Korean Culture and Information Service lists it as free to visit. You can reach it by a short walk from its own car park on the far side, or by **ferry** from the village (4,000 won round trip), but the ferry only runs when the weather and river level allow.

## The Hahoe mask dance schedule

**Hahoe Byeolsingut Talnori** started as a village rite to the local guardian spirit, and the masked play was staged to entertain the spirit. It became a National Intangible Cultural Heritage in 1980. The comedy mocks the aristocrats: a monk who breaks his vows, and a yangban and a scholar arguing over status while their servants make fun of them both. It is performed in Korean, but the slapstick is easy to follow without understanding the words.

The permanent schedule published by the village and the preservation society:

- **March–December:** Tuesday to Sunday, **14:00**, about one hour
- **January–February:** Saturday and Sunday only, 14:00
- **Mondays:** no show
- **Free**, but it takes place inside the village, so you need the 5,000-won ticket

Since June 2025 the main performance hall has been under renovation, and shows moved to a temporary basement hall with about 200 places, first come, first served. The village notice says that hall has stairs and cannot take wheelchairs or strollers. The renovation was due to finish around April 2026, but no notice since then confirms that shows have moved back. Check hahoemask.co.kr or call ahead before you go. On a weekend, be at the door when it opens at 13:30.

To catch the show, look at the bus table above. From downtown, the **12:30 bus is the last one that reliably gets you there before 2 p.m.** After the show, buses leave Hahoe for Andong at 15:45, 16:30 and 17:00.

Each autumn the Andong Maskdance Festival adds more performances. In 2026 it ran from September 24 to October 4, and dates change every year.

## Eating and sleeping in Andong

Andong's best-known dish is **Andong jjimdak**: chicken braised with glass noodles and vegetables in a sweet-salty soy sauce. Some restaurants make it spicy, so ask before you order. You can also try **gangodeungeo**, Andong's salted mackerel, and many restaurants near the Hahoe car park serve both as a set. There are no restaurants inside the village, so eat before or after your walk. The traditional meal to look for is **heotjesatbap**, rice with seasoned vegetables and clear soup. Its name comes from the old custom of holding a mock ancestral rite just to eat the ritual food.

If you stay the night, you have time for Byeongsan Seowon and the river at dusk. The village office lists many **hanok minbak** (guesthouses run by residents), and at the higher end there is Rakkojae Hahoe Hanok Hotel inside the village. Book directly and confirm check-in times, because the village gets quiet early once the day visitors leave.

If you are building a longer trip, Yangdong Village, Hahoe's partner in the UNESCO "Historic Villages of Korea" listing, is near Gyeongju. Our [Gyeongju from Seoul](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-gyeongju-from-seoul-the-ktx-the-bus-to-bulguksa-and-which-tombs-to-see-first.html) guide covers the KTX, the buses to Bulguksa and which tombs to see first.

## Your Hahoe day-trip checklist

1. Book a **KTX-Eum from Cheongnyangni** on Korail Talk, and book the return at the same time.
2. Make sure it isn't a **Monday**, or a **weekday in January–February**, if you want the mask dance.
3. At Andong Station, look for **bus 210**, not 246, and carry a transport card or 1,500 won in cash.
4. Leave downtown by the **12:30 bus at the latest** for the 2 p.m. show, or by 10:20 or 11:00 to see the village first.
5. Buy the **5,000-won ticket** at the office, then take the free shuttle in.
6. Eat near the car park. There are no restaurants inside the village.
7. Be at the mask dance hall by **13:30** on weekends.
8. Note the **last entry time** (16:30 in winter) and your **return bus**: 15:45, 16:30 or 17:00 after the show.
9. If you have time, take the ferry to **Buyongdae**, or go by road if the ferry isn't running.
10. Finish with **Andong jjimdak** back in town before your train.

faq.question: Which bus goes from Andong Station to Hahoe Village?
faq.answer: City bus 210. It replaced the old 246 in March 2022, takes about 50 minutes from downtown Andong, and costs 1,500 won in cash on the village office's table. It stops at the ticket office, and from there a free shuttle takes you to the village entrance.

faq.question: What time is the Hahoe mask dance and is it free?
faq.answer: The show is at 14:00 and lasts about an hour. It runs Tuesday to Sunday from March to December, and only on Saturdays and Sundays in January and February. There is no show on Mondays. The show itself is free, but you need the 5,000-won village ticket to get in.

faq.question: How long does the KTX-Eum take from Seoul to Andong?
faq.answer: About 2 hours from Cheongnyangni Station on the Jungang Line. There are only a few trains a day, so check the timetable on the KORAIL website or the Korail Talk app and book both directions in advance.

Korean BBQ restaurants: two-portion mini.title: Korean BBQ Rules, From Two Portions to the Fried Rice Finish
Korean BBQ restaurants: two-portion mini.description: Korean BBQ explained for first-timers: the two-serving minimum, who grills, how to build a one-bite ssam wrap, and ordering fried rice in the pan.
Korean BBQ restaurants: two-portion mini.image_query: Korean BBQ samgyeopsal grill Seoul restaurant
Korean BBQ restaurants: two-portion mini.body:
It's 7 p.m. at a neighborhood samgyeopsal restaurant in Seoul. Two friends sit down at a table with a gas grill built into the middle, point at "삼겹살" on the wall menu, hold up one finger, and wait. The server holds up two fingers back. A few minutes later raw pork lands on the table with tongs and a pair of kitchen scissors, and nobody comes back to cook it. By the time the meat is gone, the next table is scraping rice into their pan, and the two visitors have no idea how to ask for the same thing.

None of this is complicated. Korean barbecue simply runs on a few house rules that nobody prints in English. This guide covers the four things that trip up first-timers: why you have to order two portions, who is supposed to grill, how to build a ssam wrap, and how to finish with fried rice made in the same pan.

## Why the menu says one serving but the table needs two

At a Korean barbecue restaurant (고깃집, gogi-jip) meat is sold by the serving, written 1인분 (il-inbun, "one person's portion"). Most places require at least two servings, 2인분 (i-inbun), to start the grill. That is a house policy, not a law, but nearly every pork-belly and beef restaurant enforces it, and some only mention it when you order. The logic is cost: lighting a tabletop grill and setting out free side dishes for a single small portion doesn't pay.

What one serving actually weighs varies by restaurant. A common range is roughly 150 to 200 g for pork and 120 to 150 g for beef, and restaurants are required to show the meat price per 100 g, often alongside the weight and price of one serving. Use the per-100 g price to compare two restaurants, because a cheaper serving is sometimes just a smaller one.

**What to order first.** For a table of two, start with 2인분 of samgyeopsal (삼겹살, pork belly). Korea's official tourism site describes it as one of Koreans' favorite pork cuts, grilled on a hot plate and eaten with chili and soybean paste or sesame oil and salt. If you want variety, the usual add-ons are:

- **Moksal (목살):** pork neck or collar, leaner and less greasy than belly.
- **Hangjeongsal (항정살):** pork jowl, a small premium cut with a chewy, marbled bite.
- **Dwaeji-galbi (돼지갈비):** pork ribs, usually marinated in soy or chili sauce.
- **Galbi (갈비) and chadolbagi (차돌박이):** beef short rib and paper-thin brisket. Chadolbagi cooks in seconds and is usually dipped in sesame oil and salt.

Order in waves: two servings first, then add one or two more if the table is still hungry. Ordering everything at once leaves meat sitting out. To add more, say "삼겹살 1인분 추가요" (samgyeopsal il-inbun chuga-yo).

**Hanwoo or imported?** Korean law requires restaurants to show the country of origin for beef and pork on the menu or a posted sign, and for beef to state the type, such as 국내산 한우 (domestic hanwoo). Imported beef must name its country, such as 호주산 (Australian). Domestic beef that is not hanwoo is labeled 국내산 육우 (beef cattle) or 국내산 젖소 (dairy cattle). Hanwoo costs far more, and Korean beef is graded 1++, 1+, 1, 2 and 3, mainly by marbling. If you want to know the grade at a beef restaurant, ask "몇 등급이에요?" (myeot deunggeup-ieyo, "what grade is it?").

**Eating alone?** The two-portion rule is the main reason solo travelers get turned away. Look for signs saying 1인 가능 (one person OK), or read our guide to [eating alone in Korea](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-eating-alone-in-korea-which-restaurants-refuse-solo-diners-and-where-honbap-works.html) for where honbap works.

## Who does the grilling

At most neighborhood pork restaurants, you grill your own. Staff light the grill, drop off the meat, and leave the tongs and scissors with you. Among Korean groups, the informal custom is that the youngest person at the table takes the tongs, and at a company dinner the most junior employee usually does it. Among friends the job rotates.

Premium restaurants work differently. At mid-range and high-end beef places, staff often grill at the table or at least start the meat for you. If a server picks up your tongs, let them work. Reaching in usually just gets in the way. If you can't tell which kind of restaurant you're in, watch the next table.

A few grilling habits help:

- **Use the scissors.** Cut big strips into bite-size pieces right on the grill. Scissors are a normal table tool here, not a sign you're doing it wrong.
- **Don't season raw pork.** It is served plain on purpose. You season each bite with ssamjang, the sesame-oil-and-salt dip, or the scallion salad.
- **Aim for golden, not black.** Flip when one side is browned. Burnt edges taste bitter.
- **Ask for a new grill plate.** When the plate gets heavily charred, or before you switch from plain to marinated meat, say "불판 갈아주세요" (bulpan garajuseyo). Sugar in marinades burns fast on a dirty plate.

**Calling staff.** Many tables have a call bell. Press it once and wait. Some restaurants use a tablet at the table for orders instead, which works much like a [restaurant kiosk](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-unmanned-kiosk-ordering-in-korea-why-humans-are-disappearing-from-the-counter.html). Otherwise, "여기요" (yeogiyo, "over here") gets attention politely.

## Building a ssam wrap

Next to the meat you'll get a basket of lettuce (상추, sangchu) and often perilla leaves (깻잎, kkaennip), plus garlic, green chili, ssamjang (쌈장, a thick fermented soybean and chili paste) and side dishes called banchan. Banchan are free, and staples like kimchi and pickled radish are refilled at no charge. Ask "이거 더 주세요" (igeo deo juseyo, "more of this, please"). Specialty sides can cost extra, and some places have a self-serve bar where you refill lettuce and banchan yourself.

To build a ssam:

1. Hold a lettuce leaf flat in your open palm. Add a perilla leaf on top if there is one.
2. Add one or two pieces of grilled meat.
3. Dab on a little ssamjang. Add a slice of garlic, raw or grilled on the plate, and some scallion salad (파절이, pajeori) or a ring of chili if you like heat.
4. Fold it shut and eat it in one bite.

The one-bite rule is the main one. A wrap that takes three bites falls apart in your hands. If you can't close your mouth around it, use less meat. Not every bite has to be a wrap, either. Dipping a piece straight into sesame oil and salt is normal, especially for beef.

## The fried rice finish

Korean barbecue rarely ends when the meat runs out. Most tables order a closing dish, and the common options are:

- **Bokkeumbap (볶음밥):** fried rice made on the still-hot grill plate with rice, chopped kimchi and the leftover meat juices. Staff usually make it, or bring the ingredients and show you how. Don't drop plain rice onto the grill yourself mid-meal. Ask for it as the final round.
- **Naengmyeon (냉면):** cold buckwheat noodles, a palate cleanser and a summer favorite, served in broth (물냉면) or spicy and mixed (비빔냉면).
- **Doenjang-jjigae (된장찌개):** fermented soybean stew, often with a bowl of rice (공기밥, gonggi-bap). It's probably the most common closer of all.

These are common but not universal, so check the menu for 볶음밥 or ask whether they make it. If you're out with Korean colleagues, expect someone to order a closer. Skipping it can feel like ending the meal early.

When you pay, don't leave cash on the table. Tipping isn't part of Korean restaurant culture, as our [tipping guide](https://landinkorea.com/posts/korea-tipping-and-service-charges.html) explains.

## Smoke, smell and your coat

Tabletop grilling means smoke, and the smell gets into clothes. Some barbecue restaurants hand out plastic bags for coats, or have seats that open up as storage bins. Use them. Leave the nice jacket at the hotel if you can, and don't hang a scarf over the back of your chair near the grill.

## Your Korean BBQ checklist

1. Order at least 2인분 (two servings) to start, and check the per-100 g price and the serving weight on the menu.
2. Begin with samgyeopsal, then add moksal, hangjeongsal or galbi in a second round.
3. Check the origin sign if you're paying for beef: 국내산 한우 means hanwoo, 국내산 육우 or 젖소 is domestic but not hanwoo, and imported beef names its country.
4. Grill your own at neighborhood places. Let staff take over at premium ones.
5. Cut meat with the scissors on the grill, and ask "불판 갈아주세요" for a clean plate before marinated meat.
6. Build each ssam small enough to eat in one bite.
7. Ask for banchan refills with "이거 더 주세요".
8. Finish with bokkeumbap in the pan, naengmyeon or doenjang-jjigae.
9. Put your coat in the bag or storage seat before the grill gets going.
10. Pay at the counter with no tip.

faq.question: Can I order just one serving of Korean BBQ?
faq.answer: Usually not. Most Korean barbecue restaurants require at least two servings (2인분) to start the grill. It is a house policy rather than a law. Solo diners should look for signs saying 1인 가능 or choose a restaurant known for solo dining.

faq.question: Do I have to grill the meat myself at a Korean BBQ restaurant?
faq.answer: At most neighborhood pork restaurants, yes. Staff light the grill and leave the tongs and scissors with you. At mid-range and premium beef restaurants, staff often grill at the table or start the meat for you. If a server takes the tongs, let them work.

faq.question: How do you get fried rice at the end of Korean BBQ?
faq.answer: Ask for bokkeumbap (볶음밥) once you've finished the meat. Staff usually fry rice, chopped kimchi and the leftover juices on the hot grill plate. Not every restaurant offers it, so check the menu. Naengmyeon and doenjang-jjigae are the other common closers.
